text:
This week, millions of Americans woke up to hazy skies and scratchy throats under air quality alerts, not because of anything happening in their own local communities or states, but because smoke from the hundreds of wildfires burning in Canada drifted across the border. Across the Atlantic seaboard to the Midwest, Americans were told to stay indoors. Seniors and people with respiratory conditions faced increased health risks. Kids enjoying their summer break watched their outdoor plans get cancelled. Families on vacation were stuck inside.

America’s own regulatory system allows forests to grow dangerously overgrown, letting dead trees and dense underbrush pile up for years while environmental reviews drag on before a single chainsaw ever starts. Meanwhile, drought intensifies conditions and one lightning strike, or a careless spark, can turn into an inferno. This is the opposite of environmental stewardship and neglect dressed up as caution.

Americans deserve policies that help prevent catastrophic fires before they start, protect our communities when fires do occur, and ensure our environmental laws actually improve the environment instead of burying commonsense solutions in years of bureaucratic delay.

TRUMP BLAMES CANADA FOR WILDFIRE SMOKE, SAYS POLLUTION COSTS SHOULD BE ADDED TO TARIFFS

Under the Clean Air Act (CAA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has established regulations for six critical air pollutants, the majority of which are found in wildfire smoke.

We passed two pieces of legislation on a bipartisan basis to support states in their efforts to mitigate, respond to, and recover from wildfires.

The Fire Improvement and Reforming Exceptional Events (FIRE) Act rests on a simple truth: preventing catastrophic wildfires is itself an environmental win. Prevention beats response every time, and waiting for disaster to strike is almost always the most expensive, and most dangerous option on the table. The FIRE Act allows states to perform prescribed burns, the most effective tool to mitigate wildfires and their emissions, without being penalized for those mitigation efforts. It also directs the EPA to conduct regional analyses when multiple states are affected by the same wildfire or event, which will reduce regulatory burden and streamline federal action. This bill rewards proactive forest management while protecting public health, and is a commonsense solution to a problem that shouldn’t have existed in the first place.

AIR QUALITY CONCERNS FROM CANADIAN WILDFIRES FORCE RESCHEDULING OF TWO PROFESSIONAL SPORTS GAMES

The Foreign Emissions and Nonattainment Clarification for Economic Stability (FENCES) Act clarifies that states should not be held accountable for foreign emissions beyond their control and excludes foreign emissions when the EPA determines whether a state complies with air quality standards to ensure states aren’t penalized for emissions originating outside of the United States. The FENCES Act protects states, energy producers, and manufacturers from costly and unnecessary compliance requirements. When Canadian wildfire smoke degrades air quality in American communities, it’s an injustice to hold those states accountable for outside pollution and does nothing to solve the underlying cause of the air emission.

The Senate already has what it needs. The FIRE Act clears the way for states to manage their own forests, the best tool we have to address wildfires, without years of bureaucratic sign-off and fear of facing extreme economic sanctions. The FENCES Act makes sure no state foots a federal penalty for emissions it never created. Passing both isn’t optional anymore.

Canadian researchers themselves have noted that wildfire smoke is becoming a recurring feature of Canadian summers. It is simply unacceptable for American communities and businesses to continue being punished and burdened by wildfires raging outside of our own borders.

POOR AIR QUALITY DUE TO WILDFIRES FORCES LOGISITCAL CHANGES AT SEVERAL MLB GAMES, INCLUDING POSTPONEMENT

Our states know the cost of catastrophic wildfires firsthand. We’ve watched communities lose homes, businesses, treasured public lands, and, tragically, lives. We’ve seen tourism suffer, infrastructure damaged, watersheds contaminated, and local economies disrupted. Even after the flames are extinguished, the impacts linger for years through erosion, flooding, degraded wildlife habitat, and diminished water quality. To hold states accountable for pollution originating from another country is just salt in the wound.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The smoke currently blanketing much of the United States offers a powerful reminder that poor forest management doesn’t stay contained within political boundaries. Air pollution doesn’t ask whether you’re a Democrat or Republican before affecting your family. It doesn’t stop at state lines or international borders. It impacts millions of Americans regardless of where the fire started.

The best way to improve air quality across the country is to prevent these catastrophic events from happening, and legislation like the FIRE Act and FENCES Act ensure that a future without these disasters and their lasting negative impact to our environment and communities is possible. That’s why these bills matter, and why we’re urging our colleagues in the Senate to pass this legislation quickly. Every day we wait is another day that preventable risks are allowed to grow. We can’t control every wildfire, but we can make it easier to reduce their frequency, severity, protect our communities, and restore healthier forests.

We didn’t start the fire. We’re just done punishing American communities for our neighbors to the north’s mess.

text:
Gov. Bill Lee last week joined 22 Republican governors in signing onto President Donald Trump’s “Ratepayer Protection Pledge,” a voluntary agreement to hold companies responsible for the costs of building, maintaining and powering data centers.

The Trump administration has publicly touted the pledge as sparing taxpayers from tax and electricity rate hikes tied to data centers, even as communities across Tennessee and the U.S. push back on plans for the massive data infrastructure projects in their own backyards.

Tech companies including Google, Meta and OpenAI have also signed onto the pledge, which positions data center expansion as essential to the nation’s future.

“America’s continued economic and technological leadership depends on reliable, large-scale data center infrastructure built here at home,” the pledge says.

On Friday, Lee posted a message of thanks to Trump for introducing the pledge.

“Tennessee has shown we can lead the nation in innovation while protecting hardworking families from higher utility bills, & we’re grateful for your leadership to advance policies that strengthen our economy & secure America’s future,” Lee posted on X.

There may be an appetite among voters for ratepayer protections with more teeth, according to Sarah Hunt, president and CEO of Rainey Center, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit public policy research organization.

“Only 9% of voters that we polled had even heard that these tech companies had voluntarily signed onto this pledge that the White House had put together, and 61% of voters, after we tell them about it, want to see Congress make the Ratepayer Protection Pledge binding law,” Hunt said during a July Infrastructure Summit hosted by the Tennessee Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has declined to set nationwide environmental standards for data centers, instead leaving regulatory decisions to states and local governments.

Tennessee lawmakers this year passed a law stipulating that owners of data centers that require at least 50 megawatts of power must pay for any infrastructure upgrades needed to produce the electricity the data center demands. Sen. Brent Taylor, a Shelby County Republican and the law’s senate sponsor, said the law is meant to protect ratepayers from power bill increases.

But the law has some caveats: if the infrastructure upgrades benefit other ratepayers or follow normal rules that apply to all large electricity customers, utilities can help data centers cover the cost.

The law alternatively allows data centers to power themselves using equipment like gas-powered turbines — without state or local oversight — raising concerns from environmental groups and community coalitions who say these turbines pollute the air and emit continuous sound. Data centers may also purchase power from independent producers that operate outside of public utilities.

Tennessee lawmakers did not pass six other bills introduced this year that would have set up guardrails for data centers, ranging from registration and permitting requirements to mandatory reporting on water, electricity and fuel use.

text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Friday that four American nuclear energy startups have successfully proven their technologies as part of an Energy Department pilot project that began last year.

At an Oval Office event, the president said the country had exceeded its goal of three cutting-edge reactors starting up safely by the Fourth of July.

“Most believed the goal was impossible, but I’m delighted to say that four companies succeeded in meeting that deadline — four of the greatest in the world at this subject,” the president said at an event where he was joined by the leaders of the companies and Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

They are the first new privately funded advanced reactors to be activated in the United States in more than 50 years, according to White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios.

The milestone comes 14 months after Trump signed four executive orders to quadruple U.S. nuclear capacity by 2050. The orders sped up the approval process for new reactors and set the country’s 250th anniversary as the deadline for advanced reactor projects to achieve so-called criticality.

“In the last 30 or 40 years, the American nuclear industry has been quiescent,” Wright said Friday. “Most of the reactors built around the world have been built by Russia and China, both in their countries and abroad. President Trump said enough of that. America’s going to be back as the leader in the nuclear space.”

Some Democratic lawmakers have criticized Trump’s nuclear energy executive orders for ramping up nuclear power while reducing public input and oversight by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Rep. Salud Carbajal, D-Calif., said in a statement last year that the executive orders were “reckless” and could weaken the NRC’s ability to ensure safety in the communities near nuclear plants.

“At Antares, we look forward to being a resilient energy source for Golden Dome, its high-powered assets in space and eventually undersea autonomy,” said Jordan Bramble, co-founder and chief executive of Antares Nuclear, based in Torrance, California. “This is a strategic technology for our nation, and what we look forward to doing is putting reactors on our military installations before 2028.”

The Golden Dome is Trump's proposed missile defense system to shield the U.S.

Among the four nuclear energy executive orders Trump signed last year was a Defense Department directive to deploy advanced microreactors for military bases.

“This is going to be historic, and people will look back and say this is how the tide turned on nuclear energy and how we unlock cheap and abundant energy,” Deployable Energy CEO Bobby Gallagher said at the event.

According to the World Nuclear Association, 94 nuclear reactors in 28 states supplied about 18% of U.S. electricity in 2024. The Energy Department describes nuclear power’s potential as “substantial,” as electricity demand surges because of artificial intelligence data centers.

While nuclear power proponents hail the technology as providing around-the-clock reliability and zero-emission energy generation with a very small land footprint, detractors say it is expensive and comes with the risk of catastrophic accidents.

The most recent nuclear disaster was at the Fukushima Daiichi plant in Japan in 2011, when a massive earthquake and tsunami caused the power plant to suffer a blackout that stopped the reactor from properly cooling and released radioactive materials into the ocean, soil and atmosphere.

“This year we’re going to be raising a billion dollars, moving into a million-square-foot facility, and our target market is data centers,” said Matt Loszak, the co-founder and CEO of Aalo Atomics in Austin, Texas, which was the last of the four data centers to meet the July 4 deadline when it achieved a sustained nuclear fission chain reaction at 12:20 a.m. at Idaho National Laboratory.

“In all my years, I’ve never seen government, private industry and the laboratories working together this effectively,” Idaho National Laboratories Director John Wagner said Friday.

description:
A comment from reader “Jon’s Thoughts,” however, made me realize how much electric bikes (ebikes) are important to enabling more biking in hilly and mountainous places.

In places where people bike a lot, the introduction of ebikes is naturally going to spread by word of mouth quickly.

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

I’m a flatlander who was born and raised in Florida. A comment from reader “Jon’s Thoughts,” however, made me realize how much electric bikes (ebikes) are important to enabling more biking in hilly and mountainous places. He wrote:

“In the past we lived on a hill that made a regular bike a pretty strenuous trip, suitable for a good workout but not great for a casual trip to the store. The ebike definitely reduced the number of car trips for us. I suspect that there may be a number of folks living in hilly terrain that have reduced car trips with an ebike.”

I just took a brief trip to Western North Carolina. While I have been there several times and spent one summer in the mountains of North Carolina, I forgot the extent of the hills and mountains there. Just driving up and down, up and down, up and down was challenging. Biking — for me and most other people — would be out of the question. Ebikes must make biking a real option all of a sudden, and bring the opportunity to bike for transportation purposes to whole regions of people.

I did live in Chapel Hill for a few years, and I lived car-free there. I biked to work and nearby stores. When I had to go all the way up the hill to the University of North Carolina campus or downtown, though, biking was a lot of work. I was in my mid-20s and it was normally fine, but there were also many times when I just decided to put my bike on the bus. With an ebike, there’d be no waiting for buses or struggling to get up the long hill on Franklin St. Yes, I’d get my exercise in and would bike completely human-powered for some of the trip, but I’d have the option to get support from the battery and motor of an ebike (and you can be sure I’d use it).

When you think about all the places around the country and around the world where moderate to steep hills really limit most people’s ability to bike, you can see how ebikes make all the difference and open up the world to countless people.

Also, it’s really about providing the healthy habit as an opportunity to people of all ages and fitness levels. No matter how old or in/out of shape someone is, they can get on an ebike, use muscle power as much as they like, and get themselves up and down hills smoothly and conveniently.

It may take a while for this realization to spread. In places where people bike a lot, the introduction of ebikes is naturally going to spread by word of mouth quickly. In places where biking is seldom done except for recreational purposes, it may take a while for people to think about the option — but these are often the places that can benefit the most from the growth and expansion of ebikes. As noted above, hills and mountains may have stifled all but the most fringe interests in bike commuting, but ebikes provide a new option that could open up this possibility to numerous people.

text:
Indiana Department of Environmental Management Commissioner Clint Woods wrote a letter to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, asking Administrator Lee Zeldin to make changes to would weaken Northwest Indiana’s ozone regulations.

One Northwest Indiana environmental activist finds the letter unconscionable.

“The reason that they exist in Northwest Indiana is because those communities, like mine, already have elevated levels of health issues that are brought on by ozone, which include ozone-triggering asthma attacks,” said Lisa Vallee, Whiting resident and organizing director of Just Transition Northwest Indiana. “It worsens lung disease, it increases the risk of premature death. These are not small issues — these are huge issues.”

According to Woods’ July 13 letter, he asks the agency to rescind 2023 and 2024 reclassifications of the federal ozone rule. Woods claims in the letter that standards’ emissions impact is insignificant and classification changes have created regulatory burdens statewide.

“It makes me furious,” Vallee said. “Clint Woods, since he became IDEM commissioner, has been trying to change EPA restrictions throughout the state, and it’s obviously glaringly in favor of industry.”

According to the EPA website, in June, the agency proposed revisions to portions of former President Joe Biden’s EPA’s 2025 final rule, which required states to keep certain State Implementation Plan requirements to an area’s prior ozone nonattainment classification under the National Ambient Air Quality Standards.

“The (President Donald) Trump EPA is proposing to make it so that an area’s current ozone classification, not a previous one, determines the applicable SIP requirements,” the EPA website says. “This proposed change is consistent with the (Clean Air Act) that states an area can only be subject to a single classification at a given time. If finalized, EPA’s state, local, and Tribal air regulatory partners will be given renewed flexibility to better tailor their air quality strategies to current conditions, enhancing protections for human health and the environment, while reducing administrative confusion.”

Woods said in his letter that he supports the changes. He requested a 30-day extension for the EPA’s comment period — which was 30 days — to “secure additional time to evaluate and articulate potential unintended consequences.”

He also urges the EPA to review and eliminate “unnecessary requirements for vehicle inspection & maintenance programs,” arguing that the programs are no longer cost effective in Northwest Indiana, have no measurable impact on air quality, and have been superseded by the widespread use of automotive technology like onboard diagnostic systems.

IDEM declined a Post-Tribune interview request for this story.

Several public interest groups — including Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and Environmental Defense Fund — submitted a 47-page letter to the EPA expressing concerns with the Ozone Reclassification Rule.

“… the Proposal unlawfully interprets the Clean Air Act’s gradual classification scheme for ozone nonattainment areas in a way that is contrary to the plain language and purpose of the statute,” the letter said.

The groups claim that the EPA’s proposal would go against the Clean Air Act’s requirement that areas falling to meet “health-based ambient air quality standards attain those standards as expeditiously as practicable.” They say it also fails to explain how it’s consistent with the act’s language, structure, history and purpose, and it fails to “provide clarity on what nonattainment plan elements are or are not still required after reclassification.”

Michael Zoeller, senior attorney for Conservation Law Center, said his organization works with the groups that sent the letter to the EPA, but the law center doesn’t get “heavily involved” in national rulemakings.

However, he said the changes would “clearly impact” his clients in northern Lake County, where his work is focused. With Woods’ letter, Zoeller said he agrees with the 30-day comment extension because it’s a significant change.

“Which is a huge problem in northern Lake County and in the region generally,” Zoeller said. “Some people are more sensitive to high ozone levels than others, but it’s clearly a major problem in northern Lake County, and it’s not one that’s getting better.”

Ozone is measured between about March 1 to Oct. 31, Zoeller said, so extending the comment period would give agencies more time to thoroughly study ozone levels, which could help come up with something more balanced nationwide.

Overall, Zoeller said Woods’ letter is consistent with Gov. Mike Braun’s administration’s approach to environmental regulations.

“They’re concerned about the continued economic devastation wrought by the misguided and heavy-handed implementation of the 2015 (National Ambient Air Quality Standards),” Zoeller said. “I take it they mean the economic devastation on industry because nowhere in this letter is there a mention of health impacts of ozone.”

Ozone levels have been elevated in the region in July because of Canadian wildfire smoke, which led to about a week of Air Quality Action Day designations from IDEM. When the ozone levels are high, Vallee said she can’t see fully when driving through Whiting.

“We couldn’t see the steeples on the churches,” Vallee said. “That’s how smoky it was.”

When ozone levels elevate and mix with smoke from local industry, Vallee said that makes conditions worse. Vallee has lupus and asthma, and she said elevated ozone levels make her health conditions worse.

“I had to buy an expensive air purifier for my apartment because I was so scared that even using my window unit for my (air conditioning) would draw in this toxic air,” Vallee said. “I tried not to leave my house. It does impact me in really big ways. I get winded really easily, I have to use my inhaler more, and it makes my lupus flare up. I wake up, and I’m in more pain that I normally would be.”

State Rep. Carolyn Jackson, D-Hammond, expressed concerns with Woods’ letter in a Monday statement. She said Woods is asking the EPA to roll back standards “in the name of regulatory flexibility for polluters.”

“Northwest Indiana has fought for years to improve our air quality,” Jackson said in her letter. “Instead of building on the progress we’ve made to protect the air Hoosiers breathe, this letter asks Washington to take us backward and puts corporate convenience ahead of Hoosier families. … A person’s health is their most valuable commodity, and I’ll always advocate against policies that treat that commodity as expendable.”

Vallee commended Jackson for her advocacy and said she wants other elected officials to do the same for Northwest Indiana’s environment.

“We need everyone talking about this because they live here, too,” Vallee said. “This doesn’t just stay right where I live, or right where people next to the mills live. It moves, and it’s impacting the whole climate of the globe. This is not just a Northwest Indiana issue — this is a humanity issue.”

text:
(NewsNation) — Data centers in the U.S. will account for about 20% of the nation’s electricity consumption in 2035 as demand for artificial intelligence surges, according to Bloomberg research.

Given the speed at which AI is gaining momentum, Bloomberg projects data center power needs to reach 194 gigawatts in the U.S. by 2035. One gigawatt is equivalent to the capacity of a traditional nuclear reactor.

This projection is an 83% jump from its December forecast, reflecting the upward trend in AI for the next decade, according to the research.

“Every coal plant, every gas plant, every solar farm in the US — one unit of energy out of five generated by them is going to data centers,” said Lloyd Arnold, an analyst at BloombergNEF and one of the authors of the report. “So that’s the same energy that’s going to be going into powering electric vehicles, powering cities, et cetera.”

Demand from AI data centers is straining electric grids and forcing companies to find new ways to power their facilities. At the same time, local governments and political leaders are imposing environmental restrictions on their energy needs.

Electric grids are already struggling to keep up, according to the research. Annually, the record for the amount of data center capacity that can connect to the grid is 7.1 gigawatts. Even if that ability is maintained, the analysts project a 19-gigawatt shortfall by 2035.

text:
State investment unlocks additional $2M in private sector support for five projects supporting state’s first-ever maritime strategy

LANSING, Mich. — The Michigan Office of Future Mobility and Electrification (OFME) today announced the selection of five projects to receive funding through the Michigan Mobility Funding Platform (MMFP) Michigan Maritime Innovation Grant Program, supporting innovative technologies, commercialization efforts and workforce initiatives that will strengthen Michigan's maritime economy and accelerate implementation of the state's newly released Michigan Maritime Strategy. Michigan’s $1.5 million investment will leverage an additional $2 million from private industry, bringing the total investment in the five projects to $3.5 million.

"Michigan's maritime industry plays a key role in more than 350,000 shipping-related jobs across the U.S. and Canada contributing to more than $50 billion in economic activity," said Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity Director Susan Corbin. "This investment furthers Michigan’s efforts to support intermodal transportation, manufacturing, tourism, recreation and fishing and lead the way in building our workforce and infrastructure to keep our economy strong."

The State of Michigan recently unveiled the Michigan Maritime Strategy, the first comprehensive 10-year roadmap to grow the state's maritime economy by driving economic development, attracting investment, fostering innovation, creating high-quality career opportunities and protecting the Great Lakes. The strategy outlines a statewide vision for strengthening Michigan's water-based economy through investments in infrastructure, clean energy, research and workforce development and resilient ports and waterfronts.

The Maritime Innovation Grant Program supports projects advancing one or more of the strategy's four priority objectives:

Supporting economic development by modernizing maritime infrastructure, improving intermodal transportation connectivity, leveraging manufacturing capabilities, and strengthening supply chain resilience.

Accelerating the maritime sector's transition to clean energy.

Investing in maritime research, innovation, education, and workforce development.

Enhancing the sustainability, resilience, and revitalization of Michigan's ports, harbors, and waterfront communities.

"These projects demonstrate how emerging technologies, entrepreneurs and public-private partnerships can strengthen our maritime economy while accelerating real-world innovation.” said Justine Johnson, State of Michigan Chief Mobility Officer. “By investing in solutions that improve our ports, waterways and maritime operations, we're helping implement Michigan's first Maritime Strategy.”

"Michigan has all the ingredients to become a leader in BlueTech innovation, from world-class freshwater assets and maritime expertise to a growing network of entrepreneurs, researchers and industry partners," said Matt McDonough, CEO, Discovery Pier. "The projects supported through this program will help move promising technologies from concept to real-world deployment while strengthening the partnerships that make innovation possible. We're proud to work alongside the State of Michigan to help implement the Maritime Strategy and build a more competitive, resilient maritime economy."

The five selected projects include:

AquaAction – Commercializing BlueTech Innovation (Detroit)

AquaAction will launch its AquaEntrepreneur pilot-to-procurement commercialization platform in Michigan through Bedrock's Urban Tech Xchange and deployment partnerships with the Port of Detroit, Great Lakes Water Authority, Friends of the Rouge and other infrastructure operators.

Rather than serving as a traditional startup accelerator, the program creates a commercialization infrastructure that connects deployment-ready BlueTech companies with operational partners, procurement opportunities and Michigan-based jobs. Through structured pilot deployments, participating companies will validate technologies in real-world environments while accelerating commercialization across Michigan's ports, utilities and watershed infrastructure.

BlueTech Startup Studio and Electric Research Vessel (Traverse City)

This project will establish a comprehensive platform supporting emerging BlueTech startups and maritime technology companies seeking to locate research, development and operations in Michigan.

The initiative includes acquisition of a fully electric Vita Power Seal rigid inflatable boat (RIB) research vessel and an Outland Technology ROV 3000 remotely operated vehicle, providing advanced maritime inspection capabilities, workforce training opportunities and technology deployment resources while launching a dedicated BlueTech Startup Studio.

Autonomous Maritime Testing Corridor (Detroit & Alpena)

A coalition led by Newlab will establish Michigan's first autonomous maritime testing corridor, anchored by initial testing nodes at the National All-Domain Warfighting Center (NADWC) in Alpena and the Port of Monroe.

Building upon Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's Infrastructure for Innovation Initiative (Executive Directive 2024-2), the project will establish testing zones, safety protocols, regulatory pathways, and data governance frameworks for autonomous maritime technologies. The initiative is designed to convert testing activity into long-term economic growth by connecting innovators with Michigan manufacturers and creating a scalable framework capable of attracting future federal investment. This project expands upon Michigan’s existing suite of marine autonomous testing capabilities.

FORGE: Freshwater Operational Requirements to Government-Ready Equipment (Houghton)

The Freshwater Operational Requirements to Government-Ready Equipment (FORGE) project will develop and field-test an autonomous cold-water maritime first responder designed to support Lake Superior search and rescue operations.

Working alongside Keweenaw County Search and Rescue and the U.S. Coast Guard Station Portage, the project will validate technologies intended for distributed deployment in remote locations, improving emergency response capabilities in one of North America's most challenging freshwater environments.

Maritime Industrial Arts Institute (Boyne City)

The Industrial Arts Institute (IAI) in Onaway will develop a specialized training curriculum tailored to Michigan's growing maritime and naval industries.

Founded in 2013 to address advanced manufacturing workforce needs, IAI will expand its nationally recognized welding and fabrication programs to prepare skilled workers for careers supporting Michigan's maritime sector.

The investment comes as increased regional commitments to shipbuilding enterprise are creating more demand for workers skilled in maritime fabrication, safety, and non-destructive testing.

Together, these projects represent an important step toward implementing Michigan's first-ever Maritime Strategy, translating the state's long-term vision into real-world investments that strengthen ports and waterways, accelerate innovation, support workforce development and create new economic opportunities across the Great Lakes. Through the Michigan Mobility Funding Platform, OFME continues to invest in technologies and partnerships that reinforce Michigan's leadership in next-generation mobility while supporting a more competitive and resilient maritime economy.

Partner Quotes

Soula Chronopoulos, President, AquaAction: "We’re thrilled to bring our proven bluetech innovation model to Michigan. The state is full of innovative companies that often need just two things to succeed: expert guidance and the pilot opportunities that can be a golden ticket to commercialization. We’re here to provide both, and to help build a thriving bluetech economy in Michigan and beyond. We invite entrepreneurs to connect with us!"

Bradley C. Wieferich, Director, Michigan Department of Transportation: “Michigan's ports are a vital part of our transportation system and supply chain. These investments support implementation of the Michigan Maritime Strategy by advancing innovation, strengthening maritime partnerships, and helping position our ports for future opportunities and are a step toward the more sustainable funding necessary to help fulfill our ports’ true economic potential.”

Colleen Hau, Managing Director, Newlab: “The future of America's maritime industry will be built where innovation, manufacturing, and real-world deployment come together. Michigan's autonomous maritime corridor creates that ecosystem by connecting our industrial capabilities with one of the nation's most unique natural assets, the Great Lakes. As the federal government invests in restoring America's maritime strength and expanding domestic shipbuilding, this initiative ensures Michigan is not only prepared to support that resurgence but positioned to lead it, creating new opportunities for manufacturers, technology companies, defense partners, and maritime operators alike.”

Dave Kronberg, Director of Business Growth, The Northern Lakes Economic Alliance: "This investment is well timed as the Industrial Arts Institute, a highly regarded welding and fabrication trainer, looks to expand its curriculum to satisfy Michigan's growing demands for maritime manufacturing. The new Maritime Industrial Manufacturing Academy will begin graduating highly skilled workers with technical knowledge of non-destructive testing and specialized safety in Spring 2027."

Greg Kangas, President, Hawk Technologies: "Hawk’s FORGE initiative shows what Michigan's maritime and mobility leadership looks like in action: a small Upper Peninsula company, working with local search and rescue operators and Michigan Tech's Marine Autonomy Research Site, turning a life-saving operational need on Lake Superior into a scalable, production-ready solution, designed and built right here in Michigan."

title: Under-the-radar ideas to improve American energy policy that could pass Congress this year.
description:
My organization, California Forward, is helping advance an initiative that offers one solution: proactively creating development zones for clean energy industrial development.
Policies shaping its future must allow American computing capacity to grow, while promoting both affordability and clean energy.
Clean energy — rapidly scalable and cost competitive — is one of the best tools to combat both trends.
These structures can work to grow domestic clean energy capacity while protecting consumers from the financial burdens of AI.
Lynn Abramson is president of the Clean Energy Business Network, a nationwide, nonpartisan organization serving as the small business voice for the U.S. energy economy.
text:
Any Delawarean will tell you energy bills are too expensive. The price to heat and cool our homes just keeps rising.

One easy way to bring down costs quickly: Make homes more energy efficient.

We have a program that’s been doing just that for 50 years. It’s called the Weatherization Assistance Program. It saves the more than 7 million families who’ve participated an average of $300 every year by helping pay for insulation, air sealing and better HVAC systems. As those households use less energy, they reduce pressure on our energy infrastructure, helping keep prices from spiking and protecting our environment.

Weatherization is one of the rare climate policies supported by Democrats and Republicans alike. Sen. Susan Collins and I have a bill to improve the Weatherization Assistance Program and make sure it can continue through 2030. The companion bill in the House passed unanimously out of committee — and it has a real chance in the Senate, too.

If we’re going to pursue the all-of-the-above approach that’s necessary to bring down energy costs and ensure we have the energy we need to stay ahead in the race for AI, improving and strengthening weatherization assistance is an easy call.

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons represents Delaware.

The most consequential energy issue in Washington may also be the most underappreciated: permitting reform. America has the abundant low-cost resources, technology, capital and workforce to remain the global leader in energy — but our own permitting processes are standing in our way. Having spent 40 years in the private sector before coming to the Senate, I have seen firsthand how our current regulatory system — governed by well-meaning but outdated laws from the 1970s — is slowly strangling our nation’s ability to lead in this fast-paced world ahead of us.

I am encouraged by the bipartisan momentum to pass meaningful permitting reform this year — a growing coalition of my colleagues across both political parties are fed up with the status quo. We have a narrow window before the end of this Congress to enact a durable, technology-neutral plan that helps build all forms of energy infrastructure. By establishing predictable reviews, preventing the weaponization of permitting laws, and providing greater certainty after permits are issued, we can unlock private investment here in the U.S. to deliver our abundant low-cost energy without costing taxpayers a dime. This would restore America’s legacy as a nation of builders and lower utility bills, and meet the enormous energy demands of reindustrialization and the AI revolution.

Republican Sen. Alan Armstrong represents Oklahoma.

Access to more natural gas has made coal uneconomical, so the U.S. relies on it less and less to produce energy. This substitution has dramatically lowered C02 emissions. But even small methane leaks from gas production and distribution offset its climate benefits. Methane is 70 times as potent a climate agent as C02.

Notably, the oil and gas industry has made significant advances to control methane due to customer demand. Europe, Japan and Korea, where leadership is focused on reducing energy costs while combatting climate change, want “clean” natural gas. In response, industry has developed technology to detect and prevent methane leaks.

But methane regulation has been unreliable and uncertain. Obama issued rules. Trump repealed them. Biden issued rules, but Trump repealed those, too. Companies hate this back and forth, and many asked to leave the Biden regulations in place, just for certainty’s sake.

A statute that outlasts any presidency would protect the environment and give businesses certainty. Big Oil is ready. Smaller companies could get extra time, technical help and financial aid before facing fines.

Good legislation would slow global warming, help overseas sales and lower the political temperature about natural gas. Kumbaya.

Democratic Rep. Scott Peters represents California’s 50th District.

Americans are grappling with an energy affordability crisis. Utility prices continue to rise at unprecedented rates across the country as the growing demand for electricity — driven in part by AI data centers — increasingly strains the grid. While much of the debate in Washington is divided along party lines, investing in and unlocking the power of geothermal energy — a renewable source of electricity produced by drilling deep and capturing the Earth’s heat — enjoys broad bipartisan support.

Major advances in geothermal technology have been made, but the industry requires more federal support to scale up and meet the needs of the energy transition. Congress has already demonstrated bipartisan support for geothermal energy through a package of bills that have passed either in committee or the full House. These bills would provide much needed financial support in the early stages of research and development and will help bring projects online faster without sacrificing environmental protections or community engagement.

States across the country are already taking action on geothermal energy. Congress should follow suit and pass legislation that would be a positive step for U.S. energy policy.

Holly Bender is chief program officer of the Sierra Club.

Energy demand is rising fast. Supply isn’t keeping up. But new projects are increasingly facing community opposition from Americans rightly concerned that development won’t bring tangible benefits — either through local energy supply or through lower bills.

My organization, California Forward, is helping advance an initiative that offers one solution: proactively creating development zones for clean energy industrial development. Here’s how it works: In return for government support — grants, loans, procurement preferences — these zones will offer up preferential access to industrial land, interconnection, rail and logistics support, skilled workforce nearby, or other assets essential to building out critical energy infrastructure, along with clear and streamlined permitting. Zone access and governance must come from councils formed by community groups and local governments — the only people with the power to ensure priority siting and permitting, which are local land use issues in nearly every U.S. state, and the power to reduce litigation risk that can come from community opposition.

Zone-based development is familiar in international development. The Opportunity Zone program proves bipartisan appetite for this kind of approach. Let’s launch 10-15 advanced industrial zones across the country, with the goal of getting community-supported energy generation up and running within 18 months in every region. It could be the start of a new energy industrial revolution — this time with locals in the driver’s seat.

Kate Gordon is CEO of the nonprofit California Forward. She is also a strategic adviser at Advanced Industrial Zones, an initiative to promote zones that proactively align the right ingredients for industrial development.

Ask your neighbor what they think about federal permitting reform. Unless you live within 10 miles of the nation’s Capital, you’ll probably get a blank stare. But ask about their gas and electric bills, and you’re likely to get an earful.

Poll after poll shows Americans are worried about the cost of living — especially the cost of energy. What most don’t know is that a fix with genuine bipartisan support is already moving through Congress.

If energy affordability is the problem, comprehensive permitting reform is a key part of the answer.

Right now, it is difficult — and often impossible — to build large energy projects in this country. Statutes like the National Environmental Policy Act were written to protect communities. But today they are too often used to tie up pipelines, transmission lines, and other infrastructure in years of litigation — often by groups with no stake in the communities involved or the affordable energy at stake.

Meanwhile, energy demand is surging, our infrastructure is aging, and turmoil in the Middle East has reminded us why energy security matters.

The good news: the House passed the bipartisan SPEED Act in December, with members of both parties voting to modernize a broken permitting process. The Senate is negotiating now.

Midterm candidates in both parties are running on affordability this year. The ones already in office have a chance to do something rarer: deliver on it.

Mike Sommers is the President & CEO of the American Petroleum Institute.

Households across the country are struggling with skyrocketing electricity bills, and our grid is straining under the weight of natural disasters, increased demand and decades of underinvestment. We urgently need to bring more clean energy online and invest in a modernized electric grid. But in the meantime, we must make better use of the infrastructure that’s already been built.

Enter Grid-Enhancing Technologies (GETs). GETs are tools that enable grid operators to utilize existing powerlines at a higher capacity. They include higher performance conductor materials or more advanced software than what was available when the powerlines were built. For example, advanced power flow control devices enable grid operators to redistribute power away from congestion and toward lines with available capacity, which also improves reliability.

Deploying more GETs won’t address all our energy and grid needs, but it’s the fastest, lowest-cost, lowest-impact way to reduce bills today and avoid locking communities into increased pollution from new, unnecessary fossil-fuel plants. And members of Congress have already demonstrated interest: Related bipartisan legislation is actively being considered by congressional committees. Incentivizing the adoption of GETs is a commonsense step toward building an energy system that delivers affordable, reliable and clean electricity for everyone.

Meg Slattery is a staff scientist at Earthjustice.

Energy powers our economy. Policies shaping its future must allow American computing capacity to grow, while promoting both affordability and clean energy.

Artificial intelligence and clean energy adoption are transforming the global economy all at once. Data center development around the United States poses risks by increasing utility bills and local resource usage. Clean energy — rapidly scalable and cost competitive — is one of the best tools to combat both trends. In New Jersey, a new ratepayer relief plan will insulate ratepayers from rising costs by offering priority permitting for data centers that pay to reduce energy demand elsewhere in the grid, including through household energy upgrades such as heat pumps, solar panels and batteries. In Minnesota, a 2025 law imposes a fee on large-scale data centers to fund energy conservation projects for low-income households, as well as mandating that increased energy supplied to the grid for data center use does not delay the state’s commitment to 100% clean electricity by 2040. These structures can work to grow domestic clean energy capacity while protecting consumers from the financial burdens of AI.

These are reasonable reforms that allow data centers to move forward, while prioritizing clean energy. There are other options being actively debated — New York State has paused data center development and many have called for public ownership or government equity stakes — but those are another discussion entirely.

Heather Boushey is a professor of practice at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy at the University of Pennsylvania. She served in the Biden administration as a member of the Council of Economic Advisers.

After the two largest drawdowns — during the 2022 price spike and the 2026 Iran war — the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1983. Those releases showed how much emergency oil stocks still matter even though the United States is the world’s largest oil producer and a net petroleum exporter. Congress should fund a refill.

The United States long maintained the world’s largest strategic oil stockpile. But the Energy Information Administration now estimates that China controls nearly 1.4 billion barrels in strategic inventories, far more than the United States. That gap matters because reserves confer economic power during global disruptions.

Congress should also establish refined-product reserves holding gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Recent attacks on refineries have made fuel prices climb even faster than rising crude oil prices. The United States helps moderate those global prices by exporting large volumes of refined fuels. During a severe refining disruption, the United States could release stored fuel at home while allowing American refineries to continue supplying allies and global markets. Congress can strengthen domestic resilience without retreating from America’s indispensable role as an energy exporter.

James Coleman is a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

This spring, Congress overwhelmingly voted to reauthorize the Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) programs. For over 40 years, these programs have fueled American innovation by allocating 3.65% of federal research and development funding for competitive grants to help small businesses develop new technologies. This small investment has an outsized impact. The Small Business Technology Council estimates that SBIR/STTR programs return $12 to the economy for every $1 invested and have supported more than 2,100 firms that have been acquired and over 800 that have gone public. The programs have advanced technology such as Bluetooth, LASIK and GPS — and the digital satellite communications that catapulted Qualcomm to success.

But Congress’ work is not done. The Department of Energy recently moved its SBIR/STTR programs into the Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC), which is working to streamline application and award requirements and strengthen commercialization. Congress should provide robust funding to OTC in FY2027 to support these efforts and other technology acceleration programs under its purview and reauthorize OTC to reflect its growing mission. DOE’s applied research and development offices also need stable funding to ensure an adequate SBIR/STTR set-aside.

Finally, legislative guardrails are essential to protect these investments amid recent project cancellations and a proposed regulation expanding grant termination authority. These steps are politically feasible and urgently needed to strengthen America’s economy, energy security and competitiveness.

Lynn Abramson is president of the Clean Energy Business Network, a nationwide, nonpartisan organization serving as the small business voice for the U.S. energy economy.

title: Trump's EPA Wants Fewer People Asking Questions About Data Center Pollution
authors: Molly Taft, Dharna Noor, Amy Qin, Flávio Pessoa, Maya McDaniel, Sophie Hurwitz, Anna Merlan, Laura C. Morel, Alex Nguyen, Emily Jones
description:
The proposed rollback comes as data centers face greater pushback across the US, with many communities using the permitting process to try to slow down development.
The data center boom there has driven a massive buildout of private gas plants, many of which rely on minor pollution permits.
Since coming into power, the Trump administration has gone all in on artificial intelligence, removing multiple roadblocks for data center development at the federal level.
Companies are also spending vast sums of money on the data center buildout: Spending on data center construction outpaced spending on public transportation infrastructure for the first time in June.
“I think it’s part of a package of rules that the Trump administration is pushing through to make it easier for AI data centers to be constructed,” she says.
text:
This story was originally published by Wired and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The Trump administration is quietly considering a rule change that could make it easier for polluters to build facilities—including certain gas plants and diesel generators that power data centers—with little to no notice to the public.

On Wednesday, the Environmental Protection Agency held a public hearing on a proposed rule change that would hand the power to states to decide how the public participates in the permitting process for certain new sources of air pollution. The proposed rollback comes as data centers face greater pushback across the US, with many communities using the permitting process to try to slow down development. Any changes could have major consequences for how ordinary people are given notice about new or expanded polluting facilities coming into their neighborhoods.

“As someone actively working in communities with data centers, I know this to be fundamentally true: People want to have a say,” Vanessa Lynch, a Pennsylvania organizer with Moms Clean Air Force, said at the EPA hearing.

Companies building any kind of facilities that release air pollution are required to get permits under the Clean Air Act. Polluting sources can either be put through a “major” permitting process, meaning that they meet or exceed thresholds for certain pollutants, or a “minor” one for those that don’t.

Major sources of pollution are reviewed by both federal and state regulators and have extensive requirements before and after construction. However, there’s less oversight of minor sources. The scope of what gets permitted as a minor source is extremely broad and can include everything from dry cleaners and auto body shops to diesel and gas engines. The latter two are increasingly being used to power data centers, with operators such as xAI and Meta using minor source permitting processes to build behind-the-meter gas plants.

The Clean Air Act does require the public to be involved in permitting processes; Congress has specified that major sources need to have several public steps, including a public hearing. EPA rules require some public participation for minor source permits. But thanks to a patchwork of state enforcement laws, that engagement process—and whether state agencies are actually complying with EPA requirements—varies across the US.

If the proposed rule is finalized, “it would put state and local agencies most familiar with local issues in the driver’s seat to determine whether, when, and for how long to provide opportunities for public participation for proposed new minor sources and modifications,” an EPA spokesperson tells WIRED, noting the rule wouldn’t alter emissions standards.

These state-by-state differences can make a big difference in how the public gets involved. Keri Powell, an Atlanta-based attorney at the environmental legal advocacy group Southern Environmental Law Center, says that groups like hers often end up taking on cases in states like Georgia, which, she says, has a more robust public notification and participation process for minor sources. Earlier this month, the group alerted the state utility about construction issues at a data center, based on information they’d gotten from the companies’ public air permit applications. But if the EPA removes the federal requirement, community and legal groups in the state could get little to no heads up about upcoming projects and be shut out of participation and review.

“Georgia is an example of a place where I can say I’m concerned,” Powell says.

Sara Lips, the director of communications at Georgia’s Environmental Protection Division, says that the agency is “determining whether proposed federal rule changes would affect the public participation requirements per the state regulations.”

Kentucky also has stronger public participation laws for minor source permits. Byron Gary, a senior attorney at the Kentucky Resources Council, says state agencies have made an “informal commitment” behind the scenes to keep their public participation rules the same, even if the EPA changes its rules. But, he says, that could shift: “Who knows [if] the next administration, whether they would actually change it.”

Texas is an example of what lower levels of engagement look like. The data center boom there has driven a massive buildout of private gas plants, many of which rely on minor pollution permits. The state’s lower levels of enforcement have left some communities living in the shadows of data centers surprised at the scope of fossil fuel infrastructure being installed near their homes.

Since coming into power, the Trump administration has gone all in on artificial intelligence, removing multiple roadblocks for data center development at the federal level. That includes efforts at the EPA, which is working to make the US “the AI capital of the world,” the agency spokesperson says.

Companies are also spending vast sums of money on the data center buildout: Spending on data center construction outpaced spending on public transportation infrastructure for the first time in June. Given that public opposition is creating a new bottleneck for data center development, the timing of the rule revision, Powell says, is probably not an accident.

“I think it’s part of a package of rules that the Trump administration is pushing through to make it easier for AI data centers to be constructed,” she says.

text:
New data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), analysed by the Sun Day Campaign, shows that renewable energy generation increased by 10.1% in the first five months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Renewables accounted for 30.3% of total US electricity generation during the period, up from 28.2% a year earlier.

Wind generation increased by 4.8% year-on-year, while solar, including utility-scale and small-scale installations, recorded stronger growth. Together, wind and solar supplied more than 22% of US electricity generation, producing 57% more electricity than coal plants and 26% more than nuclear power plants during the first five months of the year.

Renewable capacity continued to expand, with almost 45 GW added between June 2025 and May 2026. Wind capacity increased by 10,253 MW, while utility-scale solar grew by almost 28 GW and small-scale solar by 6,664 MW. Battery energy storage capacity also increased by 16,552 MW during the same period.

EIA expects renewable energy capacity growth to continue over the next year. Utility-scale renewable capacity is projected to increase by 53.7 GW by May 2027, including 9.4 GW of new wind capacity, of which 3.4 GW will come from offshore wind projects. Utility-scale solar is expected to add nearly 44 GW. Over the same period, fossil fuel capacity is forecast to decline by 4.7 GW, while nuclear capacity remains unchanged.

Including small-scale solar, renewable energy capacity could surpass natural gas capacity by 2027. Battery storage capacity is also expected to grow significantly, with EIA forecasting an additional 23.2 GW by June 2027, bringing total installed battery capacity to around 72 GW.

text:
In Louisiana's so-called Cancer Alley, plastic pollution is not a distant environmental problem. Advocates say it is in the air near homes and inside people's bodies.

The fight over plastic is now being framed as a public health alarm, rather than just a story about waste, litter, or recycling.

What's happening?

Judith Enck, a former EPA regional administrator who now heads Beyond Plastics, said plastic is woven into daily life and is now turning up inside the human body as well.

Speaking with Paloma Beltran for Living on Earth, shared by Inside Climate News, Enck said plastics connect several overlapping issues, including climate change, ocean pollution, environmental justice, and public health.

Enck said the harms linked to plastic span its full life cycle. She noted that just 5% to 6% of plastic gets recycled, while much of what remains is burned, buried in landfills, or released into the environment.

As cleaner transportation and electricity options grow, large oil and gas companies have leaned more heavily on plastics as a business opportunity.

"We are seeing plastics emerge as plan B for the fossil fuel industry," Enck said.

Why does it matter?

According to Enck, the health concerns are driven in part by microplastics, tiny fragments measuring no more than about 0.2 inches, or five millimeters, that can be inhaled or swallowed.

She said researchers have found these particles in blood and in multiple organs and tissues, including the lungs, kidneys, liver, placenta, breast milk, and testicles.

"Our babies are being born pre-polluted," Enck said.

Enck pointed to a New England Journal of Medicine study that found microplastics attached to plaque in neck arteries, which was associated with a higher risk of stroke, heart attack, or premature death. She also cited newer research suggesting microplastics can cross the blood-brain barrier.

Many people are exposed in small, repeated ways through packaging, bottle caps, food containers, and polluted air, while health agencies and regulators are still catching up to the science.

Residents near petrochemical plants are exposed to toxic chemicals "24/7," Enck said, highlighting Louisiana's Cancer Alley as an example. She cited a Johns Hopkins study that estimated cancer risk in the area at seven times the national average.

What's being done?

Enck said advocates have gained momentum from single-use plastic bans and producer responsibility programs, even as negotiations over a United Nations plastics treaty have stalled.

She said community-level organizers are still making progress even where broader policy has lagged. Among the notable difference-makers, Enck cited Sharon Lavigne, founder of Rise St. James in Louisiana, who helped stop a major Formosa Plastics proposal; Diane Wilson, a fourth-generation shrimper in Texas fighting pellet pollution in local waters; and Debby Lee Cohen, a New York City parent who helped push the nation's largest school district away from polystyrene cafeteria trays.

Personal action can reduce risk, but it is not a full solution.

"People are paying for all of this plastic with their health," Enck said. "This is quite a serious health issue for all of us."

description:

While consumers may groan at the thought of yet another monthly bill, the financial incentives for auto executives are far too massive to ignore.
text:
For over a century, the automotive business model was simple: build a car, sell it to a dealership, and hope the customer buys another one in five years. Once the keys were handed over, the automaker’s chance to make real money on that vehicle was largely over.

Those days are rapidly fading. Second-quarter 2026 earnings reports from two of the world's biggest automakers— Tesla and General Motors—confirm a fundamental shift in how Detroit and Silicon Valley view the driveway. Like it or not, the modern automobile is turning into a rolling software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform, powered by monthly recurring fees.

The Q2 Numbers: Software Margin vs. Hardware Margin

Why are auto executives so obsessed with software? Look no further than their quarterly balance sheets. Selling traditional physical cars typically yields modest profit margins—often between 4% and 10% per vehicle dollar. In contrast, GM recently revealed that its software business retains roughly 70 cents of every dollar brought in, a eye-watering 70% margin that looks far more like Apple or Microsoft than a traditional Detroit factory.

Both manufacturers posted massive software numbers in Q2 2026:

Tesla FSD Adoption is Exploding

Tesla’s FSD adoption has followed a clear, steady upward trajectory. Total paid users grew from 400,000 in 2021 to 500,000 in 2022, reaching 600,000 in 2023, 800,000 in 2024, and surpassing 1.1 million by year-end 2025. That momentum accelerated into 2026, with active users jumping from 1.28 million in Q1 to 1.48 million in Q2. Compared to the 0.95 million users recorded in Q2 2025, Tesla has achieved an impressive 56% year-over-year increase in its FSD subscriber base.

"Like Elon mentioned, one of the key factors for our vehicle demand has been FSD," said Tesla CFO Vaibhav Taneja on the most recent earnings call. "Our sales data suggests one of the main reasons customers are coming and looking at the car is because of FSD. In Q2, we had, in North America, about 55% of our deliveries had FSD subscription at the time of delivery enabled. Overall, FSD attach rates continue to improve, reaching nearly 1.5 million paid customers globally, of which 55% is upfront purchases and the remaining 45% is subscriptions. We expect that the bulk of the growth in FSD monetization will come from subscriptions as we’ve removed the purchase option in most markets."

The EV Factor: Replacing Lost Maintenance Income

While this aggressive push into software is partially about profits, it’s also a defensive survival tactic.

As the industry transitions to electric vehicles (EVs), traditional profit centers are evaporating. EVs have significantly fewer moving parts than internal combustion engines. They don't require routine oil changes, spark plug replacements, or complex transmission flushes. That lack of maintenance cuts deeply into the reliable repair work that dealerships and auto giants have relied on for decades.

That said, the cost of diagnosing complex computer systems is likely to keep dealerships making fortunes for decades to come.

To fill any potential financial void, automakers are locking in digital recurring revenue:

General Motors is bundling baseline safety and connectivity features (OnStar Basics) for up to eight years on new 2025+ models, enticing buyers before converting 30% to 40% of them into paid Super Cruise subscribers once their free trial period ends.

Tesla went a step further by removing basic lane-keeping features and phasing out the lump-sum purchase option for FSD, forcing new buyers toward the $99 monthly subscription model as the primary gateway to hands-free navigation.

Wall Street rewards predictable, recurring cash flow. When GM announced its software margins and OnStar growth during its earnings call, investors drove the stock up 8.8% in a single day.

The Road Ahead: Features Over Hardware

By leaning into over-the-air (OTA) updates, car manufacturers can sell software additions to the second and third owners of a vehicle long after it leaves the assembly line.

Whether it is Ford’s BlueCruise ($49.99/month), GM's Super Cruise ($39.99/month), or Tesla’s FSD ($99/month), driver-assistance tech has proven to be the "killer app" that consumers are actually willing to pay for repeatedly - even though they consistently say they won't.

While consumers may groan at the thought of yet another monthly bill, the financial incentives for auto executives are far too massive to ignore. The physical car is no longer the final product, it is merely the hardware vessel that delivers the software.

text:
BREAKING: Trump admits in federal court he canceled billions in grants purely because those states didn't vote for him

They finally said it out loud. In court.

For months the Trump administration insisted that canceling more than $7.5 billion in clean energy grants was about stopping waste and protecting taxpayers. It was never true, and now their own lawyers have admitted it in writing.

In court filings this month, federal officials conceded they terminated the funding "based solely" on politics. Not performance. Not cost. Not fraud. They targeted projects in states that voted for Kamala Harris and had two Democratic senators, and they left Republican states alone even when the Energy Department itself had recommended cutting those grants too.

The Energy Department reviewed its spending last fall and flagged more than 600 grants across both red and blue states. But when Russell Vought's budget office pulled the trigger in October, it killed 284 of them, and almost every single one landed in a state that voted for Harris.

A government lawyer admitted the cancellations had nothing to do with "any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor." In plain English, the only thing these projects had in common was how their state voted.

This directly contradicts what Trump's own officials told Congress under oath. Energy Secretary Chris Wright stood in front of a House hearing in June and said, "No decisions were made on politics." The court record now says otherwise.

The projects they killed were not abstract. Grid upgrades in California and Oregon. Efforts to stop methane leaks in Colorado. Clean hydrogen hubs in the Pacific Northwest. Real jobs, real infrastructure, all wiped out to punish states for their votes.

Senator Patty Murray of Washington and Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio called it exactly what it is.

"This is an astounding admission that the president and his team corruptly abused their power to kill good jobs and punish hard-working families because of their political views."

And it gets worse. The White House is now finalizing new rules that would give Trump's political appointees the power to review, block, or revoke more than $1 trillion in federal grants every year. The same people who just admitted to punishing states over their votes want the authority to do it across the entire government.

Your tax dollars are supposed to belong to all of us. They are supposed to fund roads, research, and jobs regardless of which way your state leaned in the last election. What Trump admitted in court is that he sees the federal budget as a weapon to reward friends and punish everyone else.

text:
Europe’s battery electric vehicle market recorded a strong first half of 2026, with registrations exceeding 1.2 million across 17 tracked markets.

June was a standout month. A total of 275,060 new battery electric vehicles were registered, representing a 39.5% increase from June 2025, according to a bulletin from New AutoMotive, Fier Automotive and E-Mobility Europe.

BEVs accounted for 25.6% of new registrations across the markets included in the report. The estimated share across the European Union was slightly higher at 27.4%.

The figures point to a broader shift in the European automotive market. Electric vehicle adoption is no longer being driven solely by a small group of established markets. Growth is spreading into countries where BEV penetration has historically been lower, bringing new commercial opportunities alongside infrastructure and policy challenges.

Record BEV Growth Spreads Across European Markets

Registrations reached 1,241,916 during the first six months of 2026, up from 928,800 in the same period of 2025.

Italy recorded the fastest year-over-year growth, with registrations increasing by 97.9%. France followed with growth of 61.3%, while Germany rose 48.6% and Spain increased 31%.

Several countries also delivered their strongest monthly results to date in June.

France registered 55,851 battery electric vehicles, giving BEVs a 29.6% share of its new-car market. Spain recorded 14,559 registrations and an 11.3% market share. Slovenia and Czechia set records for both monthly volumes and BEV penetration.

Belgium, Denmark, Portugal and Finland reported their highest monthly BEV registration totals, although not all reached record market shares.

This wider geographic spread matters for manufacturers, energy providers and infrastructure operators. It suggests that investment decisions can no longer be based primarily on mature Northern European EV markets. Charging demand, fleet electrification and grid planning are becoming relevant across a much larger part of the region.

Some European countries are already reporting adoption rates above China’s June BEV market share of 42.8%.

Norway remained the regional leader, with electric vehicles representing 96.5% of new registrations. Denmark reached 79.1%, followed by Ireland at 51.2%, Finland at 48.9% and the Netherlands at 43.5%.

These percentages should be viewed in context. National vehicle markets differ significantly in size, tax structures, incentive programmes and consumer behaviour. China continues to operate at a much larger scale in terms of EV production, battery manufacturing and total vehicle sales.

Europe’s rate of growth was nevertheless stronger in June. BEV registrations across the tracked European markets increased by almost 40% year over year, compared with reported growth of around 6% in China’s domestic BEV registrations.

For automakers, the expansion brings both demand and competitive pressure. Manufacturers must increase the availability of electric models while managing vehicle pricing, production costs, supply-chain exposure and uncertainty around national incentive schemes.

Greater new-vehicle supply may also support the development of Europe’s used-EV market. As more electric cars enter company fleets and private ownership, a larger number should eventually become available at lower price points.

That could make electric vehicles accessible to a younger and more cost-conscious group of buyers, including consumers who are interested in switching but remain priced out of the new-car market.

Charging, Grid Capacity and Policy Become the Next Test

text:
In Louisiana's so-called Cancer Alley, plastic pollution is not a distant environmental problem. Advocates say it is in the air near homes and inside people's bodies.

The fight over plastic is now being framed as a public health alarm, rather than just a story about waste, litter, or recycling.

What's happening?

Judith Enck, a former EPA regional administrator who now heads Beyond Plastics, said plastic is woven into daily life and is now turning up inside the human body as well.

Speaking with Paloma Beltran for Living on Earth, shared by Inside Climate News, Enck said plastics connect several overlapping issues, including climate change, ocean pollution, environmental justice, and public health.

Enck said the harms linked to plastic span its full life cycle. She noted that just 5% to 6% of plastic gets recycled, while much of what remains is burned, buried in landfills, or released into the environment.

As cleaner transportation and electricity options grow, large oil and gas companies have leaned more heavily on plastics as a business opportunity.

"We are seeing plastics emerge as plan B for the fossil fuel industry," Enck said.

Why does it matter?

According to Enck, the health concerns are driven in part by microplastics, tiny fragments measuring no more than about 0.2 inches, or five millimeters, that can be inhaled or swallowed.

She said researchers have found these particles in blood and in multiple organs and tissues, including the lungs, kidneys, liver, placenta, breast milk, and testicles.

"Our babies are being born pre-polluted," Enck said.

Enck pointed to a New England Journal of Medicine study that found microplastics attached to plaque in neck arteries, which was associated with a higher risk of stroke, heart attack, or premature death. She also cited newer research suggesting microplastics can cross the blood-brain barrier.

Many people are exposed in small, repeated ways through packaging, bottle caps, food containers, and polluted air, while health agencies and regulators are still catching up to the science.

Residents near petrochemical plants are exposed to toxic chemicals "24/7," Enck said, highlighting Louisiana's Cancer Alley as an example. She cited a Johns Hopkins study that estimated cancer risk in the area at seven times the national average.

What's being done?

Enck said advocates have gained momentum from single-use plastic bans and producer responsibility programs, even as negotiations over a United Nations plastics treaty have stalled.

She said community-level organizers are still making progress even where broader policy has lagged. Among the notable difference-makers, Enck cited Sharon Lavigne, founder of Rise St. James in Louisiana, who helped stop a major Formosa Plastics proposal; Diane Wilson, a fourth-generation shrimper in Texas fighting pellet pollution in local waters; and Debby Lee Cohen, a New York City parent who helped push the nation's largest school district away from polystyrene cafeteria trays.

Personal action can reduce risk, but it is not a full solution.

"People are paying for all of this plastic with their health," Enck said. "This is quite a serious health issue for all of us."

description:

In this effort, the European Union is playing a leading role — at home, with partners, and in multilateral cooperation.
Within the European Union, the energy transition is being advanced through ambitious climate and energy legislation, large-scale deployment of renewable energy, stronger energy efficiency measures, and investment in grids, storage and innovation.
The EU has demonstrated that climate action, competitiveness and energy security can and must go hand in hand.

text:
President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, colleagues,

I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the EU and its Member States.

We meet at a defining moment for the global energy transition. Ten years after the Paris Agreement entered into force, the world has made important progress, but it remains far from the pace and scale required to keep 1.5°C within reach.

The challenge before us is clear: to turn commitment into implementation. The UAE Consensus set out a shared direction — to triple global renewable energy capacity, double energy efficiency by 2030, and transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly and equitable manner. Our collective task now is to deliver.

In this effort, the European Union is playing a leading role — at home, with partners, and in multilateral cooperation.

Within the European Union, the energy transition is being advanced through ambitious climate and energy legislation, large-scale deployment of renewable energy, stronger energy efficiency measures, and investment in grids, storage and innovation.

The EU has demonstrated that climate action, competitiveness and energy security can and must go hand in hand. The recent energy crisis only reinforced this lesson. It exposed the vulnerabilities of fossil fuel dependence, while accelerating efforts across Europe to diversify energy sources, reduce demand, and scale up clean, domestically produced energy.

But Europe’s responsibility does not stop at its own borders. If we are serious about energy transition, we must do much more to support partner countries, especially in Africa and in fragile contexts.

At the London Climate Action Week, the EU joined forces with COP31 and COP32 Presidency and other partner countries to expand electrification and reduce methane emissions.

Through Global Gateway, the EU supports sustainable, high-quality and trusted investments that connect energy with transport, digital, health, education, water, jobs and local value creation. By investing in clean energy alongside grids, storage, connectivity, skills, governance and resilient local systems, we aim to maximise positive spillovers for communities, strengthen resilience, and ensure that the green transition also supports poverty reduction, gender equality, climate action and sustainable growth.

The European Union stands ready to continue working with all partners to accelerate progress. Let this dialogue help move us from intention to implementation, from fragmented efforts to stronger cooperation, and from uneven progress to shared momentum.
