text:
Environmental groups are demanding the resignation of the Board of Environmental Safety’s newest member, Rhys Williams, because of his work as a lobbyist for a firm that represents clients that handle toxic materials.

The board decides appeals involving hazardous waste facilities permitted by the Department of Toxic Substances Control. Lawmakers created the board in 2021 to strengthen oversight of the department, increase transparency, and give communities disproportionately burdened by hazardous waste a stronger voice.

Gov. Gavin Newsom appointed Williams in January. Until recently Williams served as Newsom’s deputy chief of staff. In a letter addressed to Williams and copied to the board and the department, environmental groups expressed concerns with Williams’ work for a lobbying firm, Axiom Advisors. Axiom’s client list includes Clean Harbors, a hazardous waste management company, and GKN Aerospace, the company at the center of a chemical incident that prompted an evacuation order for thousands of Orange County residents in May.

Williams did not immediately respond to CalMatters’ requests for comment. At the board’s Thursday meeting, Williams did not comment on the letter.

Williams has not been accused of any wrongdoing, and his appointment was within the bounds of the law, experts say.

According to the governor’s office, Williams has been thoroughly vetted, and his work with Axiom is not a conflict of interest because he does not take on clients with matters before the board. Williams has also agreed to recuse himself from matters involving Axiom clients.

“Rhys Williams is an exceptionally qualified public servant with years of experience helping California navigate some of its most complex infrastructure, emergency management, and environmental challenges,” Newsom spokesperson Anthony Martinez said in an email. “His appointment reflects his deep subject matter expertise, professionalism, and longstanding commitment to public service.”

Advocates say his work for the lobbying firm undermines public confidence that he can act impartially to protect communities from environmental harms.

Environmental groups “were alarmed by just the audacity of appointing somebody who is or has been tied to the toxic waste industry,” said Bradley Angel, executive director of Greenaction for Health and Environmental Justice. “It does not bode well for impartiality or for upholding the stated mission of the Board of Environmental Safety, which is to protect the public from toxics and promote environmental safety, not promote polluter profits.”

Questions about impartiality

According to Williams’ LinkedIn profile and lobbying disclosures on the secretary of state’s Cal-Access website, Axiom Advisors hired Williams in May, four months after his appointment to the board.

Axiom Advisors announced the hire in June on LinkedIn. “This appointment brings something very important to Axiom’s clients,” the post reads. “Rhys’ extensive experience with the agencies that can move projects forward is invaluable to companies looking to do business here.”

The firm’s client list includes GKN Aerospace, which uses the hazardous chemical methyl methacrylate to make cockpit canopies, passenger windows and other transparent aerospace materials; Clean Harbors, a company that oversees one of the state’s two hazardous waste landfills, and the California Building Industry Association, an advocacy group for developers and homebuilders.

As a lobbyist with Axiom, Williams has attended meetings between GKN and legislative staff for Senator Tom Umberg, an Orange County Democrat, who is leading a proposal to hold the company accountable and offer relief for residents, according to a source familiar with the conversations. The Department of Toxic Substances Control does not primarily regulate GKN, an aerospace manufacturer, though it may have an oversight role if the company temporarily stores or transports hazardous waste.

Williams began working for Newsom as chief of staff in the lieutenant governor’s office in 2014, and has held various roles advising Newsom on infrastructure and emergency preparedness since he became governor in 2019.

Williams was earning close to $200,000 as deputy chief of staff in the governor’s office until January 2026, when he left for the board appointment, a part-time role paying $93,135. The governor later also appointed Williams to a position on the Board of Forestry and Fire Protection, which comes with a $100 per diem.

Asked in January why Williams was leaving the governor’s office, spokesperson Izzy Gardon wrote the aide had “earned his freedom :)” after more than a decade working for Newsom.

Board faces criticism

Williams joined the five-member board which, five years into existence, already faced sharp criticism for its questionable oversight of polluting facilities. In coming months, the board will vote on several appeals related to permits and permit modifications for some of the state’s largest hazardous waste facilities.

The board’s creation followed decades of complaints from communities and environmental advocates, who criticized the Department of Toxic Substances Control for delays in permitting facilities and for failing to protect communities from environmental harm.

The department’s handling of the decades-long Exide lead battery disaster in Los Angeles was one incident that drove reforms. Regulators determined that Exide Technologies was contaminating soil with lead and arsenic near thousands of homes over decades. The battery recycling plant operated with only a temporary permit for more than 30 years. State officials documented more than 100 violations at the plant and continued to allow it to operate.

In 2015, as part of an earlier bankruptcy, Exide agreed to permanently close the Vernon plant and pay $50 million toward cleanup. The company filed for bankruptcy again in 2020, and a federal judge approved a settlement allowing the company to abandon the site altogether – over the objection of state officials – shifting responsibility for the ongoing cleanup to the state.

Critics say the department’s slow permitting processes, and its pattern of permitting facilities with a history of violations, has continued.

Clean Harbors’ permit expired in 2006, but the company continued operating on an administrative extension for 20 years before DTSC renewed the permit last month.

Phibro-Tech, a hazardous waste treatment and recycling facility in Santa Fe Springs, operated on a permit that expired in 1996 for nearly 30 years until DTSC issued a renewed permit in 2025. The board will rule on appeals of the permit by the company and by environmental advocates in October.

Ecobat Resources, the only lead battery recycling plant west of the Rockies, operated on an administrative extension of its permit for ten years after it expired in 2015. DTSC finally issued a new permit in 2025. The board will rule on various permit appeals for the company in January.

Phibro-Tech and Ecobat are not Axiom clients.

“The BES was supposed to be our firewall to safeguard communities,” said Matt Holmes, a co-coordinator with the California Environmental Justice Coalition, referring to the Board of Environmental Safety.

Holmes added that although the board has improved dialogue with communities, “we’ve been disappointed that the (board) really hasn’t been the firewall for toxic communities to get equal treatment from the state.” The letter asking for Williams’ resignation, he said, “was a matter of us making it clear what we expect the (board) to be.”

What does the law say?

Legal experts said it’s neither illegal nor uncommon for state board members to also work as lobbyists. But they can run into trouble if they advocate for companies they also rule on as board members.

There’s no evidence Williams has violated specific conflict-of-interest laws: GKN Aerospace holds no hazardous waste handling or storage permits overseen by DTSC, and it’s unclear he has any connection to Clean Harbors or any other Axiom clients environmental groups have raised questions about.

Still, Williams may run afoul of the more broad common-law conflict-of-interest law, said Frank Zerunyan, a USC professor in government ethics.

“The fact that this person lobbies for a particular interest, does that make the people of California, which relies presumably on this person to be an objective commissioner or a board member for the purpose for which he is appointed, less trusting of California, or less trusting of that organization?” he said. “That is the question.”

For environmental groups, whether Williams ever votes on Clean Harbors, GKN, or other Axiom clients, is beside the point. They argue that the association alone is enough to erode public trust in his ability to rule fairly on appeals.

“For the duration of your tenure with the Board, the public may question whether your statements and activities (or lack thereof) could be consciously or subconsciously influenced by the interest of current Axiom clients, as well as the interests of potential clients Axiom may hope to attract,” the groups wrote in their letter to Williams.

Newsom appoints allies to state boards

Williams is one of more than a dozen of Newsom’s top staffers or close political operatives the governor has appointed to paid and unpaid positions on California’s sprawling collection of state boards and commissions.

Such appointments are commonplace, especially as governors prepare to leave office, and are known as comfortable landing pads for legislative staffers and political aides looking to leave full-time state service. They also give the governor continued influence over policy decisions and high-profile matters.

“It is a time-honored tradition for California governors to appoint high-ranking staff to plum positions as a ‘reward’ for working in high-pressure, 24-7 jobs in the administration,” said Sacramento Democratic consultant Steve Maviglio, who in 2003 received such an appointment to the Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board from outgoing Gov. Gray Davis.

Maviglio, Davis’ press secretary, spoke generally, saying it makes sense for governors to appoint staffers who are “loyal and battle-tested,” but that sometimes “appointments are made for the sake of qualifying for pension benefits.” Davis’ successor, Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, vowed to overhaul boards and commissions but later appointed several of his staffers to them.

Ford and Geely announced this week that they plan to create a joint venture at Ford’s assembly plant in Spain to build a new generation of multi-energy vehicles for the European market under both brands. Is “multi-energy” another way of saying “plug-in hybrid”? Apparently so. According to The Detroit News, Ford will own 66 percent of the partnership and Geely will own the remaining 44 percent.

“For nearly 50 years, Valencia has built some of the most-loved cars in our history, and now this team will help build our future,” Jim Baumbick, president of Ford of Europe, said in a statement. “That’s why we’re building a flexible, cost effective industrial system with a capable partner in Geely Auto. Together we can fully utilize a best-in-class plant with a great workforce and match the industry’s new cost benchmark. This partnership shows how automakers are strengthening Europe’s industrial base, but we can’t do it alone.”

Ford’s On The Road blog this week carried this message: ”Through this strategic, European focused joint venture, the new company will manufacture Ford and Geely multi-energy passenger vehicles for the European market — pooling production volume across two automakers to use the plant more fully, lower the cost of every vehicle we build there, and strengthen the local Valencia economy.

“The world class lineup of new electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles that Valencia produces will deliver the rally-bred thrills and enable the offroad adventures that are part of Ford’s unique appeal to European drivers. This isn’t just a partnership. This is our blueprint to win in an environment where intense competition, European electric vehicle mandates and industrial costs create challenges that no single company can solve alone. We are making the Valencia plant an automotive manufacturing powerhouse in Europe. ”

He added: “The joint venture is expected to produce an all new multi-energy crossover for Ford, in addition to a new member of the Bronco family, plus two electric Geely SUVs, with production starting in 2028. Kuga production continues uninterrupted. The collaboration accelerates Geely Auto’s European expansion, and supports Ford’s product offensive to bring five new passenger vehicles to European showrooms by 2029.”

V Is For Valencia

The Valencia factory has an annual capacity of 500,000 vehicles and is expected to start building a new Bronco for the European market in 2028. A multi-energy family crossover designed by Ford and jointly developed with Geely will follow by 2029. The popular Ford Kuga — which is available with a plug-in hybrid powertrain already — is currently assembled at the Valencia factory. It will continue in production while the factory is being reconfigured. Geely also plans to produce two electric SUVs in Valencia, with the first arriving in 2028.

“This JV with Ford in Europe reflects our commitment to open, collaborative product development as part of our growth strategy, deepening our local presence and commitment to customers in Europe,” Alex Nan, vice president of Geely Auto, said in a statement. “We are dedicated to delivering vehicles that European customers will choose on merit, on industry leading features, on high quality, and on actively contributing to Europe’s green future. Put simply, we are building cars in Europe, for Europe, alongside a trusted partner.”

Condemnation Ensues

Blowback was swift. Soon after the announcement, John Moolenaar, a congressperson from Michigan, criticized the deal. “Ford is actively helping the Chinese Communist Party advance its ambitions to dominate global automotive supply chains and increase the world’s dependence on China,” said Moolenaar, who is chairman of the House Select Committee on China.

“This partnership with Geely will further enable China’s decimation of auto markets in Europe as Chinese automakers set their sights on North America,” he said. “Ford’s decision (on Geely) is incomprehensible as its seeks protection from Chinese automakers coming to the United States. Ford should work with our nation’s allies, not our adversaries.”

Moolenaar, despite his xenophobic rhetoric, has a point. Virtually every automaker in the US is screaming for protection from Chinese competition while lobbying for further rollbacks in exhaust emissions standards. China is portrayed as the big bad wolf, but the US government has also been far more susceptible to political pressure than the European Union. Ford, like every other special interest group, will use any lever it can find that gives it an advantage.

Ford spokesperson Dave Tovar fired back in a statement that said Ford builds more vehicles annually in the United States than its domestic and foreign rivals that import millions of vehicles from Asia. “No company has done more to advance the US auto industry than Ford. Over in Europe, the landscape is changing fast and we are competing head-on with the Chinese and every other major global automaker. This new reality is forcing every car company to get radically leaner and smarter, which is exactly what we’re doing with our plant in Valencia, Spain.”

“While other US automakers chose to exit Europe altogether,” Tovar added, “we’re building strategic partnerships with companies like Renault, Volkswagen and Geely to build a sustainable future in Europe.” That “other US automakers” remark is clearly aimed at crosstown rival General Motors, which hastily dumped its European operations on Opel and beat feet for the border a decade ago. Last December, Ford announced a partnership with Renault to build two EV models for Europe. It also once intended to utilize the Volkswagen MEB platform for some European models, but that collaboration has gone mostly dormant recently.

An Existential Threat

Ford CEO Jim Farley has said that Chinese automakers are an “existential threat” to the US automotive industry, thanks to low priced, heavily subsidized electric vehicles and other advantages. In response, Ford has developed a next-generation platform for affordable EVs in the United States that will launch next year. Its first offering will be an as yet unnamed electric pickup truck that will be significantly smaller and less expensive than the F-150 Lightning. But Farley has also expressed an interest in an international partnerships to help it compete in markets where Chinese competitors are rapidly increasing their market share and European government regulations are requiring reductions in carbon emissions.

Ford has also suffered a mountain of criticism for its battery licensing agreement with CATL to produce batteries for its next-generation EVs in Marshall, Michigan. In the US today, it is popular to bash the Chinese for taking battery, solar, and wind technologies invented in America and making them commercially viable. Yet in the words of Harry Truman, “America was not built on fear. America was built on courage.”

So far, Ford and other US based manufacturers have shown precious little courage as they continue to prioritize monstrous gas hogs and fight any exhaust emissions standards that are more stringent than those from 30 years ago. This latest joint venture shows Ford knows what to do; now it needs to do it — not just in Europe, but in America as well.

text:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission explored reforms to PJM governance and stakeholder processes during a daylong technical conference Thursday featuring two-dozen speakers.

Following commissioners’ remarks, the audience heard from James P. Danly, deputy secretary of the U.S. Department of Energy and a former FERC chair, and Peter Lake, senior director of power for the White House National Energy Dominance Council.

Any reform should strengthen PJM’s ability to act, said PJM President and CEO David E. Mills, who participated in the first panel, “PJM Governance Mechanics – Board Authority, States’ Role, Filing Rights and Document Architecture.”

FERC Chair Laura V. Swett ended that session by asking panelists to briefly state specific changes that would improve PJM governance and the stakeholder process.

Mills advocated for more resources for state perspectives and participation by the Organization of PJM States (OPSI). Mills said PJM also seeks expanded rights to petition FERC, when necessary, to propose speedy consideration via what is known as a section 205 petition under the Federal Power Act.

“I would create an augmented OPSI organization that speaks for the totality of the states, and I would afford the PJM Board [section] 205 rights on the Operating Agreement and transmission planning,” Mills said.

Mills’ comments at the conference reflected PJM’s submitted testimony (PDF) to FERC, in which PJM expressly acknowledged the need for change and for a stakeholder process that advances solutions with greater efficiency.

“The PJM region is experiencing rapid load growth, tightening supply-demand conditions, changed resource economics and upward pressure on consumer costs,” the PJM testimony stated. “In this environment, governance and stakeholder processes play a direct role in determining how quickly and effectively PJM can respond to changing system needs. PJM is committed to meeting this moment, and the Commission is appropriately examining whether aspects of PJM’s governance and stakeholder processes should evolve to better enable our ability to do so.”

That PJM testimony was among dozens received by FERC prior to Thursday’s conference. In seeking comments from panelists and the public, FERC sought feedback “with a particular focus on identifying and evaluating concrete, actionable reforms to improve PJM’s ability to address operational and market needs in a timely and efficient manner” and “specific governance features and stakeholder processes in PJM that impact timely action on operational and market needs.”

PJM Signals Action To Preserve Reliability

After the panel, Mills further shared factors beyond PJM’s control that contribute to resource adequacy challenges amid concerns about extraordinary load growth and affordability.

“The binding constraint and largest risk are the failure to bring new generation online and into PJM’s auctions, with permitting, siting, interconnection and financing all contributing causes. The last two auctions produced lackluster new generation, even though more than 50 GW of resources have cleared PJM’s planning process and executed interconnection agreements,” he said.

Mills also signaled the imminent announcement of PJM proposals to FERC to maintain reliability and affordability amid extraordinary load growth. Determined by the PJM Board, the proposals to FERC reflect feedback and participation by diverse PJM Members, state regulators, consumer advocates and more from the recently concluded Critical Issue Fast Path – Reliability Backstop Procurement – Connect & Manage stakeholder process.

Mills noted that PJM will announce a September 2026 backstop auction with a 15-year term to help close the reliability gap in the coming days.

Mills stated, “The deeper issue may be investor confidence, weakened by repeated market-model changes; external interventions such as price caps; and broader narratives about leaving, dismantling or breaking up PJM.”

Joining Mills on the first panel were:

Pat Wood III – Hunt Energy Network, Executive Chairman and Former FERC Chair

Kelsey Bagot – Virginia State Corporation Commission, Chair

Jacob Finkel – Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s Office, Deputy Secretary of Policy

He was joined by:

title: Viewpoint: Delaware Must Build Its Innovation Economy by Design
description:
We’re building what comes next,” Governor Matt Meyer said in outlining Delaware’s economic future.
Building an innovation economy requires sustained work in areas where Delaware has distinctive strengths and the ability to compete.
Delaware’s innovation economy should be statewide in purpose, market-focused in strategy and regional in execution.
Tourism, agriculture, food and coastal innovation should be centered in southern and central Delaware and connected to the broader Delmarva economy.
Each needs its own leadership team and plans for capital, talent, commercialization, corporate engagement and measurable results.
text:
“We’re not just defending what we have. We’re building what comes next,” Governor Matt Meyer said in outlining Delaware’s economic future.

That is the right ambition—and the work has begun. In his first year, Governor Meyer has worked with the Delaware Prosperity Partnership to complement business recruitment with a stronger focus on innovation and entrepreneurship, while advancing other important elements of Delaware’s economic agenda such as the recent banking reforms. The next priority is to connect these efforts through an even more focused, market-driven strategy with clear priorities, coordinated leadership and practical mechanisms for execution.

Building an innovation economy requires sustained work in areas where Delaware has distinctive strengths and the ability to compete. Because biotechnology, advanced materials, tourism and financial technology operate in fundamentally different markets, each requires its own strategy, capabilities and path to growth. Delaware should therefore organize its efforts around four priority growth areas: (1) life sciences and biotechnology; (2) tourism, agriculture, food and coastal innovation; (3) advanced materials, chemistry and clean energy; and (4) financial services, corporate infrastructure and digital technology.

Each growth area needs its own strategy, specialized capabilities and connection to larger markets. These priorities do not encompass Delaware’s entire economy, but they can provide a strategic center of gravity for innovation. Good strategy requires choices, and these areas offer strong opportunities for differentiated growth across all three counties.

Traditional economic development remains essential. Delaware should continue attracting and expanding major employers in manufacturing, corporate operations, healthcare and selective logistics and data centers, while investing in transformative institutions such as the state’s planned first four-year medical school. These investments create jobs, strengthen talent pipelines and communities, and broaden our tax base.

But recruitment alone cannot define our long-term strategy. Delaware must also attract entrepreneurs to start companies here and create the policies, programs, capital and incentives that help high-growth startups take root, scale and stay. Innovation creates companies and value, attracts outside capital and ambition, and develops the experience and talent already here. It gives Delawareans a meaningful role in building—and benefiting from—the next generation of growth.

That growth also strengthens Delaware’s Main Street businesses. As startups form, hire and scale, they create demand for local suppliers, professional services, restaurants, retailers, salons, housing and everyday services. The value generated by innovation does not remain within individual companies; it circulates throughout the broader economy, supporting small businesses, strengthening communities and creating new opportunities across Delaware.

Delaware is not starting from scratch. We have globally respected companies, strong universities and healthcare institutions, entrepreneurs, experienced leaders and civic organizations, along with connections to regional and national sources of investment capital. These assets reach across the state, with important institutional and economic strengths in each of Delaware’s three counties.

The opportunity is to connect these assets into a more intentional system. When they operate independently, progress slows and opportunities can be lost. When companies, institutions, capital and talent are aligned around shared market priorities, ideas can move more efficiently from discovery to commercialization and scale.

Any strategy must reflect how markets work. State borders matter for policy, funding, taxation and political accountability, but talent, capital, supply chains, research, customers and entrepreneurial networks rarely stop there. For a small state like Delaware, regional connection is a strategic advantage.

Delaware’s innovation economy should be statewide in purpose, market-focused in strategy and regional in execution.

Life sciences and biotechnology should position Delaware as a company-building and translation hub within Greater Philadelphia’s life sciences cluster. Our opportunity is not to replicate Philadelphia, but to collaborate with it. Delaware combines specialized laboratory and manufacturing infrastructure, university and healthcare connections, experienced industry leadership, and the capacity to move biomedical and industrial biotechnology companies from research to pilot-scale and commercial operations. Its ability to move more nimbly from decision to development can make Delaware a leading place to turn discoveries into companies and help science-based ventures grow.

Tourism, agriculture, food and coastal innovation should be centered in southern and central Delaware and connected to the broader Delmarva economy. These sectors may receive less attention than life sciences, advanced technology or financial services, but they are no less important to Delaware’s future. They bring outside value into the state, support small businesses, strengthen communities and create distinctive employment and entrepreneurial pathways.

Advanced materials, chemistry and clean energy build on one of Delaware’s clearest global strengths. Our scientific, corporate and university heritage gives us a right to compete in advanced materials and materials science, materials-enabled energy, sustainable chemistry, specialized ingredients, biomaterials, water technologies, advanced manufacturing and other hard-tech markets. Delaware can support these companies with specialized laboratories, pilot facilities, process engineering expertise, manufacturing partners and industrial customers. Northern Delaware provides scientific and corporate density; central and southern Delaware contribute sites, workforce, infrastructure and demonstration opportunities.

Financial services, corporate infrastructure and digital technology should build on two distinct but complementary Delaware strengths. The first is our globally recognized incorporation and corporate-governance system, which supports a broad ecosystem of business and professional services. The second is Delaware’s longstanding banking and financial services industry, now positioned for renewed growth through modernized laws. Delaware’s opportunity is to protect and strengthen both platforms while using fintech, legal technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and compliance tools to make the state an even more trusted and efficient place to form, finance, govern and secure companies.

These growth areas cannot be effectively supported through one generic innovation program. Biotechnology and fintech require different investors. Clean-energy manufacturing and artificial intelligence require different talent pipelines. Therapeutic companies and financial-technology platforms face different regulatory environments.

Each needs its own leadership team and plans for capital, talent, commercialization, corporate engagement and measurable results. They should still share statewide strengths such as entrepreneurial education, university connections, data, policy alignment and coordinated economic development.

Delaware needs both focus and connection. Market-focused growth areas provide the focus. Natural economic clusters provide the geography. A statewide strategy provides the connection.

One practical way to support that work would be to establish four time-limited leadership councils—one for each priority growth area—and charge each with developing a strategy and helping drive execution. Each council should be chaired by a respected individual with the credibility to convene the right people, the independence to think beyond any one institution and the trust to maintain momentum.

Each council should have a working budget, clear deliverables and a timetable. It should identify the markets Delaware can realistically win, map our assets, benchmark competing regions, identify gaps and recommend the investments and partnerships needed to deliver results.

These strategies cannot sit on a shelf. They should guide decisions about talent, infrastructure, commercialization, entrepreneurship, public investment and regional partnerships. Progress should be measured publicly through company formation, capital attracted, jobs created, technologies commercialized, businesses scaled and new value brought into Delaware.

No single organization can build this alone. Success will depend on government, universities, industry, entrepreneurs, investors and communities aligning around shared priorities and contributing what each does best.

Delaware’s size gives us a rare advantage: we can bring the right people together, make decisions and move quickly. But that advantage matters only if we use it with focus, discipline, public accountability and shared ownership.

The task now belongs to all of us: choose the markets where Delaware can lead, organize the teams, align the resources, commit to sustained political and institutional support, and deliver measurable results.

Not by chance. By design.

text:
Attorney General William Tong helped win a lawsuit forcing the EPA to identify areas with unhealthy soot pollution levels

A federal judge ruled the EPA broke the law by failing to make those identifications, giving it six months to comply

The ruling follows Canadian wildfire smoke blanketing the East Coast and comes with major projected public health benefits

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong recently announced that his office, alongside attorneys general from 11 other states, won a lawsuit against the Trump regime that requires the Environmental Protection Agency to implement air quality standards.

A rule in 2024’s Clean Air Act strengthened National Ambient Air Quality Standards for soot, a pollutant emitted from numerous sources like vehicles, factors and construction sites, CT News Junkie explained. These particles can invade the body through the lungs and attack the rest of a body; they’ve been linked to serious health problems including heart attacks and cancer.

Under that rule, the EPA was legally required to identify areas that fail to meet the stricter standards, but failed to do so, Inside Climate News reported. A federal judge ruled that the EPA now has six months to implement the enhanced standards.

The ruling in the lawsuit comes several days after Canadian wildfires spread vast amounts of soot across the northern and eastern United States, reinforcing the serious health risks that polluted air can cause.

“There is nothing more vital to public health than the air we breathe, and we cannot take that for granted. We sued to force the EPA to do its job, and we’re going to stay on them until it gets done,” Tong said.

Should the new standards be implemented by the new deadline, areas designated as failing to attain healthy air will receive attention from state-level programs to reduce dangerous pollution levels, Tong’s office said.

According to the EPA’s own estimates, the first year of full implementation of these better air quality standards would significantly improve public health. Improvements would include 4,500 fewer premature deaths, 2,000 fewer emergency room visits, 5,700 fewer asthma diagnoses and 800,000 fewer triggerings of asthma symptoms.

text:
A new Thinking Minnesota poll from the Center of the American Experiment has recently come out that shows affordability is the top issue for Minnesotans, of all political stripes, in the upcoming 2026 state elections. In fact, as per the first graphic below, 87% of total voters consider it a factor, be it a major one of 59% or a minor one of 28%.

Source: Meeting Street Insights

Issues

The poll also shows that energy is a top ten affordability issue, as seen in the second graphic below. “Lowering energy costs” is 8th place with 10%. However, energy is more like 5th place, given it is a sixth of both 4th place “lowering housing costs” of 20%, and at least half, and probably more, of “reducing gas taxes and transportation costs” at 9%.

Source: Meeting Street Insights

Affordability

As can easily be seen in the first chart below, for all Minnesota electricity customers combined (i.e. residential, commercial and industrial), overall affordability has been shockingly bad in the 21st century, especially since 2002, the first year of the state’s transition to renewables. The lowlights from 2002 to 2025 were as follows:

electricity price inflation of +118.4%;

electricity use deflation of -14.6%, noting that less use was not efficiency but poverty;

electricity bill unaffordability of +86.6%.

Source: EIA.gov electricity price (cents/kWh), use (kWh/customer) and bill (dollars/customer)

Index: 100.0 = 2002

Price

The second chart below compares electricity prices of Minnesota to the Midwest and Nation. The Midwest is comprised of: 1.) Illinois; 2.) Indiana; 3.) Iowa; 4.) Michigan; 5.) Minnesota; 6.) Nebraska; 7.) North Dakota; 8.) Ohio; 9.) South Dakota; and 10.) Wisconsin. From 2002 to 2025:

Minnesota electricity price inflation of 118.4%, 22.2% and 29% worse than the next two;

Midwest electricity price inflation of 96.2%;

National electricity price inflation of 89.4%.

Source: EIA.gov eelctricity price (cents/kWh) Index: 100.0 = 2002

Use

The third chart below compares electricity use of Minnesota to the Midwest and Nation. From 2002 to 2025:

Minnesota electricity use deflation of 14.6%, 8.9% and 9.7% worse than the next two;

Midwest electricity use deflation of 5.7%;

National electricity use deflation of 4.9%.

Source: EIA.gov electricity use (kWh/customer) Index: 100.0 = 2002

Bill

The fourth chart below compares electricity bills of Minnesota to the Midwest and Nation. An electricity bill is price times use. It is good when a bill goes down because of price deflation. It is bad when it goes down because of price inflation. The latter happened from 2002 to 2025:

Minnesota electricity bill unaffordability of 86.6%, only 0.5% and 6.4% worse than the next two, because of higher price inflation inducing greater use deflation;

Midwest electricity bill unaffordability of 86.1%;

National electricity bill unaffordability of 80.2%.

Source: EIA.gov electricity bill (dollars/customer) Index: 100.0 = 2002

Proposals

The new affordability poll canvassed voter preferences on five potential policy proposals, as can be viewed in the third graphic below. Three of the five proposals were fiscal policy, that being the 1st, 2nd and 5th placed ones. The other two, the 3rd and 4th, were regulatory policy. Unfortunately, although the 5th called for subsidy removal, the 2nd called for more subsidies.

Source: Meeting Street Insights

Subsidies

Mainstream static economics teaches that taxpayer subsidies, such as to Minnesota renewables, will increase supply and lower prices. It also teaches that rising input costs, say in such renewables, will decrease supply and escalate prices. Dynamic incentives are the missing link.

Free market economics, like in Murray Rothbard’s Power and Market, argue that subsidies will cause both effects, of increasing supply and rising input costs. But the latter effect will tend to overpower the former. Thus, prices will tend to be high and rising as time goes by.

The reasons for this are: 1.) inefficient businesses are the ones who are incentivized to seek subsidies or rent seek; 2.) these subsidies incentivize such businesses to stay inefficient or worsen; 3.) more resources are diverted into #1, leading to more #2. Rinse and repeat.

Solutions

On June 8, American Experiment published “41 concrete steps policymakers can take to make Minnesota more affordable” in the report Supplying Hope and Demanding (Real) Affordability: An agenda for Minnesota’s future. Those 41 steps included 5 concrete ones “to improve electricity affordability.” Thus, “Minnesota’s state government should:

Repeal the mandates for 100 percent renewable energy.

Repeal costly subsidy programs for energy conservation, small-scale renewable energy, electric vehicles and vehicle chargers, and similar wasteful programs.

Reduce state-authorized taxes on electricity, natural gas, propane, gasoline and diesel fuel, which would provide immediate relief to consumers.

Repeal the state’s ban on building new nuclear power plants.

Reduce mandates and taxes on natural gas.”

Conclusion

Both Republican and Democrat candidates for state office, especially legislative and gubernatorial ones, should take heed of this pocketbook policy poll. And, as the index numbers on electricity prices, usage and bills above confirm, Minnesotans are ‘too right‘ to be alarmed about energy affordability. Only good economics, policy and politics can fix it.

text:
(NewsNation) — President Donald Trump delivered remarks Friday in his push to revive America’s nuclear power industry, as the administration announced four advanced nuclear reactors have reached criticality and officials weigh opening federal waters to offshore nuclear projects.

“America is building again, America is dreaming again, and we’re leading the world in pioneering the next generation of nuclear power,” he said.

Trump was joined in the Oval Office by nuclear energy executives to mark the achievement, which the White House tied to a series of executive orders the president signed in May 2025.

“President Trump has done more than any other president in history to advance civilian nuclear energy development, innovation, and technology,” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. “In this Golden Age of America, President Trump has unleashed a nuclear energy renaissance to meet the nation’s growing energy needs while keeping prices low.”

Trump previously said he wants to quadruple U.S. nuclear capacity by 2050 to meet rising electricity demand driven largely by data centers.

Nuclear power’s share of U.S. electricity generation stood at 18% in 2026, down from 19.7% a decade earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration.

Four advanced reactors reach criticality

Trump’s May 2025 orders directed Energy Secretary Chris Wright to launch a pilot program requiring at least three advanced reactors to achieve criticality by July 4, 2026 — the nation’s 250th anniversary.

The Department of Energy said it met that goal, with the reactors representing the first privately funded, non-light-water advanced reactors to come online in the U.S. in more than four decades.

“I directed Secretary of Energy Chris Wright to establish a pilot program for advanced reactors and see at least three cutting-edge reactors started up safely by the Fourth of July and what we’ve done has been pretty much of a miracle,” Trump said.

“Most believe the goal was impossible, but I’m delighted to say that four companies succeeded in meeting that deadline,” he added.

He touted reactors from Antares Nuclear, Deployable Energy, Aalo Atomics and Valar Atomics.

Antares Nuclear announced it had gone critical June 4, followed by Valar Atomics on June 18, according to NPR. A third company followed in the weeks after.

Other firms in the program, including Radiant, were still working toward criticality as the deadline approached, though Radiant’s chief nuclear officer, Rita Baranwal, said the company expected to have its reactor operating soon even if it missed the July 4 target, NPR reported.

Attending Friday’s Oval Office event was Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy; Jarrod Agen, executive director of the National Energy Dominance Council; Wright; Interior Secretary Doug Burgum; and the chief executives of Antares Nuclear, 3rd Deployable Energy, Aalo Atomics, Valar Atomics and Stealth, among others.

Feds may allow nuclear plants in offshore federal waters

The Interior Department’s Marine Minerals Administration said this week it signed an agreement with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to coordinate oversight of potential nuclear projects in federal waters on the Outer Continental Shelf.

“Submerged reactor systems have been safely deployed in naval applications for decades, demonstrating their potential as a reliable source of energy in demanding marine environments,” MMA Acting Director Matt Giacona said in a statement.

No commercial offshore nuclear projects are currently planned, the agencies said, but they will coordinate on any future industry requests.

The move follows other recent efforts by the Interior Department to open federal waters to industrial activity, including proposals for seabed mining off American Samoa and space launch infrastructure.

The Center for Biological Diversity criticized the offshore nuclear proposal.

“The Trump administration seems to have a never-ending store of terrible ideas for mistreating ocean life, and nuclear reactors on rusty old oil platforms is one of its worst,” said Nick Katkevich, an oceans campaigner with the group.

Are there safety concerns with the nuclear reactors?

The rapid pace of the reactor pilot program has drawn criticism from some nuclear safety experts.

Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, called the push “essentially an exercise in public relations” and said regulatory rollbacks tied to the program risk undoing decades of safety lessons.

“This is taking us back to the 1950s, and that is not progress,” Lyman told NPR.

The Energy Department rewrote its safety and security standards for the pilot program and exempted participating reactors from environmental review, consulting with companies but not the public, NPR reported.

The department has said the changes were designed to cut unnecessary regulation without compromising safety.

Nick Touran, chief nuclear officer at Ocean Atomics, which is developing nuclear power for civilian ships, said the pace of progress under the program has been unprecedented. “We haven’t done anything this fast, basically ever,” he told NPR.

text:
North Carolina Hydropower Day

2026

By The Governor Of The State Of North Carolina

A Proclamation

Whereas, the State of North Carolina recognizes August 24 as North Carolina Hydropower Day to honor hydropower’s longstanding contribution to our state’s economic prosperity and its continuing role in providing reliable, renewable, and affordable electricity while preserving North Carolina’s natural resources; and

Whereas, North Carolina is home to 37 conventional hydropower facilities and one pumped storage hydropower plant, generating nearly 2,000 megawatts of electricity; and

Whereas, hydropower is the second-largest source of renewable electricity in North Carolina, supporting energy and grid reliability for homes, businesses, and industries across the state; and

Whereas, the resilience and reliability of hydropower resources are particularly important to western North Carolina communities as they continue to recover and rebuild from the impacts of Hurricane Helene and strengthen infrastructure for future generations; and

Whereas, the continued modernizations and responsible management of North Carolina’s hydropower facilities and dams support public safety, environmental conservation, workforce development, and technological innovation; and

Whereas, the hydropower industry creates high-quality jobs, supports rural and mountain communities, and contributes to North Carolina’s economic growth and clean energy future; and

Whereas, the State of North Carolina encourages all residents to recognize and celebrate the vital role of hydropower in strengthening our energy security, supporting economic opportunity, enhancing grid reliability, reducing carbon pollution, and preserving our state’s natural resources for future generations;

Now, Therefore, I, Josh Stein, Governor of the State of North Carolina, do hereby proclaim August 24, 2026, as “North Carolina Hydropower Day” in North Carolina and commend its observance to all residents.

name: Indiana Environment
title: Renewable Energy Policy After the Federal Retreat - Legal Planet
description:
In some ways, the fact that those states are staying the course is good news for the industry.
But 40% of the states have taken steps to make it more difficult to develop new renewable energy projects than it was before the return of Trump.
Despite all of this, there are already 28 gigawatts of installed renewable generating capacity in the state.
The solar industry reports that Indiana was third overall among the states for new installed solar capacity in 2025.
These things make it easier for the renewables industry to thrive everywhere.
text:
That doesn’t mean that all of the other 40 jurisdictions are rejecting renewables or that the solar and wind industries have ground to a halt. Some states that have taken no new steps had already created ambitious programs to support renewables. In some ways, the fact that those states are staying the course is good news for the industry. In addition, the economics for many renewables has become favorable in recent years, leaving the industry in a competitive position in most states.

It is also important to note that states such as Texas, while not declaring an intention to abandon fossil fuels, have paved the way for very substantial renewables development by simplifying permitting processes and expanding the transmission system.

But 40% of the states have taken steps to make it more difficult to develop new renewable energy projects than it was before the return of Trump. In the words of the report, “they are doing this through legislation that creates barriers to wind and solar development, mandates that prop up fossil fuel generation, restrictions on local clean energy rules, or outright bans on certain technologies. Missouri and Kentucky fall into this category, as do the growing number of states where utility commissions have delayed coal retirements, rolled back net metering, or weakened existing renewable standards.”

The roster of states that are weakening support for renewables includes Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, the two Dakotas, Iowa and Missouri. Add in Tennessee, Indiana, Ohio, West Virginia and others. All of the states in the Southeast are moving backward or standing still.

Even in those states, however, it is not uniformly bad news for solar and wind. Take Indiana, as an example. Indiana is a coal-producing state with a governor (Mike Braun) who is a close ally of the President’s. The state has no requirement that its utilities develop or procure renewable power. County governments, which have to issue permits for the construction of new solar and wind farms, are free to create moratoria on new development, or set such draconian conditions on new projects that they are discouraged from going forward. As of the writing of our report, 64 of Indiana’s 92 counties have enacted bans or prohibitive restrictions on new development. Despite all of this, there are already 28 gigawatts of installed renewable generating capacity in the state. There are about three gigawatts of other projects under construction. The solar industry reports that Indiana was third overall among the states for new installed solar capacity in 2025.

How can all of this happen in a state that is not enthusiastic about renewables? While this question is worthy of a study of its own, some factors are likely: the industry as a whole has benefited from mandates in many states and tax credits that have recently expired. These things make it easier for the renewables industry to thrive everywhere. Not unrelated, the cost of solar and wind (as well as battery storage) have gone down dramatically over the last few years, making these technologies cost competitive with fossil generation. In addition, Indiana borders Illinois, which has a substantial appetite for renewables to meet its requirements. Finally, it is often faster to procure and install new renewables than to build a gas-fired plant of a similar size.

Today, the institute engages, through various programs, with nuclear power plants in the U.S., Canada, China, Mexico, Romania, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates.
The company officially began construction on the project in April after receiving Nuclear Regulatory Commission approval of its construction permit in March.
Levesque added in this newest press release that the company’s membership in INPO reflects “TerraPower’s unwavering commitment to safety, performance, and reliability that INPO has championed for decades.” INPO CEO Bob Willard added that, “As the first advanced reactor company accepted into INPO membership, TerraPower is demonstrating a commitment to the principles of operational excellence, safety, reliability, and continuous learning that have defined commercial nuclear operations for decades.”
text:
Some history: Shortly after the partial meltdown of Three Mile Island-2, a consortium of utilities created INPO to address “one of the central problems revealed by the TMI accident, the need to have qualified and competent people to operate and manage nuclear power plants,” as explained in the March 1981 issue of Nuclear News (p. 47). That lengthy NN article goes on to say that INPO would soon establish standards of quality and competence; evaluate operating practices at nuclear plants; set criteria for personnel qualification, training programs, and instructors; and analyze operating experience.

While INPO was created independently, without federal direction, it quickly gained a significant nod from the government by way of the Kemeny Commission, a 12-person group established by the Carter administration and charged with investigating the causes and any consequences of the TMI accident. In its final recommendations, that commission noted that INPO could be an appropriate vehicle to set standards and conduct independent evaluations of the industry.

Fast forwarding: In the decades since its creation, INPO has followed through with its originally established objectives and become an indispensable—if frequently overlooked—part of the global nuclear ecosystem. Today, the institute engages, through various programs, with nuclear power plants in the U.S., Canada, China, Mexico, Romania, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates. INPO also works closely with the World Association of Nuclear Operators.

In January of this year, in an interview with Nuclear News, Jeff Place (INPO’s executive vice president for industry strategy) explained that the institute focuses on four main challenge areas: industry performance, industry sustainability, teaching and learning, and data science and analytics. “We implement that work through our operating model that includes our continuous monitoring program, accreditation activities, and various courses and seminars,” he explained.

While Place acknowledged, at the time, that there were a number of nuclear newcomers that INPO had yet to interact with, he added that “We believe it is important for new nuclear entrants to understand the social license that each of our utilities has to run these plants and that if something significant happens at any nuclear plant—new entrants included—it creates challenges for the entire industry.”

TerraPower’s entrance: In a press release, TerraPower CEO Chris Levesque said that the company has joined INPO as an operating member in support of Kemmerer-1, in Wyoming. That project will feature the first deployment of its Natrium power plant, a 345-MWe sodium-cooled fast reactor with an integrated molten salt–based heat storage system that can temporarily boost power output to 500 MWe. The company officially began construction on the project in April after receiving Nuclear Regulatory Commission approval of its construction permit in March.

Earlier this week, in a public NRC meeting, TerraPower announced that it is planning to submit a Part 50 operating license application for the project by March 2028.

Levesque added in this newest press release that the company’s membership in INPO reflects “TerraPower’s unwavering commitment to safety, performance, and reliability that INPO has championed for decades.”

INPO CEO Bob Willard added that, “As the first advanced reactor company accepted into INPO membership, TerraPower is demonstrating a commitment to the principles of operational excellence, safety, reliability, and continuous learning that have defined commercial nuclear operations for decades.”

text:
Social media advertisements released this week by fossil fuel advocacy front group Consumer Energy Alliance (CEA) are boosting Arizona Public Service’s (APS) recently announced proposal to convert two units at its retired Cholla Power Plant from coal to methane gas. According to a CEA internal budget document obtained by EPI via public records request, APS paid $15,000 for its membership in the organization in 2025.

APS noted the project, “will need to go through formal permitting and planning processes.” The chair of the regulator responsible for the final determination in that permitting and planning, Nick Myers, was onsite at the northeast Arizona plant for APS’s announcement.

Myers, Chair of the Arizona Corporation Commission (ACC), the agency which regulates investor-owned utilities in the state, was vocal in his support of the plant conversion in the days following the decision, stating that, “[c]onverting a retired coal-fired plant to natural gas is an important step in strengthening Arizona’s energy future.” Myers ran for reelection this year with his fellow incumbent commissioner, Kevin Thompson, who reposted CEA’s advertisement on his social media account saying that Myers and he “have pushed for natural gas since we were sworn into office. The fruits of our labor have paid dividends as we see APS announce the conversion of Cholla.”

Myers and Thompson also issued press releases about APS’s proposal, highlighting their roles in influencing the proposal. Thompson stated, “Chair Myers joined me in encouraging APS to consider the priorities of this Commission with decisions like Coronado and Springerville as they contemplated the future of Cholla.” The ACC approved the conversion of the Coronado and Springerville generating stations from coal to methane gas earlier this year.

Myers and Thompson faced Dr. Ralph Heap in a competitive Republican primary on July 21. Heap narrowly beat Myers for the second slot on the ballot after Thompson, with the support of conservative groups such as Turning Point Action and the Arizona Free Enterprise Club. Heap blamed the current ACC for the shutdown of the Cholla coal plant.

APS executives stated there was no definitive plan for Cholla weeks before their announcement

APS’s general rate case is currently under evaluation at the ACC. APS Chief Operating Officer Jacob Tetlow testified on May 26 about the company’s plans for Cholla, stating that APS did not “have a definitive plan” and that the company was “evaluating different alternatives.” The hearing in the rate case concluded on July 7, just days after the Cholla announcement. Parties are expected to submit briefs in late August and early September, and a decision from the ACC is due no later than December 31, 2026.

APS also plans to submit an integrated resource plan (IRP) to the ACC in August, assessing the company’s required energy needs and potential resources over the next 15 years. If the conversion of Cholla from coal to methane gas use is the lowest cost alternative, the company may use the IRP to help make its case. If the conversion is motivated by pressure from the ACC or the federal government, customers may end up paying the price.

Front group CEA has funded efforts in Arizona before

CEA is operated out of the offices of the Houston-based public relations and lobbying firm HBW Resources (HBW). According to CEA’s IRS 990’s, since 2010, the front group has allocated 56% of its $46.9 million revenue to HBW. The 990s also reveal that CEA has no staff; nearly all the representatives listed on CEA’s website are HBW employees. Recent CEA Board of Directors documents obtained by EPI show robust representation by the utility sector for CEA’s advocacy. In 2025, the group allocated more than $900,000 to support utility advocacy in several states including Arizona. This allocation also included dedicated funds for advocacy on behalf of the Edison Electric Institute, the utility industry’s national lobbying association.

CEA’s Southwest Director, Matthew Gonzales, celebrated the Commission days before its 2024 election, which ushered in a 5-0 Republican majority, including current Vice Chair Rachel Walden, who was recruited to run for her seat by Myers.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy announced that it will make up to $218.5 available to federally recognized tribes and corporations for energy efficiency upgrades for tribal homes.

The funding is part of the High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate (HEEHR) Program, created under the Inflation Reduction Act to help reduce household energy costs through rebates for qualifying electric appliances, heating and cooling systems, insulation, wiring and other efficiency improvements. Under the tribal program, each tribe is eligible for a formula-based allocation.

The DOE recently released updated guidance for the HEEHR program. The agency also released tribes’ formula funding allocations and extended the application deadline to Dec. 11. DOE said the revised guidance is intended to streamline program administration and give tribes more flexibility in designing rebate programs.

The DOE will host an online informational session on the program, updated guidance and next steps towards application for applying on July 28 at 2 p.m. EDT. Tribes and tribal organizations can register through the program’s registration page.

Additional assistance and implementation support are also available for tribes that want to participate in this program.

description:
— President Trump announced that 200 additional entities involved in developing and powering AI data centers have signed on to his voluntary ratepayer protection pledge first announced in March.
The President of Meta, CEO of Louisiana utility Entergy, and Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry were among those who joined the President for the announcement at the White House yesterday.
Signing on to Trump’s pledge is meaningless without legitimate transparency and enforceable protections,” said Susan Stevens Miller, senior attorney at Earthjustice.
People deserve strong, enforceable protections against data centers’ enormous impacts, not empty promises.” Many questions remain about President Trump’s pledge, as well as iterations of ratepayer protection pledges that governors have introduced across the country.

text:
—

President Trump announced that 200 additional entities involved in developing and powering AI data centers have signed on to his voluntary ratepayer protection pledge first announced in March. The President of Meta, CEO of Louisiana utility Entergy, and Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry were among those who joined the President for the announcement at the White House yesterday. The announcement comes as Americans continue to push back against the rapid proliferation of AI data centers that are causing utility bills to skyrocket, straining grids, and harming their communities and the climate.

In Louisiana, Earthjustice, representing the Alliance for Affordable Energy and the Union of Concerned Scientists, intervened in a case in front of the Louisiana Public Service Commission challenging Entergy Louisiana’s proposal to build seven additional gas power plants, through a fast-tracked proceeding, for Meta’s second hyperscale data center in Richland Parish. Recently, an administrative Law Judge (ALJ) granted Earthjustice’s request ordering Meta to turn over key information it has hidden from the public about Entergy Louisiana’s proposal.

But the trillion-dollar company subsequently filed motions to challenge that ruling in an effort to continue hiding critical information about Entergy Louisiana’s proposal, including how it determined how much energy its data center will actually need and how much those costs will be shifted onto Louisianans. If Meta and Entergy actually care about ratepayers in Louisiana as they pledged to, why are they trying to ram through these gas plants without oversight and accountability?

“Right now, Meta and Entergy are fighting tooth and nail to fast-track approval of seven new gas plants for its massive data center project in Richland Parish, all while hiding critical information from the public about how much the project will cost ratepayers and what jobs it will actually bring. Joining Trump for a press conference in support of an unenforceable ratepayer protection pledge while actively picking the pockets of ratepayers is a slap in the face to Louisianans. Signing on to Trump’s pledge is meaningless without legitimate transparency and enforceable protections,” said Susan Stevens Miller, senior attorney at Earthjustice.

“We support real consumer protections, but a voluntary pledge doesn’t guarantee the benefits Meta and Entergy are touting will ever materialize,” said Logan Burke, Executive Director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy. “This pledge is a publicity stunt. Meanwhile, Meta and Entergy are hiding behind NDAs and fighting a judge’s subpoena that requires them to disclose key information the public needs to evaluate the supposed benefits. The Public Service Commission needs to stand on transparency, because they are the ones who will ultimately have to enforce this pledge.”

“Entergy and Meta have continually fought basic transparency and cost-saving measures in their ongoing efforts to build more costly and polluting gas plants that won’t benefit the public,” said Paul Arbaje, senior analyst at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “Without intervention by regulators or legislators, both companies will continue putting Louisianans health, wallets and environment at risk. People deserve strong, enforceable protections against data centers’ enormous impacts, not empty promises.”

Many questions remain about President Trump’s pledge, as well as iterations of ratepayer protection pledges that governors have introduced across the country. Ultimately, these pledges and guidelines, whether at the federal or state level, will require enforcement from state regulators. Without protective, binding, enforceable policies from state regulators, the companies racing to power data centers will continue to inflate costs across the system. Unenforceable pledges are no substitute for meaningful regulatory oversight.

Without protective, binding, enforceable policies from state regulators—like developing special rates for data centers—the companies racing to power data centers will continue to inflate costs across the system, from wholesale and capacity market prices to the price of fuel, even if they build their own power and assume all costs.

name: American Energy
title: Advocates, regulators both call for reforms at power grid operator PJM - Maryland Matters
authors: Mayah Nachman, Christine Condon, Peter Hall
description:
As federal energy officials met Thursday for a daylong conference on PJM Interconnection, Maryland legislators and advocates rallied outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to express concerns about the multistate grid operator.
Inside the packed conference, FERC officials appeared sympathetic to the need for change at PJM, the nation’s largest regional power grid operator, calling for improved transparency, faster decision-making and affordability for customers.
Consumer advocates from PJM states are ex officio members with voting rights on certain committees.
But otherwise, state leaders have no formal role, though they can participate in stakeholder processes and at the Organization of PJM States, or OPSI.
“Within individual states, PJM may hear from governors, utility commissioners, legislators, consumer advocates and other public officials who each hold diverging views.
text:
As federal energy officials met Thursday for a daylong conference on PJM Interconnection, Maryland legislators and advocates rallied outside the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to express concerns about the multistate grid operator.

“PJM has lost sight of who its customers are,” said Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery).

“Every decision they make affects the 67 million ratepayers, yet PJM’s governance is primarily accountable to its market participants, those who have a financial stake in the outcome, not the people who are paying those residential bills,” she told a small crowd outside FERC headquarters.

Inside the packed conference, FERC officials appeared sympathetic to the need for change at PJM, the nation’s largest regional power grid operator, calling for improved transparency, faster decision-making and affordability for customers.

“Frustrations are mounting,” said commission Chair Laura Swett. “Put plainly, market participants have lost confidence in PJM’s decision-making abilities.”

FERC put on the conference in response to growing frustrations over PJM’s governing structure, which lawmakers and advocates say gives unfair voting power to companies, including utilities, that have a financial stake in the outcomes of its decisions.

Maryland lawmakers, and Gov. Wes Moore (D), have been among those pushing for state officials to have a greater say at PJM, as their constituents grapple with ever-increasing utility bills. PJM, the nation’s largest electricity grid, includes all or part of 13 states and the District of Columbia.

Hester, who is leading a bipartisan, multistate coalition of legislators pushing for reform at PJM, was joined Thursday by Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery), Pennsylvania Rep. Joe Webster (D-Montgomery) and environmental advocates.

Fry Hester submitted a proposal on behalf of the coalition, outlining ways in which PJM should overhaul its governing structure. They call for ensuring PJM prioritizes affordability and reliability, formalizing states’ roles in decision making and strengthening transparency. They also recommend creating ways to speed up decision-making process and strengthening board independence and accountability, including by requiring FERC to evaluate PJM using specific performance markers.

Charkoudian said PJM’s slow decision-making process and governance structure have undermined states.

“When we look at each of these areas where states are trying to move policy forward on reliability, on decarbonization and on affordability, and where PJM has overridden our ability to do that, we have to ask the question of who is calling the shots,” Charkoudian said. “The people calling the shots are the folks who have money to make when each of these solutions do not succeed.”

Both Fry Hester and Charkoudian thanked the FERC for convening the conference, with Fry Hester noting that she heard commissioners express views that aligned with the collaborative’s recommendations.

Many of the concerns stem back to an energy auction that PJM held in 2024, which ended with a record clearing price an astounding 800% higher than a year before. The reason was an imbalance between energy supply and energy demand, caused in part by massive amounts of demand projected to come from data centers. The auction increased Maryland customers’ bills by varying amounts, with BGE customers faring the worst, with a $21 monthly increase in 2025.

After the auction, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) sued PJM, backed by Moore, and a January 2025 settlement established a new price cap for the auction, which has been extended several times. Each subsequent auction has hit the cap, and consumers are estimated to have saved tens of billions. At the auction for 2028 and 2029, held earlier this month, PJM also wound up securing less energy from suppliers than it had hoped, leaving it with slimmer energy reserves should an emergency affect the grid.

PJM Interconnection electricity price hits cap again in latest auction

Critics have long complained about PJM’s clogged interconnection queue that keeps new projects from connecting to the grid expeditiously. PJM’s procedures were built for a time when a smaller number of large power plants were coming online. These days, with renewable energy projects like solar, wind and battery storage facilities, a much larger quantity of small projects want to come online.

PJM is governed by a board of managers with nine voting members and the PJM CEO, currently David E. Mills. The members must have expertise in various areas, including corporate leadership and transmission systems, but they cannot have any relationship with or financial stake in a member company.

PJM’s more than 1,000 members include transmission owners, generation owners, electricity distributors and others. Consumer advocates from PJM states are ex officio members with voting rights on certain committees. But otherwise, state leaders have no formal role, though they can participate in stakeholder processes and at the Organization of PJM States, or OPSI.

In a comment document prepared by PJM officials for Thursday’s FERC conference, the grid operator notes that when PJM formed, the states chose not to be members, “so as to not be placed in a position to vote or otherwise opine on matters that may subsequently come before them in their role as state commissioners.”

“More recently, the energy politics in each of the PJM states has become more complex,” reads the document. “Within individual states, PJM may hear from governors, utility commissioners, legislators, consumer advocates and other public officials who each hold diverging views. The range of diverse voices speaking for each of the states can make it difficult for PJM to determine how best to incorporate any given state’s view into its decision-making.”

PJM said it has shown “great deference” to the states, including by agreeing to the settlement establishing a price cap for its auctions.

“PJM is open to discussions around how PJM can enhance opportunities for state participation and better define roles and responsibilities,” the document reads. “But such proposals should be paired with an appropriate level of responsibility and accountability based upon our states’ very important role – especially in maintaining resource adequacy for the region.”

name: EVs
title: NEVs' coming of age-- Beijing Review
description:
The end of the exemption is a coming of age for China's new-energy vehicle (NEV) industry, as it transitions from policy-protected infancy to the arena of market competition.
In February 2015, China exempted lithium-ion batteries from the consumption tax in order to support its nascent battery industry and associated industries such as NEVs.
More than a decade later, China has become the world's largest producer and consumer of lithium-ion batteries and NEVs, which include battery electric vehicles, plug-in hybrid vehicles and fuel-cell vehicles.
The decision to levy a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries addresses both the need for the industry's sustainable growth and a range of broader considerations.
This may incentivise more automakers to extend their business upstream into the lithium-ion battery sector, accelerating the integration of the NEV industry.
text:
The Ministry of Finance, the General Administration of Customs and the State Taxation Administration have announced the end of a decade-long tax exemption on lithium-ion batteries. The agencies will introduce a 2-percent consumption tax on the batteries on September 1 and will increase it to 4 percent on September 1 next year. The end of the exemption is a coming of age for China's new-energy vehicle (NEV) industry, as it transitions from policy-protected infancy to the arena of market competition.

In February 2015, China exempted lithium-ion batteries from the consumption tax in order to support its nascent battery industry and associated industries such as NEVs. More than a decade later, China has become the world's largest producer and consumer of lithium-ion batteries and NEVs, which include battery electric vehicles, plug-in hybrid vehicles and fuel-cell vehicles.

The decision to levy a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries addresses both the need for the industry's sustainable growth and a range of broader considerations.

The new tax is a step toward equal taxation for gasoline and electric vehicles, which is currently advocated by the market. For a long time, gasoline-powered vehicles have borne taxes such as a refined oil consumption tax as well as a vehicle and vessel tax. The former is included in the price of gasoline to support road maintenance costs. The latter is paid annually by vehicle and vessel owners and, as an incentive, currently does not apply to NEVs. However, exemptions on certain types of NEVs will be canceled as of January 1, 2027.

As NEV sales surpassed 50 percent of China's new car sales in 2025, the NEV industry is now no longer a "seedling" that requires special protection, but rather needs to assume the same responsibility for road maintenance as gasoline vehicles do. Maintaining the current asymmetrical tax burden on gasoline and electric vehicles would distort market competition. Additionally, within China's lithium-ion battery manufacturing industry, profits grew 48.5 percent year on year in 2025, a clear sign it has moved beyond the initial startup phase that required financial support.

Another motivation is curbing excessive competition within the industry. Over the past few years, too many players have entered the industry, resulting in a surplus of low-end production capacity. Levying a consumption tax of 2-4 percent will eliminate low-end production capacity that relies heavily on tax exemptions and make development healthier and more sustainable.

Based on the current average price of lithium iron phosphate cells, a type of lithium-ion batteries widely used in electric vehicles, a 2-percent tax rate will increase NEV production costs by about 400-600 yuan ($59-88) per unit, while a 4-percent tax rate will increase costs by around 1,300 yuan ($191). Such an increase accounts for less than 1 percent of the total vehicle price, far lower than the impact of lithium-ion battery price fluctuations in the past.

However, the long-term impact of the new tax cannot be ignored. According to the policy, lithium-ion batteries that are produced and used by the same entity are exempt from tax. This gives automakers such as BYD, which use self-produced batteries, a greater cost advantage compared to other automakers that purchase batteries externally. This may incentivise more automakers to extend their business upstream into the lithium-ion battery sector, accelerating the integration of the NEV industry.

Since the consumption tax applies only to lithium-ion batteries produced and sold within China, the policy may prompt some Chinese battery producers to build overseas production capacity, reshaping the geographical distribution of the global lithium-ion battery supply chain. Should this happen in the future, it is unlikely to alter China's dominant position in the global supply of lithium batteries.
