name: Clean Energy
title: A Market-Based Approach to Scaling Clean Cooking in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)
description:
Launched in February 2026, FOREST’s Results-Based Financing (RBF) mechanism is mobilizing private sector companies across the full value chain, from manufacturing and distribution to after-sales service and sustained usage of clean cookstoves.
The first phase is already on track to deliver over 110,000 cookstoves this year.
The program’s objective is to equip 500,000 households – or a total of 2.5 million people – with clean cooking solutions, with a target of 25% of recipients being female-headed households.
More affordable energy for households: Households spend less on energy when stoves burn fuel more efficiently.
Together, these efforts illustrate how global expertise, national leadership, and innovative financing can come together to accelerate clean‑cooking access and deliver lasting development impact.
text:
In a modest workshop in Kinshasa, Florence Kavire is building a business that is changing how families cook. As CEO of Yawe Nissi, one of a growing number of local enterprises partnering with the World Bank's Forest and Savanna Restoration Investment Program (FOREST), she is part of an ambitious effort to put clean cookstoves in the hands of 500,000 households across the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) — delivering cleaner air, lower energy bills, new jobs, and relief for the country's beleaguered forests, all at once.

Backed by $20 million co‑financed by the International Development Association (IDA) and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP), the FOREST Program spearheads a major expansion of clean cooking access in the DRC, contributing to the country’s Mission 300 commitment of reaching 40 million people with clean cooking by 2030. FOREST builds on the foundation laid by the other programs, notably the World Bank’s Improved Forested Landscape Management Project (IFLMP), which delivered more than 80,000 clean cookstoves across targeted communities. Drawing on operational lessons, the program is focusing on market-based approaches that can scale sustainably and reach more households.

Launched in February 2026, FOREST’s Results-Based Financing (RBF) mechanism is mobilizing private sector companies across the full value chain, from manufacturing and distribution to after-sales service and sustained usage of clean cookstoves. The first phase is already on track to deliver over 110,000 cookstoves this year. This effort will generate wide-ranging co-benefits including job creation, improved industry capacity and efficiency, reduced deforestation, improved health, and better access to energy. Phase II is underway, aiming for sales of 390,000 additional units. The program’s objective is to equip 500,000 households – or a total of 2.5 million people – with clean cooking solutions, with a target of 25% of recipients being female-headed households.

Under the RBF mechanism, companies are paid for verified results – the number of cookstoves sold to households – rather than for inputs or activities. This directly aligns financing with measurable outcomes, incentivizes performance and innovation, and helps de-risk investments for local enterprises. It also encourages competition on quality, service, and affordability.

Four Wins for People, Planet, and Prosperity

By coupling RBF with local private sector capacity and complementary investments in sustainable wood energy, FOREST is advancing a model that delivers fourfold wins:

Better health: More efficient cookstoves reduce indoor air pollution – a leading environmental health risks linked to an estimated 2.9 million premature deaths globally every year. Cleaner combustion means less exposure to smoke for women and children, who are most often responsible for cooking and fuel collection in the DRC.

Reduced emissions from deforestation: Improved cookstoves reduce charcoal and fuelwood consumption. In the DRC, this complements FOREST’s investments in 120,000 hectares of agroforestry, to provide a sustainable alternative source of wood energy and help ease pressure on primary rainforests.

More affordable energy for households: Households spend less on energy when stoves burn fuel more efficiently. Lower charcoal consumption translates into direct cost savings, freeing up resources for other essential needs.

Job creation: FOREST is partnering with local enterprises across the full value chain, from manufacturing and distribution to after-sales service, to build long-term market capacity for clean cooking solutions. As of today, 295 new jobs have been generated by supported clean cooking operators, with a target of 2,000 full-time equivalent jobs by 2030 – at least 10% for women. The program also supports a Kinshasa-based lab to strengthen stove quality testing and industry standards.

Drawing on Global Knowledge, Building Local Capacity

With financing and technical support from ESMAP, the DRC draws on a global reservoir of experience in clean cooking, leveraging lessons learned from diverse country contexts. Building on this global knowledge base, the DRC is strengthening the foundations for a market capable of delivering cleaner, safer, and more affordable cooking solutions at scale.

During a recent visit to the country, Michelle Hallack, Coordinator of ESMAP’s Clean Cooking Fund, joined the World Bank team, government counterparts and key stakeholders to take stock of progress and identify next steps. Discussions focused on strengthening cookstove testing and standards to ensure quality and consumer safety, as well as on progressively refining the RBF mechanism. As markets evolve, the RBF framework can be further adapted to different technologies and market segments, creating a pathway toward more outcome‑based financing to support the country’s Energy Compact targets.

The dialogue also highlighted emerging opportunities, including the potential role of carbon finance, synergies with new forest‑related funds, and stronger integration with the health system, particularly through awareness‑raising campaigns and capacity building. Together, these efforts illustrate how global expertise, national leadership, and innovative financing can come together to accelerate clean‑cooking access and deliver lasting development impact.

Dive Brief:

California’s Cap-and-Invest program — a carbon-pricing mechanism that places a firm cap on major sources of greenhouse gas emissions throughout the state — has generated $36.2 billion for climate investments since its inception in 2013, according to a new report from the California Air Resources Board.

CARB, the agency tasked with managing the program and implementing California’s climate laws, noted in the report that $15.5 billion from this figure has already been deployed across 122 programs to back over 600,000 projects that aim to deliver clean air, energy efficiency, affordability and emissions reductions.

The report, released to the state legislature on Monday, also noted that 76% of the funding deployed specifically targets disadvantaged and low-income communities and households.

Dive Insight:

Covered entities, which include major polluters like power plants and oil refineries, are required to surrender a tradeable permit for every metric ton of carbon they emit.

The program was revised earlier this year with the aim of bringing statewide emissions down to meet California’s target of a 40% reduction in emissions by 2030, compared to 1990 levels.

The Cap-and-Invest program also drove emission reductions worth 130.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, according to the report. CARB said this would help bring California closer to achieving its climate and air quality goals.

CARB’s report also noted that the program delivered around $44.4 billion in cost savings from decreased fuel consumption, lower transit expenses and reduced household energy bills.

text:
Paqtnkek, Nova Scotia, July 24, 2026 — Ten Mi’kmaw communities in Nova Scotia are generating their own renewable energy after an investment of more than $4.8 million from the federal government and the communities.

The project, which is now complete, included the installation of net metered solar panels. Net metering allows the communities to generate their own electricity and supply it to the electrical utility. As a result, they only pay the “net” amount of electricity, which is the difference between what their solar systems produce versus the amount of electricity that they actually consume from the grid.

Each community will reduce their energy costs and carbon footprint while creating employment opportunities in the renewable energy sector and giving the Mi’kmaw more control over their energy and environmental future.

Ulnooweg Development Group, a not-for-profit organization that supports Indigenous businesses in Atlantic Canada, managed the funding agreement on behalf of the ten participating First Nations communities: Acadia, Annapolis Valley, Eskasoni, Glooscap, Millbrook, Paqtnkek, Pictou Landing, Potlotek, Wagmatcook, and Waycobah.

Two majority Indigenous owned renewable energy construction companies, Bayside Renewables and Eskasoni Renewables, successfully installed all of the solar systems across the ten communities, building capacity for future renewable energy projects.

text:
This Week in Cleantech is a weekly podcast covering the most impactful stories in clean energy and climate featuring Paul Gerke of Factor This and Tigercomm’s Mike Casey.

This week’s episode features special guest Alexa St. John from The Associated Press, who discusses how automakers are increasingly turning their EVs and hybrids into home backup power sources as EV sales growth slows.

This week’s “Cleantecher of the Week” is Cora Stryker, co-founder of Bright Saver. The nonprofit just started selling zero-markup, plug-in balcony solar kits, starting at about $300, with shipping to 47 states kicking off in August. Cora said that nonprofits are often willing to stomach financial losses in the near term, because its mission is to get solar into the hands of more people, so they can lower their energy bills and carbon pollution. Congratulations, Cora!

1. Data Center Troubles Stoke Industry’s Fear of Coming Distress — Bloomberg

A new survey from consulting for AlixPartners finds the data center industry bracing for a wave of financial distress. In a poll of more than 400 respondents, 68% said they expect distressed situations in the industry to increase over the next 12 to 18 months, up from 66% in 2025. AlixPartners says it’s not one bad input causing the pessimism. It’s rising energy costs, thin cash flow, and falling compute prices all hitting the balance sheet at the same time. Labor shortages and equipment logjams are compounding the problem, with skilled trades like electricians and plumbers especially hard to find.

Read here.

2. Why States Are Making It Harder to Save Money With Solar Panels — The New York Times

More than a third of U.S. states have changed the rules over the last decade to let utilities pay homeowners less for the solar energy they send back to the grid. Under old-school net metering, homeowners get credited at the same retail rate they pay for power, often 10 to 30-plus cents per kilowatt-hour. Under the newer “net billing” model, utilities buy that extra power back at just 2 to 10 cents.

Arkansas made that switch in 2024, and it cut roughly $500 a year off the savings for a typical solar household, even though homeowners who already had panels were grandfathered in. Utilities argue the shift is fair since solar households still rely on the same poles and wires as everyone else, but pay less for grid upkeep.

Read here.

3. The Key to Solar and Wind Power Is Battery Storage, and China Is Dominating — The Wall Street Journal

Five years ago, China’s grid-scale battery storage was under 4 gigawatts. Today it’s around 155 gigawatts, and Beijing is targeting 300 by 2030. That buildout is what lets China lean so hard into solar and wind, which now make up 22% of the country’s power mix. Storage banks the extra sun and wind for when the grid actually needs it.

Chinese companies aren’t just building at home. The world’s top 10 storage battery-cell makers are all Chinese, and together they hold 90% of the global market. And even Tesla’s Megapack business runs through this supply chain. Its Shanghai plant sources cells from CATL for markets outside the U.S.

Read here.

4. State legislatures are getting better at clean-energy permitting policy — Canary Media

A new tally from the Siting Solutions Project looked at more than 200 state bills across 40-plus states this year, and the picture is a lot better than 2025’s wave of restrictive siting laws. Out of 86 bills that would’ve made it harder to permit solar, wind, and battery projects, only one became law: a scaled-back Utah measure limiting tax credits for solar on certain farmland. Last year, 10 restrictive bills passed across six states.

AI-driven demand growth plus an affordability crunch means legislators — even in red states — are looking for the fastest, cheapest way to add power to the grid, and that’s solar, wind, and batteries. Broad coalitions of developers, industry groups, and even agriculture and labor interests have been showing up to kill restrictive bills.

Read here.

5. Need backup power? Automakers want you to look no further than their vehicles in your driveway — Associated Press

Automakers like Ford, Kia/Wallbox, Tesla, and GM are increasingly turning their EVs and hybrids into home backup power sources, letting drivers plug vehicles into their houses to keep the lights on during outages. Ford’s newest option lets F-150 PowerBoost hybrid and Lightning owners connect via an adapter and cable straight to their electric meter, powering select circuits for two to five days depending on the model and usage, at an installation cost starting around $1,100 versus thousands for a standby generator.

This push comes as EV sales growth has slowed (down 23.8% year-over-year in the first half of 2026) and grid demand keeps rising, giving automakers a new business angle for their EV investments beyond car sales. Challenges remain, including required safety certification, utility approval for interconnection (which can take years), and the fact that owners need to actively manage a new power source in their home, but industry experts expect vehicle-to-home and vehicle-to-grid capability to keep growing in popularity.

Read here.

text:
Today, the Justice Department, on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the Arkansas Department of Energy & Environment, Division of Environmental Quality (ADEQ) lodged a proposed settlement with Domtar A.W. LLC resolving alleged Clean Air Act and Arkansas Water and Air Pollution Control Act violations involving the company’s kraft pulp and paper facility in Ashdown, Arkansas.

Under the proposed consent decree, Domtar will pay a $1.5 million civil penalty, divided between the United States and the state of Arkansas. In addition, the company will implement projects to address excess emissions from its operations and correct its inadequate inspection and monitoring practices. The projects include installing the proper pollution controls on Domtar’s brown stock washer, updating leak detection and repair procedures to ensure compliance with the regulations, increasing the frequency of monitoring for leaks, and conducting performance testing on the boilers. The estimated cost to complete the required injunctive relief and bring operations into compliance is at least $2.6 million.

“Today’s settlement demonstrates the Justice Department’s commitment to protecting public health and the environment,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson of the Justice Department’s Energy and Natural Resources Division (ENRD). “Domtar is moving in the right direction to resolve its Clean Air Act violations by committing to properly control pollution and monitor for leaks and substandard facility performance.”

“This settlement ensures that Domtar will take the necessary precautions to maintain and control its facility’s pollution controls among other corrective actions,” said Administrator Scott Mason of EPA Region 6. “I would like to thank the DOJ and ADEQ for their coordination on this matter and we appreciate Domtar’s cooperation in adhering to environmental laws.”

This settlement resolves Domtar’s failure to follow federal and state requirements to capture and control air emissions from its brown stock washer. A brown stock washer is used in the pulp and paper industry to separate and wash the waste liquid from pulp fibers. The complaint filed in the case alleges that Domtar did not install the appropriate pollution controls (required under the Clean Air Act’s New Source Performance Standards and the National Emissions Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants) on its brown stock washer. Without the proper controls, the brown stock washer can leak hydrogen sulfide into the air. Hydrogen sulfide has a strong rotten egg smell and is harmful to human health.

The complaint also alleges that Domtar did not follow mandatory inspection and monitoring requirements. The complaint alleges that, in one instance, Domtar failed to inspect for 53 days and failed to detect a leaking valve emitting uncontrolled and illegal amounts of pollutants. Domtar also did not conduct adequate performance testing for two of its boilers. Without proper monitoring and performance testing, the extent of the excess hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) that Domtar emitted into the air is unknown. The HAPs include volatile organic compounds (VOCs), methanol, carbon monoxide, and chlorinated compounds, including chlorine dioxide and hydrochloric acid.

Under the settlement, Domtar is taking the necessary steps to ensure that its systems control pollutants from the brown stock washer. The settlement also requires a third-party to review and revise the leak detection and repair plan to ensure Domtar’s compliance with environmental regulations. These actions will significantly reduce harmful emissions from the company’s operations.

Domtar is also undertaking two emission reduction projects to mitigate the environmental and public health harm attributable to its violations. First, Domtar will install capping valves to help prevent VOC and HAP emissions leaks. Domtar will also update its biological wastewater treatment system to capture HAPs and VOCs before they are emitted to the air.

Domtar A.W. LLC is limited liability company registered in Delaware and a wholly owned subsidiary of Domtar Corporation. Domtar is a manufacturer of diversified forest products, which includes production of pulp, paper, packaging, and tissue. Domtar describes its Ashdown Mill as one of the largest fluff pulp production facilities in the world.

The consent decree was filed with the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Arkansas and is subject to a 30-day comment period. The complaint and the proposed consent decree are available at www.justice.gov/enrd/consent-decrees.

The EPA and Arkansas Department of Energy & Environment, Division of Environmental Quality, investigated this matter.

Attorneys with ENRD’s Environmental Enforcement Section are handling this matter.

text:
The agreement marks an expansion of Fulcrum Point Holdings’ energy partnerships to include geothermal development alongside its ongoing work in nuclear energy, advanced manufacturing, and workforce development. Fulcrum Point and Rodatherm will initially focus on planning and developing a flagship geothermal project in the Brigham City region, with the potential for a phased development of up to 200 megawatts of generating capacity.

“Utah’s growing energy needs will require multiple sources of reliable and locally produced power,” said Chris Hayter, President of Fulcrum Point Holdings and Co-Founder of Hi Tech Solutions. “This collaboration expands our energy partnerships into geothermal and brings another important technology into the state’s energy ecosystem, which supports Governor Cox’s Operation Gigawatt initiative. By combining Rodatherm’s geothermal expertise with HTS’s engineering, operations, maintenance and workforce capabilities, we can help develop projects that create jobs, strengthen communities and deliver dependable energy for Utah.”

“Utah is fortunate to have a diverse portfolio of energy resources, including significant geothermal potential,” said Joel Ferry, Utah Director of the Department of Natural Resources. “Partnerships like this can help responsibly develop those resources while supporting reliable energy and economic opportunity for communities across the state.”

Rodatherm is a geothermal developer, owner and operator whose proprietary Waterless Geothermal Systems™ technology is designed to support baseload and dispatchable electrical power generation, energy resiliency systems, as well as district heating and cooling systems. The company is pursuing projects throughout the Western United States, especially in Utah and Idaho.

“This collaboration represents a transformational opportunity for Box Elder County and the State of Utah,” said Curtis Cook, President and CEO of Rodatherm Energy Corporation. “By combining Rodatherm’s patented Waterless Geothermal Systems™ technology and Fulcrum’s integrated development platform, we can deliver energy security that supports Utah’s long-term economic growth. ”

Under the agreement, Fulcrum Point and Rodatherm intend to collaboratively lead project development, strategic planning, financing, government and community engagement, and long-term operational planning. Hi Tech Solutions would support plant operations, maintenance and technical services, and help develop the skilled workforce necessary to support the projects. Rodatherm will lead the development of the geothermal resource including project design, permitting, technology deployment and geothermal operations planning.

The companies intend to begin with the commercial deployment of an initial 10-megawatt capacity development in the Brigham City area, with construction currently targeted to begin in late first quarter 2027. They also plan to negotiate a broader strategic development alliance supporting future projects throughout the Mountain West. The companies will continue to engage local leaders, stakeholders, and community members throughout each stage of the evaluation and development process for feedback and review.

text:
OKLAHOMA CITY -

The EPA has changed the regulations regarding diesel exhaust fluid (DEF) previously enacted by the Biden administration.

In a recent move by the EPA, those regulations were dangerous due to engine slowdowns caused by deratements.

EPA Region 6 Administrator Scott Mason, who represents Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas and 66 Tribal Nations, spoke with News 9 about how Oklahoma influenced the new regulations and what Americans can expect under the new rules.

“This is really exciting for anybody who owns a diesel vehicle. And we’ve heard big conversation started last about a year ago in western Oklahoma. And that was really one of the catalysts to drive this national change,” Mason said.

Can you explain the change in DEF regulations?

Mason: Over the last year, Administrator Lee Zeldin has heard this in his visit to all 50 states. President Trump has heard about this. We have leaned in and started working on this. The issue is with farmers, ranchers, truck drivers or anyone who has a diesel vehicle, who currently get a deratement if you run low on diesel exhaust fluid (DEF.)

We have now proposed a new rule that the DEF deratement would be a thing of the past. You will still be protecting the environment because DEF would remain, but now you’re not at the whim of your own engine.

Why is it important to change these regulations?

Mason: The stories that we have heard have been that this has crippled farmers who are stranded in the field because they get an automatic deratement, and their tractor may slow to a crawl, or truckers who are driving on I-40 or I-35 or any interstate system in Oklahoma or across the country. It hampers the economy because they’re having to take time out of their day to deal with that. Sometimes they’re stranded.

Now, they can simply take that in on their own time and deal with it.

Why is it exciting? Who does it actually benefit?

Mason: It’s exciting because diesel is what runs our economy. And so, I mean, if you think about the commerce that has moved through this state alone, every single day, this is a major improvement for the lives of truckers and for industry, for farmers and ranchers. They can deal with this on their own time, and they’re not at the whim of having to automatically be stranded, stuck in the field, having to deal with this immediately. They can continue their work, and then they can fix it on their own time. And time is money.

Does this eliminate DEF entirely?

Mason: Eliminating DEF entirely would take an act of Congress through the Clean Air Act. We are taking this as far as the law will allow, and this EPA is leaning in on the best reading of the law, and we will follow the law to the maximum extent, but when we talk about DEF, we are doing as much as we possibly can to improve the lives of farmers, ranchers, truck drivers, anyone with a diesel-powered vehicle. The president is all in on this, Administrator Zeldin, and we are delivering for the American people.

How are new and existing vehicles affected?

Mason: The elimination of deratement is for new vehicles, on- and off-road engines going forward. As far as existing vehicles, we’ve also announced right to repair and freedom to fix. So you can now fix that; you can take that into your own local auto shop that you may know the local person there rather than having to deal with it at the manufacturer. Or if you know how to fix it, you can fix it.

Can people give feedback on these changes?

Mason: Currently, we’re in a 45-day comment period, so we invite anyone, any member of the public to comment, give us your feedback, your thoughts, your concerns, just your ideas of how you think we could do better with doing away with DEF or deratements.

Comment now. We will review every one of those. If modifications need to be made at the end of the 45-day comment period, we will do that. But going forward in the future, DEF deratements will be a thing of the past under our proposed new rule.

———

Comments can be submitted at epa.gov or regulations.gov.

text:
A South Carolina federal judge this week ordered the Environmental Protection Agency to resume distributing funds designed to address environmental and health challenges in underserved communities.

In June, U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel voided the Trump administration’s termination of the $2.8 billion Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program. But the court ruling did not explicitly require the Environmental Protection Agency to resume distributing the block grants.

Although Gergel ruled that the government’s internal actions terminating the grants were “unlawful,” he declined to order the EPA to immediately restart the program, saying such a move would be “impractical.”

Last month, emails between the EPA and the Southern Environmental Law Center, which filed the lawsuit in partnership with the Public Rights Project, showed that government officials believed that no “specific agency action is required to comply” with Gergel’s ruling.

After reviewing additional court filings from both sides, Gergel confirmed this week that the EPA must resume distributing the grant funds. He rejected the Trump administration’s argument that his decision “required no further agency action.”

In his latest order, Gergel wrote that the Trump administration’s interpretation of the initial ruling relied on an interpretation of the facts the court had already “specifically rejected.”

“The court made it clear that EPA has to follow the law, not keep making the same arguments the court has already rejected,” Toby Merrill, the litigation director for Public Rights Project, said in an email. “When federal agencies ignore court orders, communities pay the price.”

Gergel ordered that the agency “must comply with its statutory obligations to administer the [Environmental and Climate Justice] Program” through the end of September, when the grants were originally scheduled to expire under President Joe Biden.

Since the latest order was issued, Kym Meyer, the Southern Environmental Law Center’s litigation director, said her organization “hasn’t heard” from the EPA.

The Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program, created under the Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act, was designed to help communities address problems like air pollution and extreme heat and bolster local infrastructure, according to federal budget documents.

At the start of his current term, President Donald Trump issued executive orders that put the disbursement of Inflation Reduction Act funds on hold and directed agencies to eliminate environmental justice offices and positions, to the maximum extent allowed by law. An EPA official told the court that he decided to terminate the program in February 2025 because of “policy reasons,” court documents show.

One $500,000 grant was intended to help CleanAIRE NC, a North Carolina-based nonprofit, install air quality monitors throughout Mecklenburg County, which includes Charlotte. Residents there face health impacts from air pollution because of their proximity to major highways and industrial activity.

“While the EPA has tried to evade the court’s order, families in north Mecklenburg were left waiting for basic transparency about the air they breathe,” said Jeffrey Robbins, the executive director of CleanAIRE NC, in an email. “We are ready to put these critical air monitoring resources to work in north Mecklenburg the moment the agency complies.”

In response to questions from Inside Climate News, a spokesperson for the EPA said in an email that the agency “is reviewing the decision and working to comply with the court’s order.”

description:
President Donald Trump announced a non-binding pledge by U.S. power producers and data centers on Thursday to fund or build energy infrastructure that would meet massive AI-related power needs while shielding consumers from high electricity costs.
But data centers’ demands on overloaded transmission lines, compounded by the power sector’s labor shortages and plant retirements, have made rising energy costs a volatile issue for voters going into November’s midterm elections.

text:
President Donald Trump announced a non-binding pledge by U.S. power producers and data centers on Thursday to fund or build energy infrastructure that would meet massive AI-related power needs while shielding consumers from high electricity costs.

Consumer advocacy groups and other administration critics, however, dismissed the pledge as an empty promise to consumers as Trump tries to balance his support for power-guzzling data centers against public anger over rising utility bills.

Trump has been pushing an aggressive build-out of AI-related infrastructure, as part of an economic agenda that includes winning the AI race against China.

But data centers’ demands on overloaded transmission lines, compounded by the power sector’s labor shortages and plant retirements, have made rising energy costs a volatile issue for voters going into November’s midterm elections.

“Under this groundbreaking plan, America’s largest tech companies have formally committed to fund or build all energy infrastructure required to meet the demand they are placing on the grid,” Trump said at an Environmental Protection Agency event attended by Republican governors, power sector CEOs and data center developers.

“So they’re going to be funding all of those electric needs, and we’re giving them the right to build their own power plants.”

Average annual residential electricity prices are predicted to rise by 5.1% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, before inflation, the Energy Information Administration said.

Community meetings in many states have lasted into the wee hours as residents oppose development of data centers they view as noisy, bad for the environment and a factor in rising electric bills.

Trump’s take was more positive.

“You have communities that really want the data centers, and frankly those are the smart communities,” he said.

Critics, meanwhile, have questioned whether the voluntary pledge will prevent higher bills as AI power demand accelerates. Jesse Lee, senior adviser at advocacy group Climate Power, criticized the pledge’s lack of enforcement triggers, calling it a “pinky promise.”

“Instead of allowing affordable, scalable clean energy onto the grid, Trump has actively pressured tech companies to power their data centers with fossil fuels that will increase utility costs and expose Americans to toxic pollutants,” Lee said.

Josh Levi, president of the Data Center Coalition, defended the industry, which he said powers essential services such as telehealth appointments, digital classrooms, secure banking systems and air traffic control networks.

Republican governors from Georgia, Idaho, Louisiana and Nebraska attended Thursday’s event, along with chief executives Drew Marsh of Entergy Corp and Chris Womack of Southern Co. Marsh and Womack are among a group of CEOs at the 15 largest U.S. power companies sitting on nearly $1 billion in ‌stock-based pay, according to a Reuters analysis. That value is poised to keep rising as firms invest to fix the U.S. electrical grid.

At the center of the political battle over data centers is PJM Interconnection, the largest U.S. grid operator.

“PJM is the face of a national problem,” according to analysts at Siebert Williams Shank, who cited its struggle to withstand unprecedented power consumption, along with power plant retirements, transmission line congestion and construction bottlenecks.

“AI data centers did not create every challenge facing electric systems, but they have amplified nearly all of them.”

PJM is battling escalating costs on several fronts as it manages the flow of electricity for 67 million people from Washington, D.C., to Chicago.

In PJM’s latest capacity-market auction, which secures power from generating sources for peak demand times, data centers accounted for $6.3 billion of capacity-market charges, or nearly 40% of the total. Those charges ultimately show up in customers’ monthly bills.

(Reporting By Tim McLaughlin in Boston, Jacob Bogage in Washington and Jarrett Renshaw; Editing by Timothy Gardner and Edmund Klamann)

title: Kept in the dark: How Louisiana weakened community air monitoring as industry pushed back
description:
As reported by Verite News, ten of the state’s heaviest air-polluting facilities operate without a single public air monitor within five miles.
No public monitors track ammonia, even though CF Industries’ Donaldsonville plant reported emitting more than 7 million pounds of it in 2024.
“If large emissions from these facilities are happening far away from the air monitors, they’re often going to go unnoticed,” DeCarlo told Floodlight.
Since 2020, Louisiana has lost four air monitoring stations, and spending by the LDEQ division that oversees air monitoring fell nearly 15% between 2020 and 2026, a drop of more than one-third when adjusted for inflation, according to the investigation.
The two closest public monitors, each about five miles away, measure only lead and ozone.
text:
In Louisiana’s petrochemical belt, some of the people most exposed to toxic air have the least information about what they are breathing. A new investigation by the nonprofit newsroom Floodlight, produced in partnership with The Guardian and with contributions from the Louisiana Illuminator, finds that the state’s public air monitors are frequently located miles from major industrial polluters and fail to test for some of the most dangerous chemicals released along the corridor between Baton Rouge and New Orleans.

That stretch of roughly 85 miles, widely known as “Cancer Alley,” is home to dozens of refineries and chemical plants and to many predominantly Black communities. According to the reporting, cancer rates from toxic air pollution there are among the highest in the country, yet residents living near heavy industry often have no reliable way to learn what is in the air around their homes.

What the analysis found

Floodlight identified Louisiana’s top 25 industrial air polluters using emissions companies self-report to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, then measured each plant’s distance to the nearest public monitor and checked which pollutants those monitors actually track. As reported by Verite News, ten of the state’s heaviest air-polluting facilities operate without a single public air monitor within five miles.

The gaps extend to specific chemicals. Dow Chemical’s plastics factory in Plaquemine, one of Louisiana’s biggest air polluters, releases pollutants including ethylene oxide, a known carcinogen, but the nearest monitoring station is about eight miles away and measures only ozone. No public monitors track ammonia, even though CF Industries’ Donaldsonville plant reported emitting more than 7 million pounds of it in 2024. And the three chemicals researchers concluded account for the large majority of the area’s cancer risk, ethylene oxide, chloroprene and formaldehyde, are not monitored by the state at all.

The chemical findings echo peer-reviewed science. In 2023, atmospheric scientist Peter DeCarlo and other Johns Hopkins University researchers drove a mobile laboratory through the corridor. In 14 of the 15 locations they studied, cancer risks from toxic emissions exceeded EPA figures, in some places by up to 11 times, according to their work later published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. “If large emissions from these facilities are happening far away from the air monitors, they’re often going to go unnoticed,” DeCarlo told Floodlight. “But that doesn’t mean they’re not gonna have an effect on the people who live there.”

A system that misses emergencies

The limits of the network were on display during a fire at Marathon’s Garyville refinery in August 2023. After a naphtha leak was reported to the Coast Guard in the evening, more than six hours passed before the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality began monitoring the air, according to the reporting. The leak ignited the next morning, two nearby schools opened anyway, and residents within two miles were not ordered to evacuate until more than 15 hours after the leak began. A Guardian investigation found at least 29 residents were later treated at area hospitals.

The nearest state monitor measured ozone, not the volatile organic compounds released in the fire, and the plant’s own fenceline monitoring tracked a single chemical, benzene. By contrast, Marathon’s Los Angeles refinery continuously monitors more than 15 pollutants, as California rules require. Wilma Subra, a MacArthur-honored environmental chemist who examined the fire’s emissions, said the state’s network is “not adequate to protect the health of the community living in close proximity to these industrial facilities.”

Adrienne Katner, a Louisiana State University associate professor and former state environmental health scientist, concluded in 2022 that roughly 400 high-emission facilities in Louisiana had no public air monitoring, calling the situation “a public health emergency waiting to occur.” She argues the data gap protects polluters: “The theme is, if you don’t look for it, you won’t find it.”

Fewer monitors, less money

Even as advocates pushed for more coverage, the state moved the other way. Since 2020, Louisiana has lost four air monitoring stations, and spending by the LDEQ division that oversees air monitoring fell nearly 15% between 2020 and 2026, a drop of more than one-third when adjusted for inflation, according to the investigation. The agency operates 35 permanent stations and describes its network as “robust,” but acknowledges it is not designed to monitor pollution in fenceline communities and that “financial and technical constraints limit full monitoring coverage” of toxic pollutants.

Some reductions were deliberate. In 2022, regulators shut down a temporary monitor in New Orleans’ Irish Channel that had recorded elevated particulate matter, even after the EPA later urged the state to make it permanent. Louisiana’s 2022 monitoring plan included a section on “Environmental Justice Considerations” describing monitors in communities such as St. Rose and the Irish Channel; a year later, both the section and the St. Rose monitor were gone. When the EPA pressed the state on environmental justice, LDEQ replied that such considerations were “beyond the scope” of the plan.

Industry’s role in the legislature

For years, former state Sen. Cleo Fields, a Democrat now serving in Congress, filed bills to require major polluters to monitor emissions at their property lines and report the results. Each attempt died. “I got so frustrated because every year this was opposed by industry for no good reason,” Fields told Floodlight, adding that regulators “were working totally in concert with industry.” A more recent effort this year by state Sen. Royce Duplessis also failed.

The Louisiana Chemistry Association, a trade group representing 70 companies operating more than 100 sites statewide, has repeatedly helped defeat such measures. It found an ally in Republican state Sen. Eddie Lambert, who chairs the Senate environmental committee that killed the bills and who has received more than $28,000 in contributions from petrochemical, oil and gas and other polluting industries since 2020. Lambert said neither those donations nor his oil investments influenced his votes: “I don’t take that into consideration at all.”

In 2024, Lambert sponsored the Community Air Monitoring Reliability Act, which bars the use of air pollution data for enforcement unless it comes from EPA-approved monitors, equipment that can cost tens of thousands of dollars, far beyond the means of most community groups. An attorney for the chemistry association acknowledged at a 2024 committee hearing that the group helped draft the bill. A top EPA regional administrator at the time called the measure “inconsistent with federal law,” but the legislature passed it anyway. Association president David Cresson has defended the law, saying it ensures data used for enforcement meets minimum EPA standards and does not stop residents from monitoring for their own information.

The effect on the ground was immediate for Kimbrelle Kyereh, who lives a few hundred feet from chemical storage tanks in St. Rose and began collecting air samples in her yard in 2023. After the law passed, she stopped. “I shut my mouth like they wanted me to,” she said. The strategy has spread: after Louisiana acted, lawmakers in Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia introduced similar bills using industry arguments, and the measures passed in Kentucky and Ohio.

Why the numbers matter

Lambert questioned the need for more public monitors, noting that plants already collect emissions data. “If we already get the information from the plants, why would we want to spend our resources there?” he asked. But under EPA rules, some facilities may report estimates rather than direct measurements, and those estimates can be far off. A 2025 ProPublica investigation found that when the EPA required temporary physical monitors, 97% of the comparisons showed facilities underreporting emissions; at Dow’s Plaquemine facility, measured vinyl chloride was more than 150 times higher than the company’s estimate.

For residents, the uncertainty is a daily fact of life. Tish Taylor lives less than a mile from the Denka Performance Elastomer plant in St. John the Baptist Parish, which suspended neoprene production in 2025 after federal regulators found its chloroprene emissions posed an “unacceptably high” cancer risk. The two closest public monitors, each about five miles away, measure only lead and ozone. When the wind carries something toxic through her garden, Taylor said, all she can do is guess: “I just have to wonder how much.”

text:
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — The African Development Bank (AfDB) has approved a $110 million loan to support the construction of Africa’s first gigafactory in Morocco, backing the continent’s push to build a domestic electric vehicle battery industry.

The loan to Gotion Power Morocco will finance the development of an integrated lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery plant in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra Free Trade Zone, the bank said Friday.

The bank said it also plans to mobilize up to $162.6 million in additional financing from development partners for the project under the New African Financial Architecture for Development initiative, where it is serving as mandated lead arranger.

Morocco's EV sector is booming. The country hosts more than 250 companies that manufacture cars or their components, including Stellantis and Renault, as well as Chinese, Japanese, American and Korean factories.

Across Africa, the use of electric vehicles is surging as soaring prices and fuel shortages compel countries to opt for cleaner and cheaper transport.

Led by China’s Gotion High-Tech Co. Ltd., the Moroccan project will establish the first integrated battery manufacturing plant in Africa, the Middle East and North Africa region. The factory is expected to produce 10 gigawatt-hours of battery cells and packs annually for electric vehicles during its first phase, with plans to expand capacity to 100 GWh.

“ Battery storage is the missing link in Africa’s clean energy transition,” Kevin Kariuki, the bank’s vice president for Power, Energy, Climate and Green Growth, said in a statement.

“A facility of this scale, powered primarily by renewable energy, strengthens the foundations for the large-scale integration of solar and wind power, which our grids increasingly depend on,” he said.

Kariuki said the project would help deliver reliable, low-carbon electricity while creating green jobs and strengthening supply chains needed to support Africa’s energy transition.

The project is also expected to boost Morocco’s industrial competitiveness, according to Achraf Tarsim, the African Development Bank’s country manager for Morocco.

“It will help foster an African industrial ecosystem for batteries and electric vehicles while promoting the local beneficiation of critical minerals essential to the energy transition,” Tarsim said.

The first phase of the project is expected to create more than 600 direct jobs and achieve a local industrial integration rate of 70%, supporting skills development and the growth of domestic manufacturing supply chains.

The investment is expected to strengthen Morocco’s ambitions to become a regional hub for electric mobility and green technology manufacturing.

text:
Two California maritime emissions waivers were sent to Congress giving the Environmental Protection Agency a possible loophole to reclassify regulations covering ocean-going ships at berth and commercial harbor craft. Because the Clean Air Act are rules, the Agency said Congress is allowed to reject newly submitted rules through a joint resolution under the Congressional Review Act.

The Agency claimed that “California’s standards could impose costs on ports, shipping and supply chains,” but “Environmental groups and California regulators dispute that interpretation, maintaining that Clean Air Act waivers have not historically been treated as rules subject to congressional repeal,” Splash Ports reported.

“The federal government’s attack on California’s At Berth and Commercial Harbor Craft waivers is a misuse of the Congressional Review Act (CRA),” Davina Hurt, climate policy director at Pacific Environment, said. “For more than 50 years, Clean Air Act waiver programs have been respected by Republican and Democratic administrations alike. Until now, no administration had attempted to use the Congressional Review Act to overturn these waivers.”

Advocates of the rules said that the 2020 At Berth Regulation “will reduce potential cancer risk for California’s port-side communities by about 60 percent,” according to Pacific Environment. An initial analysis by the California Air Resources Board (CARB)’s determined that the amended regulation will save 230 lives and prevent 73 hospital admissions and 116 emergency room visits statewide and would save $2.31 billion.

“Instead of playing politics with our health, undermining the regulatory certainty businesses rely on, and jeopardizing billions of dollars in public and private investments made under these life-saving rules, Congress should recognize this blatant overreach by the oil and gas industry to continue to put profits over people,” Hurt said. “Communities, workers, businesses and our economy will pay the cost not polluters, if Congress repeals California’s Clean Air waivers.”

text:
Certification of micro-inverters brings plug-in solar closer to being widely available

DENVER – Two companies, Hoymiles and APSystems, recently announced that their micro-inverters for plug-in solar systems were certified as complying with national product safety standards. The certification was done by the nationally recognized testing laboratory, CSA Group. The inaugural safety standard for plug-in solar, UL 3700, was adopted in December of 2025.

Micro-inverters convert energy from solar panels (direct current or DC) into electricity that can be used to power appliances in a home (alternating current or AC).

As of July 2026, no whole-system plug-in solar kit (sold in one box that includes a panel, inverter and plug) has received UL 3700 certification from a nationally recognized testing laboratory.

In response, Johanna Neumann, senior director of the Campaign for 100% Renewable Energy at Environment America Research & Policy Center, released this statement:

“Many Americans would prefer to harness the rays of the sun in their backyard to help power their homes, rather than paying utility companies for power generated by burning fossil fuels many miles away.

“America is now one step closer to a national safety certification for plug-in solar kits. I hope it is a matter of months, not years until Americans can go to a store, buy a solar kit and plug it in at home with the same ease and peace of mind as plugging in a toaster.”

text:
Kentucky cities play a critical role in maintaining the roadways that span the Commonwealth. From the economic impact of commerce to daily travel for work and enjoyment, the municipal function of sustaining the state’s roads is essential to ensuring Kentuckians enjoy a high quality of life.

Electric Vehicles: A Trending Shift on US Roads

A growing share of transportation revenue is generated by the registration and usage of electric vehicles (EVs). The International Energy Agency (IEA), an autonomous inter-governmental agency created by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), reported that sales of EVs in the United States increased by 1.6 million units in 2024, with the sales share growing by more than 10%.

Mobility Global forecasts that US EV sales may reach 40% of total passenger car sales by 2030, with more optimistic outlooks predicting 50%. Leading auto and battery manufacturers are increasing their investment into the EV market, with the goal of producing more battery electric vehicles (BEVs) with the goal of significantly increasing their output by 2030. Toyota in statements regarding its electric vehicle strategy committed to producing 3.5 million units of BEVs by 2030 and began production of its $13.9 million all-battery plant in North Carolina in 2025 [1]. They also announced an investment of $800 million over the next 5 years in its Toyota Kentucky facility to manufacturer its second battery electric vehicle [2]. According to Ford, the manufacturer plans to produce 50% of its global volume in hybrids, extended-range EVs, and electric vehicles by 2030. They will also introduce its first midsize electric truck under its new flexible universal EV platform in 2027 [3].

Federal and state governments are also investing in EV infrastructure. The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, or the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, contained $7.5 billion in new EV funding for charging stations, and made EV charging infrastructure eligible for additional federal funding programs. Kentucky has implemented many incentive programs to encourage economic development in EVs, such as Alternative Fuel Manufacturing Tax Incentives, Alternative Fuel Production Tax Incentives, and EV Charger Grants.

Kentucky has witnessed $13.1 billion in EV investments since 2020, which is highlighted by a $2 billion investment by Ford for a new Universal EV Platform in its Louisville facility, and a $2 billion battery project by AESC in Bowling Green.

The increased investment, production, and consumer demand for EVs demonstrates a growing shift in the type of vehicle that drivers will operate on Kentucky’s roads. As a result, it is imperative that Kentucky cities receive an equitable portion of the state's revenue generated from EVs.

Electric Vehicles in the Commonwealth

In Kentucky, state law defines an electric vehicle, under KRS 138.475(1), as any vehicle with plug-in charging capability, regardless of whether it is powered by an electric motor only or a combination of an internal combustion engine and electric power. Similarly to gas-powered vehicles, EV owners are required to pay an initial registration fee and an annual renewal registration fee.

Under KRS 138.475, Kentucky motorists are required to pay an electric ownership fee. Motorists must pay $120 for electric vehicles and $60 for electric motorcycles. The fee is adjusted on the same schedule as the electric vehicle power taxes under KRS 138.477, except that the adjustment is rounded to the nearest dollar and cannot go below the initial baseline fees of $120 and $60. Under KRS 138.477, the adjustment is based upon comparisons to quarterly changes in the National Highway Construction Cost Index. In 2025, the current electric vehicle ownership fee increased to $126 for electric vehicles and $63 for electric motorcycles.

According to the Office of the State Budget Director, in fiscal year (FY) 2026, Kentucky collected over $3.1 million in electric ownership fees. This was an increase of 0.5% from the previous FY total of $3.0 million. However, the fee has grown substantially since FY 2024, over 114%, when revenues totaled $1.4 million.

The growth in EV ownership and renewal fee revenue coincides with the increased number of registered EVs in the state. According to data from the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, total EV registered vehicles, excluding buses and diesel hybrids, totaled 120,724 vehicles in 2025. This was an increase of approximately 29% from the previous year. Since 2020, the number of registered vehicles has increased by over 81,000, an increase of over 200%. The table below shows the total registered electric vehicles by type from 2020 to 2025.

Kentucky’s Municipal Roads: A Connection Through the Commonwealth

Maintaining Kentucky’s city streets is one of the most critical functions of city government. With 75% of all economic output occurring within Kentucky cities and over 10,000 miles of roadway maintained, ensuring Kentucky cities have safe roadways is essential.

Cities drive Kentucky in a multitude of ways, and maintaining local roadways is crucial for the provision of city services and daily life. For Kentucky to continue to grow for future generations, it is essential that its cities receive an equitable share of the growing revenue from the increased ownership of EVs.

text:
PORTSMOUTH, Va. (WAVY) — Virginia Sen. Mark Warner recently introduced a bill aimed at creating guidelines and transparency when it comes to data centers and their construction.

The Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act was introduced as a massive boom of data center facilities is taking place across the U.S. and Commonwealth.

“We are data centers central, particularly up in Loudoun County and around northern Virginia, kind of where the Internet started,” said Mike Gerel, Virginia science manager for the Chesapeake Bay Foundation. “They have spread and they’re continuing to spread throughout the region.”

According to U.S. Data Center Map, as of July 2026, almost 2,700 data centers are currently operating in the country, with more than 1,000 under construction or are planned to be built.

Warner said many of the facilities have been built and are operating with little to no information disclosed and said his bill would work to create a national baseline of transparency going forward.

“Making sure these data centers don’t add to the consumer’s electric bill, make sure there are appropriate uses of water, and setbacks from neighborhoods,” Warner said. “They ought to be making sure that the backup power is also clean and reliable.”

Warner said data centers would be required to meet these standards as well as disclose water and energy usage among other information in order to receive certain deferral tax benefits.

“All the nondisclosure agreements need to be disclosed so the community can make the judgment,” Warner said. “You should not get this huge federal tax benefit upfront until you meet these standards. So this is a good … federal guideline.”

Geral noted the proposed legislation would help communities across the Commonwealth stay informed and decide the future of data centers in their area.

“We all are using data. It’s part of our lives,” Geral said. “But we have a role in controlling how it’s used in the Commonwealth, in the communities, and how it engages in our life. If we’re transparent about it and we use our existing public processes, we can have a greater degree of control of how the data that we all use is connected and managed in our state and in our communities.”

text:
Environmentalists and construction workers are calling for reforms to make it easier to produce clean energy in Washington state.

Despite its green reputation, the Evergreen State trails every other U.S. state in adding wind and solar power to its electrical grid, according to a 2025 investigation by Oregon Public Broadcasting and ProPublica.

“We’re 50th out of 50,” state Sen. Victoria Hunt (D-Issaquah) said at a forum hosted by the nonprofit PNW Climate Week in July. “We need to do something about this.”

“What we’re most worried about is a cold snap in a low-snowpack year,” Hunt said. “We are looking at rolling brownouts and rolling blackouts. That’s what keeps me up at night.”

Building new transmission lines has been the main holdup for expanding the state’s clean energy supply.

Environmental groups are calling on the Washington Legislature to let transmission lines run in the underused land in highway corridors. The Washington State Department of Transportation has concluded it cannot allow such use of highway rights-of-way without approval from legislators.

“Expanding the options available for siting new transmission is a critical step toward modernizing the grid and ensuring communities and businesses have access to electricity around the clock,” Nicole Pavia with the Clean Air Task Force said in a press release.

Beyond the environmental impact, labor leaders say the bottleneck has left many construction workers jobless.

“The Pacific Northwest was a leader for a long time, and we're definitely in a very deep lull right now,” said Matthew Heppner with the Certified Electrical Workers of Washington.

Heppner said unemployment in his union is about 16%, or three times the statewide average.

“The construction industry is struggling incredibly badly in Washington right now,” Heppner said. “We pushed for building clean energy. We thought we were going to do that.”

But those clean-energy projects foundered without access to transmission lines.

Oregon Public Broadcasting and ProPublica reported that the Bonneville Power Administration, which operates most of the Northwest’s electrical grid, has only added one mile of transmission lines in the past five years.

“So the only things we're really building are data centers, which really sucks right now,” Heppner said.

“BPA has been understaffed and under-resourced, especially with staff buyouts under Trump,” said Casey McLean with the nonprofit Renewable Northwest. “The inter-connection queue is huge.”

With demand for power skyrocketing, the clean-energy bottleneck has meant more climate-altering pollution from power plants that burn gas or coal.

RELATED: Microsoft's climate-warming emissions surge 25%, driven by AI

State law requires that Washington achieve a 100% clean electricity supply by 2040, a tall order made taller by data centers’ rapidly growing energy demands as use of artificial intelligence proliferates.

“Data center load is emerging as the dominant driver of long-term U.S. electricity growth,” the U.S. Energy Information Administration concluded in April in its Annual Energy Outlook 2026.

In March, the state created the Washington Electric Transmission Authority to coordinate, accelerate, and finance the construction of transmission lines. The new agency is expected to start operations in January.

McLean said the Transmission Authority is not a silver bullet.

“A lot of permitting reform is needed,” McLean said. “We have a lot of laws on the books to protect other things.”

Washington state Rep. Alex Ybarra (R-Quincy) said the town of Quincy, population 8,000, has benefited massively from the concentrated buildout of data centers southeast of Wenatchee.

“ I've got a brand-new hospital that opened up six months ago. I've got an aqua center, which is a big swimming pool, opened up four days ago. I've got a brand-new city hall, brand-new police station, a brand-new $100 million high school, the best high school in the state of Washington.”

Other electricity users have not seen their rates rise with the arrival of the energy-guzzling data centers nearby, according to Ybarra. The only downside he’s seen is one he experiences as a driver.

text:
Washington, D.C. (July 24, 2026) — This week, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sent two California Clean Air Act waiver approvals to Congress, seeking to overturn them via the Congressional Review Act. These waivers allow California to protect people living in the state’s densely populated port regions from dangerous pollution emitted by ocean-going vessels at berth and commercial harbor craft.

Following is a statement from Sue Gander, Director, U.S. Transportation, World Resources Institute:

“The federal government’s continued attacks on California’s Clean Air Act waivers are playing politics with public health. Retaining these waivers would dramatically reduce the amount of nitrogen oxides and particulate matter that pollute the air Californians breathe, while also cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

“The very agency created to protect public health is instead endangering it. In the process, it's undermining the regulatory certainty that businesses rely on and jeopardizing billions of dollars in investment in low- and zero-emission berthing and harbor operations.”

text:
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — The African Development Bank (AfDB) has approved a $110 million loan to support the construction of Africa’s first gigafactory in Morocco, backing the continent’s push to build a domestic electric vehicle battery industry.

The loan to Gotion Power Morocco will finance the development of an integrated lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery plant in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra Free Trade Zone, the bank said Friday.

The bank said it also plans to mobilize up to $162.6 million in additional financing from development partners for the project under the New African Financial Architecture for Development initiative, where it is serving as mandated lead arranger.

Morocco’s EV sector is booming. The country hosts more than 250 companies that manufacture cars or their components, including Stellantis and Renault, as well as Chinese, Japanese, American and Korean factories.

Across Africa, the use of electric vehicles is surging as soaring prices and fuel shortages compel countries to opt for cleaner and cheaper transport.

Led by China’s Gotion High-Tech Co. Ltd., the Moroccan project will establish the first integrated battery manufacturing plant in Africa, the Middle East and North Africa region. The factory is expected to produce 10 gigawatt-hours of battery cells and packs annually for electric vehicles during its first phase, with plans to expand capacity to 100 GWh.

“ Battery storage is the missing link in Africa’s clean energy transition,” Kevin Kariuki, the bank’s vice president for Power, Energy, Climate and Green Growth, said in a statement.

“A facility of this scale, powered primarily by renewable energy, strengthens the foundations for the large-scale integration of solar and wind power, which our grids increasingly depend on,” he said.

Kariuki said the project would help deliver reliable, low-carbon electricity while creating green jobs and strengthening supply chains needed to support Africa’s energy transition.

The project is also expected to boost Morocco’s industrial competitiveness, according to Achraf Tarsim, the African Development Bank’s country manager for Morocco.

“It will help foster an African industrial ecosystem for batteries and electric vehicles while promoting the local beneficiation of critical minerals essential to the energy transition,” Tarsim said.

The first phase of the project is expected to create more than 600 direct jobs and achieve a local industrial integration rate of 70%, supporting skills development and the growth of domestic manufacturing supply chains.

The investment is expected to strengthen Morocco’s ambitions to become a regional hub for electric mobility and green technology manufacturing.

text:
Versinetic supplies white-label hardware, software and load-balancing systems to EV charging companies. Now the company has launched a software tool to help EV charger manufacturers’ engineering teams decide when, and how, to migrate from OCPP 1.6 to OCPP 2.1.

“The OCPP Migration Decision Matrix provides a structured framework for evaluating technical, commercial and operational factors, including fleet size, field upgrade capability, customer requirements and product roadmaps,” the company explains.

According to Versinetic, many engineering teams encounter the same three pitfalls when planning protocol migration:

Treating OCPP 2.x as a complete platform rewrite instead of a phased evolution.

Embedding protocol logic throughout charger firmware instead of isolating it within a dedicated software layer, making future upgrades more complex.

Underestimating the interoperability challenges presented by different charging management systems and large installed fleets.

As procurement specifications increasingly reference OCPP 2.x capabilities, manufacturers must decide how and when to introduce those capabilities without disrupting development programs. Versinetic believes manufacturers should focus on adopting the capabilities that deliver genuine commercial and operational value, rather than treating migration as a race to the latest protocol version.

While OCPP 1.6 remains the most widely deployed protocol across existing EV charging infrastructure, OCPP 2.1 introduces enhanced security, a richer device model, improved diagnostics, more advanced smart charging capabilities and support for emerging technologies such as vehicle-to-grid (V2G).

“Supporting OCPP 2.1 doesn’t automatically mean rebuilding your platform,” said Ricardo Silva, Firmware Engineer at Versinetic. “The manufacturers making the fastest progress are focusing on the capabilities their customers actually need while designing their software so OCPP 1.6 and 2.x can coexist during the transition.”

Versinetic recommends a staged migration strategy, keeping proven OCPP 1.6 products stable while introducing OCPP 2.x on new platforms or selected deployments in which the benefits are clear. A modular software architecture, in which protocol logic is separated from core application functionality, enables manufacturers to support multiple protocol versions while reducing future engineering effort.

Silva concluded: “Protocol migration shouldn’t be driven by the latest version number. It should be driven by business priorities, customer requirements and an architecture that allows products to evolve without slowing development.”

title: Energy tax credit audits: What taxpayers should expect | RSM US
description:
Unlike traditional tax credits, many IRA-related incentives involve operational, engineering, environmental and labor compliance considerations that extend beyond standard tax reporting.
Transferable energy tax credits face growing audit risk The transferability rules under section 6418 have fundamentally changed the energy credit marketplace by allowing taxpayers to monetize certain credits through credit transfers.
How Loper Bright could affect energy tax credit disputes Recent developments in administrative law may also impact future energy credit controversy.
Energy tax credit audit readiness Examination readiness may help taxpayers respond more efficiently to IRS inquiries and support credit positions if a claim is reviewed.
Future IRS enforcement trends for energy tax credits The energy credit market is entering a new phase in which controversy risk, audit preparedness and administrative scrutiny are becoming increasingly important.
text:
IRS scrutiny of energy tax credits is increasing

The IRS has publicly emphasized that administration and compliance oversight remain key components of IRA implementation. Recent guidance, pre-filing registration requirements and IRS compliance campaign activity indicate an increased focus on substantiation and eligibility requirements for energy-related tax incentives.

Several factors are contributing to increased controversy risk, including significant dollar amounts associated with transferable and direct pay credits, rapid market growth and participation by new entrants, reliance on evolving administrative guidance, complex technical qualification standards, increased use of third-party studies, certifications and lifecycle modeling, and heightened political and regulatory scrutiny surrounding IRA incentives.

Unlike traditional tax credits, many IRA-related incentives involve operational, engineering, environmental and labor compliance considerations that extend beyond standard tax reporting. As a result, examinations are likely to be extremely fact-intensive and may require taxpayers to maintain documentation and support for factual and technical determinations spanning tax, engineering, environmental and labor compliance matters.

Transferable energy tax credits face growing audit risk

The transferability rules under section 6418 have fundamentally changed the energy credit marketplace by allowing taxpayers to monetize certain credits through credit transfers.

Section 6418 provides that an eligible taxpayer may elect to transfer all or a specified portion of eligible credits to an unrelated transferee. The rules establish detailed procedural and compliance requirements, including pre-filing registration, election reporting requirements and substantiation obligations.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also added restrictions prohibiting transfers of certain energy credits to specified foreign entities for tax years beginning after July 4, 2025.

While transferability has increased liquidity and investment activity, it has also introduced additional IRS controversy risks.

Potential IRS focus areas may include:

Validity of transferred credits

Adequacy of due diligence performed by credit purchasers

Registration compliance

Timing of credit generation and transfer

Excessive credit claims

Basis calculations

Prevailing wage and apprenticeship substantiation

Documentation supporting domestic content or energy community qualification

Although transferred credits generally remain subject to recapture and adjustment rules, market participants continue navigating unresolved questions regarding audit risk allocation between transferors and transferees.

As transfer markets mature, well-defined indemnification provisions and diligence procedures may provide greater clarity around audit exposure and support more efficient transaction execution.

IRS examinations may focus on section 45Z clean fuel credits

Section 45Z clean fuel production credits present particularly significant controversy potential due to the technical and evolving nature of the regime. The IRS is likely to closely scrutinize several aspects of these claims, including issues related to the emissions rate, such as lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions calculations, emissions rate determinations and provisional emissions rate applications.

The IRS is also likely to scrutinize feedstock qualification, book-and-claim frameworks, related-party sales issues, producer registration requirements and substantiation supporting fuel production volumes. In many cases, taxpayers must rely on evolving administrative guidance, technical modeling and external data sources to support credit calculations, creating uncertainty regarding the level of documentation the IRS may ultimately require upon examination.

Additionally, taxpayers operating across multiple regulatory regimes, including Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) requirements, state low-carbon fuel programs and federal tax credit frameworks, may face increased complexity in reconciling operational data and compliance positions.

How Loper Bright could affect energy tax credit disputes

Recent developments in administrative law may also impact future energy credit controversy. Following the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, taxpayers may increasingly challenge Treasury regulations and regulatory guidance governing IRA incentives.

Certain energy credit programs rely heavily on notices, FAQs, registration procedures and other forms of administrative guidance. As taxpayers and advisors continue evaluating the legal authority supporting various guidance positions, disputes regarding administrative procedure and regulatory interpretation may become more common.

This dynamic may be particularly relevant in areas involving lifecycle emissions methodologies, registration requirements, domestic content calculations, prevailing wage compliance standards, credit transfer procedures and recapture mechanics.

As a result, future controversies may involve not only technical qualification disputes but also broader challenges regarding the scope of the Treasury and IRS authority in drafting regulations.

Energy tax credit audit readiness

Examination readiness may help taxpayers respond more efficiently to IRS inquiries and support credit positions if a claim is reviewed. Readiness often involves attention to several documentation and process-related areas, including:

Maintaining contemporaneous substantiation supporting all eligibility requirements

Implementing formal governance and compliance procedures

Coordinating tax, engineering, environmental and operational documentation

Reviewing transfer agreements and indemnification provisions

Evaluating audit readiness for technical studies and third-party reports

Monitoring evolving IRS guidance and enforcement activity

Conducting periodic internal compliance reviews

Given the complexity and financial significance of IRA incentives, integrating controversy preparedness into energy credit planning may help organizations address documentation and substantiation issues before an examination begins.

Future IRS enforcement trends for energy tax credits

The energy credit market is entering a new phase in which controversy risk, audit preparedness and administrative scrutiny are becoming increasingly important. As IRS enforcement strategies related to IRA incentives continue to evolve, examination activity is likely to focus increasingly on substantiation, procedural compliance and technical qualification requirements.

Evaluating documentation and governance processes before an examination occurs may help organizations identify gaps, support credit positions and reduce disruption if IRS scrutiny increases. Early preparation may also help mitigate financial exposure and operational disruption as enforcement activity evolves.

Given the technical and operational complexity of many energy credit programs, organizations often benefit from a multidisciplinary approach to examination readiness. Tax advisors with experience in energy incentives, credit monetization transactions and controversy matters can help assess documentation, review governance and compliance processes, identify potential areas of examination risk and evaluate substantiation supporting credit claims.
