title: SEIA calls for stronger cybersecurity as US solar and storage manufacturing expands
description:
Tim Pawlenty, president and CEO of SEIA, said: “As solar and storage continue to lead the way in adding new power capacity to the grid, cybersecurity must remain front and centre.
The report identifies three priorities for improving cybersecurity across the solar and storage sector: Expanding domestic manufacturing through resilient supply chains, greater supplier transparency and trusted manufacturing capacity.
Establishing consistent baseline cybersecurity practices, including national guidance for distributed energy resources (DERs).
SEIA is advocating for national cybersecurity guidance for distributed energy resources, building on existing frameworks developed by the US Department of Energy, NIST, IEEE and other standards bodies.
However, it argues that distribution-connected solar and storage systems continue to rely largely on voluntary standards, resulting in inconsistent cybersecurity practices across the sector.
text:
SEIA said the rapid expansion of solar and storage, which accounted for nearly 80% of new US power generation capacity additions in 2025, increases the importance of securing systems against cyber threats targeting critical infrastructure.

Tim Pawlenty, president and CEO of SEIA, said: “As solar and storage continue to lead the way in adding new power capacity to the grid, cybersecurity must remain front and centre. From secure and resilient systems to expanding domestic manufacturing, this report lays out the actions our industry is taking to strengthen US energy security, protect critical infrastructure and stay ahead of emerging threats.”

Domestic manufacturing linked to cyber resilience

According to the report, US inverter manufacturing capacity has reached 55GWac following recent factory expansions. The expansion comes as US policymakers increasingly scrutinise foreign-made inverters over potential cybersecurity risks.

SEIA argues that strengthening US-based production of key technologies, including inverters, will improve supply chain resilience, increase transparency and reduce dependence on potentially vulnerable overseas supply chains.

The report identifies three priorities for improving cybersecurity across the solar and storage sector:

Expanding domestic manufacturing through resilient supply chains, greater supplier transparency and trusted manufacturing capacity.

Establishing consistent baseline cybersecurity practices, including national guidance for distributed energy resources (DERs).

Improving threat intelligence sharing and industry coordination to strengthen risk awareness and response capabilities.

Distributed energy remains a challenge

While large utility-scale solar plants connected to the bulk power system are subject to North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) standards, SEIA notes that most distributed solar and storage assets remain outside mandatory federal cybersecurity requirements.

The association warns that the rapid growth of internet-connected distributed energy resources, virtual power plants and remote monitoring systems creates additional cyber risks that require more consistent security standards.

SEIA is advocating for national cybersecurity guidance for distributed energy resources, building on existing frameworks developed by the US Department of Energy, NIST, IEEE and other standards bodies.

AI and the evolving regulatory landscape

Beyond traditional cyber threats, the report identifies supply chain security, third-party vendors and artificial intelligence as emerging areas of concern.

SEIA said reliance on cloud platforms, telecommunications providers, fleet management software and managed service providers expands the industry’s attack surface, requiring stronger vendor risk management throughout the lifecycle of solar and storage projects.

The report also warns that while AI can improve threat detection and operational efficiency, it may also enable attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities more quickly if deployed insecurely.

As previously reported in our sister journal, PV Tech Power, industry analysts have warned that AI-enabled asset management and optimisation tools could introduce new cybersecurity and operational risks for solar and storage portfolios [subscription required].

SEIA notes that the regulatory framework for utility-scale projects is becoming more stringent as NERC expands reliability requirements to cover more inverter-based resources.

However, it argues that distribution-connected solar and storage systems continue to rely largely on voluntary standards, resulting in inconsistent cybersecurity practices across the sector.

The association said it will continue working with industry, utilities and government agencies to help members navigate evolving compliance requirements while promoting proactive cybersecurity measures ahead of future regulatory mandates.

title: Manufacturing's transformation imperative - JLL
description:
Site selection is shifting, AI is transforming facility management, high-growth sectors are reshaping demand, and workforce expectations are outpacing organizational response.
Leading manufacturers have recognized this integration imperative and fundamentally changed how they approach transformation.
Minor disruptions can halt billion-dollar production lines, so manual processes meant reactive facilities management represented existential business risk.
These sustainability-driven sectors demand infrastructure beyond standard specifications: cleanroom environments, sophisticated HVAC, substantial renewable energy capacity, and specialized safety systems.
JLL's Workforce Preferences Barometer reveals 47% of manufacturing frontline employees cite "the right work environment to be productive" as their top expectation.
text:
The operational playbook that made manufacturers competitive five years ago now explains why many are losing ground. Site selection is shifting, AI is transforming facility management, high-growth sectors are reshaping demand, and workforce expectations are outpacing organizational response.

These aren't four separate challenges. They're deeply interconnected forces where progress in one area either amplifies or undermines progress in others. Leading manufacturers have recognized this integration imperative and fundamentally changed how they approach transformation.

"The organizations achieving breakthrough results aren't just executing better—they're recognizing interconnections that isolated efforts miss entirely," says Marjolein Westendorp, Managing Director - Industrial Lead at JLL.

They're asking different questions—not "Which area needs improvement?" but "How do these interdependencies create compounding advantages competitors pursuing isolated initiatives cannot replicate?"

Manufacturing site selection once followed predictable patterns: transportation proximity, favorable incentives, and low-cost labor. Today's decisions require three critical factors converging: skilled talent availability, robust infrastructure capacity, and reliable renewable energy access.

The hidden trap lies in single-variable optimization. A low-cost location without renewable energy infrastructure faces rising operating costs as decarbonization mandates tighten. A talent-rich market without adequate power capacity cannot support energy-intensive advanced manufacturing.

Koch Industries illustrates this at scale: 120,000+ employees across 50+ countries occupying 140 million square feet. Their decentralized structure meant individual business units across chemicals, energy, and technology sectors each had different real estate priorities that a one-size-fits-all approach couldn't meet.

JLL's LIFT model (Land, Infrastructure, Facilities, and Transactions) offered a menu of services—from full facility management to targeted support—letting each business unit choose what they needed while enabling portfolio-wide optimization. The result: 23 projects across three countries and eight U.S. states, now serving 19 Koch businesses across 18 countries with flexible, integrated solutions.

The shift required: Stop evaluating sites in isolation. Start mapping how location decisions across your entire portfolio either strengthen or weaken your position on all three factors simultaneously.

Artificial intelligence is transforming facility management from reactive crisis response to predictive operational excellence. JLL's 2025 Pulse Survey shows 53% of industrial organizations responding through outsourcing, while 24% deploy technology for efficiency. These strategies increasingly converge in AI-powered predictive maintenance that simultaneously reduces costs, extends asset lifecycles, and minimizes energy waste.

A Fortune 100 semiconductor manufacturer exemplifies the strategic stakes. Minor disruptions can halt billion-dollar production lines, so manual processes meant reactive facilities management represented existential business risk.

JLL's digital transformation deployed AI-powered predictive analytics across 3,000+ IoT sensor points. The results: over 5x ROI, 75% reduction in response times, 90% improvement in data accuracy, and 50% decrease in unplanned downtime.

The critical oversight: The transformation's most challenging dimension proved human, not technical. Making 200+ technicians comfortable with new systems required 18 months of comprehensive training. This explains why many digital initiatives deliver disappointing results—organizations invest in sophisticated AI while neglecting workforce adaptation.

Manufacturing real estate demand is accelerating as energy storage and semiconductor sectors fuel growth of purpose-built facilities that generic industrial space cannot accommodate. These sustainability-driven sectors demand infrastructure beyond standard specifications: cleanroom environments, sophisticated HVAC, substantial renewable energy capacity, and specialized safety systems.

As manufacturing occupies premium purpose-built space requiring substantial capital investment, operational excellence becomes critical to protecting these assets.

A global apparel manufacturer consolidating nine buildings into one facility confronted what seemed like a straightforward real estate transaction. Deeper analysis revealed storage chaos with excessive materials, poor tracking, and security vulnerabilities creating operational inefficiency and environmental waste.

JLL's Storage + Organization team applied Lean principles to reimagine workflows before the physical move, delivering an 80% increase in processing efficiency and 30% reduction in storage space requirements. After optimization, the client found "plenty of space to spare"—reducing energy footprint while creating strategic capacity reserves.

The key takeaway: Operational optimization before occupancy, not after. Purpose-built facilities represent long-term location commitments. Getting operational design right before construction means site selection decisions support rather than constrain strategy for decades.

Manufacturing's future depends on attracting skilled frontline workers in competitive labor markets where 21% of factory employees are actively considering leaving.

JLL's Workforce Preferences Barometer reveals 47% of manufacturing frontline employees cite "the right work environment to be productive" as their top expectation. Additionally, 44% want flexibility in working hours, 43% desire workplaces where they can "really be themselves," and 37% seek healthy lifestyle support.

Organizations viewing frontline experience as an HR concern rather than competitive imperative face systematic disadvantage—particularly as younger workers evaluate employers based on workplace quality and environmental responsibility alongside compensation.

Workforce preferences now directly influence other strategic decisions. Sites selected for low costs become talent deserts when workers prioritize modern facilities and sustainability commitments. AI investments fail when technicians reject new systems. Purpose-built facilities can't operate at capacity without skilled workers seeking flexibility and genuine culture.

Posted on Jul 22, 2026 in Latest Department News, Newsroom

STATE OF HAWAIʻI

KA MOKU ʻĀINA O HAWAIʻI

JOSH GREEN, M.D.

GOVERNOR

KE KIAʻĀINA

DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH

KA ʻOIHANA OLAKINO

KENNETH S. FINK, MD, MGA, MPH

DIRECTOR

KA LUNA HOʻOKELE

DEPARTMENT OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL

KA ʻOIHANA O KA LOIO KUHINA

ANNE LOPEZ

ATTORNEY GENERAL

LOIO KUHINA

STATE TAKES ON HAWAIIAN ELECTRIC FOR WALKING BACK POLLUTION COMMITMENTS

026-086

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

July 22, 2026

HONOLULU – Attorney General Anne Lopez has filed a petition on behalf of the Hawaiʻi Department of Health (DOH) challenging the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) partial disapproval of Hawaiʻi’s Regional Haze State Implementation Plan (RHSIP).

Under the Clean Air Act, states must develop RHSIPs to improve visibility and protect air quality around national parks. Haze-forming pollutants have been linked to serious health problems and environmental damage.

Hawaiian Electric Company, Inc.’s Kanoelehua Hill, Kahului, Māʻalaea and Puna generating stations were identified as the top contributors of human-caused, haze-causing pollution affecting visibility in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park and Haleakalā National Park.

Following extensive consultation, Hawaiian Electric voluntarily agreed to retire older and inefficient oil-burning units on Maui and Hawaiʻi Island currently operating with minimal pollution controls. While cost analyses found air pollution controls to be economically feasible, Hawaiian Electric proposed to retire the units instead of installing air pollution controls.

But when the EPA changed administrations in 2025, Hawaiian Electric abruptly reversed course on its commitment and notified the EPA that it no longer agreed to the retirements. On May 29, EPA issued a final rule partially disapproving Hawaiʻi’s RHSIP.

“Hawaiʻi will fight to protect our people and our environment,” said Deputy Director for Environmental Health Kathleen Ho. “Our regional haze plan was tailored to Hawaiʻi’s unique circumstances and developed through years of collaboration to improve air quality in and around our state’s national parks. EPA’s partial disapproval undermines the goals of the Clean Air Act and weakens important environmental protections designed to reduce harmful air pollution.”

“Congress enacted the Regional Haze Program to decrease haze and improve visibility in all national parks,” said Attorney General Anne Lopez. “Hawaiʻi’s national parks are culturally and environmentally significant places. Haleakalā National Park and Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park are home to unique landscapes and many species of plants and wildlife found nowhere else on Earth. Residents and visitors deserve to experience these parks with the natural air quality and visibility the RHSIP was intended to protect. We challenge EPA’s action because it is inconsistent with the goals of the RHSIP and is based on an unlawful interpretation of the Clean Air Act.”

In the disapproval, Hawaiian Electric’s voluntary retirements were characterized by EPA as “unconsented” closures. Characterizing the closures as unconsented disregards years of negotiations that resulted in the voluntary commitments incorporated into the RHSIP. Further, in disapproving Hawaiʻi’s implementation plan, EPA creates uncertainty in the retirements and other pollution remediation measures.

https://health.hawaii.gov/cab/regional-haze/

The petition was filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The state is asking the court to declare EPA’s partial disapproval unlawful and vacate the agency’s action.

The state of Hawaiʻi is represented in this litigation by Lyle T. Leonard, deputy attorney general with the Department of the Attorney General’s Health Division.

title: What to know about Ford's BlueOval City plant, 5 years later | News From The States
description:
What is BlueOval City, and what will be made there?
BlueOval City is a 6-square-mile manufacturing campus located about 2.5 miles south of Stanton, a Haywood County town of about 700 residents.
BlueOval City includes Ford’s Tennessee Truck Plant (formerly the Tennessee Electric Vehicle Center), a 4-million-square-foot electric battery plant owned and operated by SK On Tennessee, a supplier park, a railyard connection and a wastewater treatment plant.
SK On Tennessee took full ownership of the battery plant at BlueOval City in May and plans to produce automotive and energy storage systems there starting in 2028.
Ford began changing its plans for BlueOval City in August 2024, pushing back production from its initial 2025 target to 2027.
text:
Nearly five years after Ford Motor Company announced a massive electric vehicle and battery manufacturing campus poised to change the economic landscape of rural West Tennessee, the plant has yet to start production.

The project’s initial roadmap had production starting in 2025, but a series of delays, changed plans and the dissolution of Ford’s joint venture with South Korean battery manufacturer SK On pushed back hiring and production timelines for the $5.6 billion BlueOval City hub.

The campus’ future now looks different — and less electric — than the auto giant’s original pitch. But Ford and the newly minted SK On Tennessee have said they still plan to honor the commitments made in 2021 to hire 5,800 people and start manufacturing by the end of the decade.

Here’s what to know.

What is BlueOval City, and what will be made there?

BlueOval City is a 6-square-mile manufacturing campus located about 2.5 miles south of Stanton, a Haywood County town of about 700 residents.

The site lies on about 3,300 acres of former farmland that is part of the state-owned Memphis Regional Megasite. It’s sandwiched between an existing CSX railway near U.S. Route 70 and Interstate 40.

BlueOval City includes Ford’s Tennessee Truck Plant (formerly the Tennessee Electric Vehicle Center), a 4-million-square-foot electric battery plant owned and operated by SK On Tennessee, a supplier park, a railyard connection and a wastewater treatment plant.

Original plans for the campus included a manufacturing facility for Ford’s EV pickup truck and a battery plant owned and operated by BlueOval SK, a joint venture between Ford and South Korean battery manufacturer SK On. Ford and SK On announced plans to dissolve their partnership in December.

Shortly after, Ford announced that the company no longer intends to manufacture electric vehicles at BlueOval City and will instead begin producing gas-powered Built Ford Tough truck models at the renamed Tennessee Truck Plant in 2029.

SK On Tennessee took full ownership of the battery plant at BlueOval City in May and plans to produce automotive and energy storage systems there starting in 2028. The battery company will remain a tenant on the BlueOval City campus and will maintain a “strategic partnership” with Ford, including supplying batteries for Ford’s future electric vehicles, according to SK On Tennessee spokesperson Keli McAlister.

What state incentives are on the line?

Tennessee lawmakers approved a $900 million incentive package for Ford in October 2021.

Ford’s agreement with the state requires the company and the former BlueOval SK joint venture to create at least 90% of the total 5,800 jobs within 10 years. Meeting that mark secures Ford a $500 million state reimbursement for construction work.

Failing to reach 80% of the promised jobs by 2032 would trigger a “clawback” requirement forcing the company to pay back that $500 million in addition to $175 million, based on the value of the state’s donated land.

Other state contributions include:

$200 million to build a road interchange

$138 million for water treatment facilities and a wastewater line to the Mississippi River

$5 million for local government consulting

The state also agreed to pay for a new $60 million extension campus for the Tennessee College of Applied Technology located down the road in Stanton to help train future employees of the massive industrial complex. The campus opened in summer 2024.

Tennessee legislators also earmarked $725,000 to create an 11-member Megasite Authority of West Tennessee to handle development of the BlueOval City site and an additional 300 acres under state control.

Megasite Authority of West Tennessee CEO Clay Bright told state lawmakers in February that the state has met all of its commitments to Ford, including the road work needed for the first phase of the project, the water supply and the wastewater treatment plant.

The dissolution of BlueOval SK and transfer of ownership to SK On Tennessee does not change the details or accountability of the state’s agreement with the companies, Bright said in February.

Separately, Ford pledged to invest $9 million in West Tennessee communities surrounding the campus in a “Good Neighbor Plan” released in January 2025. A coalition of community members has criticized the package for lacking legally binding accountability measures.

Ford announced in April that it surpassed that goal, spending nearly $11.7 million.

How many people work there now, and what is the hiring timeline?

Ford employs about 80 people at its facility, and SK On Tennessee currently employs a core team of 100 people.

Both companies say they will ramp up hiring closer to the start of production — 2028 for SK On Tennessee, and 2029 for Ford.

Before the companies’ joint venture BlueOval SK dissolved, that entity employed around 300 people. BlueOval SK laid off 150 employees in May as it prepared to transition to SK On Tennessee.

Early projections indicated that Ford would ultimately employ about 2,300 people at the truck plant. Another 3,500 people would work at the adjoining battery plant now owned by SK On Tennessee.

Why did Ford decide not to build electric trucks at BlueOval City?

Ford stated that it dropped its plans to build a next-generation electric pickup truck at BlueOval City because the “business case has eroded due to lower-than-expected demand, high costs and regulatory changes.”

The shift came after slowing demand and the rollback of Biden-era incentives and tax credits for clean energy and electric vehicles under President Donald Trump’s second administration.

Ford began changing its plans for BlueOval City in August 2024, pushing back production from its initial 2025 target to 2027. The company planned to reduce its expenditures on pure electric vehicles from 40% to 30% after Ford’s electric vehicle unit reported it was on track to lose $1.3 billion in 2023. At the time, Ford stated that pushing production to 2027 would allow the company to implement lower-cost battery technology to make the electric pickup trucks more price-competitive.

In August 2025, Ford delayed mass production again, this time until 2028. At the time, the company said it was shifting its focus to smaller, more affordable electric vehicle models.

While Ford no longer plans to produce all-electric pickup trucks at BlueOval City, the company still intends to assemble a mid-sized electric pickup truck at its plant in Louisville, Kentucky starting in 2027.

Ford will turn its focus to producing a range of hybrids and extended range electric vehicles — electric vehicles that also feature combustion engines that act as generators to recharge the vehicle’s battery, extending range for long trips. The company expects about half of its global volume will be hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles and fully electric vehicles by 2030, Ford stated in December.

text:
Environmentalists in Texas want the state to adopt new laws and regulations governing where renewable energy projects should be built, how they should run and what they can do to minimize their environmental impact. These policy proposals would be in stark contrast to what’s been introduced in prior legislative sessions—bills designed to artificially slow renewables’ progress.

Without clear rules, ideological opponents of renewable energy have weaponized conservation concerns to justify sweeping legislative proposals that would effectively ban new solar, battery storage and wind projects, according to a new report by the Environment Texas Research & Policy Center and the Frontier Group, both progressive research organizations.

Luke Metzger, the executive director of the research and policy center, said while wind and solar can have negative impacts on Texas land and wildlife, it’s less than those of fossil fuels.

There are renewable energy developers already using best practices, Metzger said, like utilizing acoustic surveys before construction to identify high-traffic bird corridors and implementing reasonable setbacks and light and noise standards.

These approaches help minimize environmental harm on private property, where ranch and farm families have stewarded the land for generations, Metzger said. The income these families earn from leasing their land for renewable energy development often helps them keep their land intact, rather than selling it off to be subdivided.

Metzger said state policy makers should ensure that any new rules support that approach, rather than blocking clean energy altogether.

“Banning renewables doesn’t protect our environment,” Metzger said. “It means more pollution, more water strain and it undermines those landowners that depend on that income to keep their land intact.”

The nonprofit group suggests that any siting policies for renewable projects should establish clear rules and include timely decisions and should avoid draconian or non-science based regulations.

The last time Texas lawmakers convened in 2025, numerous bills were introduced seeking to restrict the growth of renewable energy sources across the state.

One proposal, sponsored by Sen. Lois Kolkhorst, a Republican from Brenham, sought to force renewable energy projects to apply for permits required of no other energy generators and added new guidelines to increase setbacks from property lines for wind power projects.

During the last session, Kolkhorst told reporters that her proposed bill was about protecting the environment and landowners. She said it was the right thing to do for Texas.

The solar, wind and battery storage industries fought off proposed legislation aimed at requiring every watt of new solar generation to be accompanied by a watt of new gas generation.

Two bills sought to force existing wind and solar companies to buy fossil fuel-based power or connect to a battery storage resource to cover the hours the energy plants are not operating. Both renewables and oil company lobbyists saw the legislation as adding unnecessary costs and opposed it.

They were sponsored by Rep. Jared Patterson, a Republican from Denton County, and Sen. Kevin Sparks, a Republican from Midland. Patterson previously chaired the House Committee on Protecting Texas LNG. Sparks is the president of a family oil and gas company in Midland.

Patterson said at the time that the aim of the legislation was to ensure producers, not consumers, bear increased costs. He also worried about relying on the “whims of nature.”

After these bills did not advance through the Legislature, the Republican Party of Texas urged lawmakers to eliminate and counterbalance all subsidies, rebates and mandates for renewable energy sources and related infrastructure. The state GOP chapter also said that the Legislature should establish a uniform reliability standard.

Texas leads the U.S. in its production of wind and utility-scale solar. On most days, solar, storage and wind are providing nearly half of the state’s electricity, said Cyrus Reed, the conservation director of the Sierra Club Lone Star Chapter. On March 14, renewables met a record 79 percent of the state’s electricity demand, according to a Solar Energy Industries Association report.

As renewable energy is meeting a larger share of the state’s daily electricity demand, it has significantly reduced air and water pollution, said Quentin Good, a policy analyst at Frontier Group and an author of the report.

As electricity consumption across the state grew between 2018 and 2023, sulfur dioxide emissions from Texas power plants went down by 50 percent and greenhouse gas emissions went down by 11 percent due, at least in part, to the growth of renewables, Good said.

The addition of battery storage as part of Texas’ independent grid has helped store electricity when conditions have become tight, adding resilience and preventing system-wide outages Texans have grown to fear during serious weather events. On March 13, batteries supplied a record 20 percent of evening electricity demand.

“The massive amount of renewable energy and battery storage in Texas is really helping deliver cleaner air and water,” Good said. “It’s helping Texas move away from some of the harmful impacts of fossil fuel production and use.”

The report also said that any statewide regulations on renewables should prioritize stewardship of Texas land and wildlife, while also allowing landowners to responsibly develop energy projects on private land.

Donate Now

A theme throughout legislative discussions in 2025 among conservative lawmakers was whether the proposed bills to curb the growth of renewables infringed on private property rights. By the end of deliberations, there was a divide among state Republicans.

Some lawmakers saw the effort to govern how Texans utilized their private land as a transgression against small government conservatism and strong private property freedoms. Other Republicans see the expansion of renewable energy in Texas as antithetical to the future of the party, one which has deep ties to the oil and gas industry and is aligned with President Donald Trump, a staunch opponent of renewable energy, especially wind.

Another recommendation the environmentalists made in the report is to set statewide baselines or ceilings for local siting requirements, like setbacks from a property line, so that localities cannot effectively ban renewables. This would increase certainty for developers, while providing a baseline for environmental projections, the report outlined.

Lastly, the report argues that lawmakers should adopt a tiered process which addresses risks specific to the technology and sensitivity of a specific site.

More environmentally sensitive areas should require stricter scrutiny, the report authors suggested, while renewable energy projects which chose their location with conservation in mind should have an accelerated review.

This could include projects that utilize existing developed land—like putting solar on rooftops and carports instead of utilizing the state’s best agricultural areas, said Garrett Bader, a smart solar specialist for the American Farmland Trust in Texas.

Lisa Gonzalez, the vice president and executive director of Audubon Texas, a chapter of the national bird conservancy group, said it’s important that developers work with agencies like Texas Parks and Wildlife and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service before a shovel ever hits the ground.

Responsible developers use advanced mapping to steer projects away from sensitive habitats and towards “low conflict areas,” Gonzalez said. There are also emerging artificial intelligence technologies being developed to curtail or slow wind blades when birds or bats are in the area.

In Texas, the effects of climate change—extreme weather, drought, rising temperatures, sea level rise and shifting seasons—are already reshaping the ecosystems that birds and other animals rely on, Gonzalez said.

As climate change is one of the single greatest long-term threats to Texas birds, from waterbirds to grassland species, Gonzalez said, shifting toward clean power is a high priority.

Texas lawmakers can start submitting their proposals for new state legislation after the fall elections. Environmentalists are preparing to argue against bills that restrict renewable energy and further incentivize fossil fuels.

title: UK's EV battery sector moves to industrial scale, but can it build a midstream? - Fastmarkets
description:
Fellow UK recycling company Recyclus was represented on the same panel by Alex Stanbury, co-founder and chief executive officer.
Today, most European and UK-origin black mass is exported, with the majority of volumes ending up in key Asian markets like South Korea, according to market sources.
In 2026, China is forecast to account for around 84% of globally announced CAM capacity, according to Fastmarkets’ research team.
South Korea is expected to be the next largest CAM producer by country, accounting for 8.60% of globally announced CAM capacity.
Government support aims to close the gap But UK authorities have shown strong willingness to back projects aiming to scale up for the battery supply chain.
text:
Key takeaways:

The UK risks losing critical battery materials and value overseas: Most battery scrap and black mass generated in the UK is still exported for refining, meaning critical minerals, jobs and commercial opportunities leave the country before re-entering the supply chain at a higher cost.

Recycling and battery manufacturing capacity are growing, but key midstream processing gaps remain: While new gigafactories and recycling projects are coming online, the UK still lacks commercial-scale refining, pCAM and CAM production needed to create a fully domestic battery supply chain.

Funding and scale-up challenges continue to slow progress: Despite strong government support and rising EV adoption, companies face financing hurdles, uncertain feedstock availability and lessons from previous industry failures as they seek to expand.

UK seeks to retain battery materials domestically

Speakers at the Battery Cells & Systems Expo (BCSE) held in Birmingham, England, on July 8-9 said that over the medium term, the UK needs to be able to retain critical minerals generated from end of life batteries at home rather than exporting battery scrap or shredded black mass overseas.

The UK currently has several pre-processing battery shredding companies turning battery scrap into black mass, and a handful of EV battery production facilities, but lacks commercial-scale refining capacity for metals salts, precursor cathode active materials (pCAM) and cathode active materials (CAM).

“Right now, if we talk about battery recycling, we take a waste battery and then we shred it and create another waste material,” Christian Marston, president, co-founder and chief operating officer of battery recycler Altilium Clean Technology, said at the event on July 9. “Predominantly, that material is exported overseas, mainly Asia.”

“When we do that, we export UK jobs, we export critical minerals needed for the energy transition, and we buy them back at a premium,” he said.

Altilium and Recyclus target domestic processing growth

Altilium has plans to scale up its hydrometallurgical recycling capacity of black mass in the UK with the start of its “ACT 3” scale-up facility in Plymouth, in southwestern England, expected to commission by 2027 with capacity to recycle 8,000 tonnes of black mass per year.

The company believes that recycled materials could supply up to 50% of the critical minerals required for the UK’s energy transition by 2040, Marston added.

Recycled metals are forecast to make up 15% of total global cathode material supply by 2030, up from 8% in 2026, according to Fastmarkets analysts.

Altilium has delivered test batches of recycled nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) CAM to the UK Battery Industrialization Center (UKBIC) for EV battery cell production and qualification, from its pilot-scale operations in Devon, in southwestern England. But commercial-scale size may be some way off, Fastmarkets understands.

It has also demonstrated an ability to produce recycled anode active materials from used batteries and black mass on pilot scale, which is an area rarely explored by most recycling firms.

Fellow UK recycling company Recyclus was represented on the same panel by Alex Stanbury, co-founder and chief executive officer. Its pre-processing nameplate capacity in Wolverhampton, in central England, is for consumption of 22,000 tonnes of scrap batteries annually.

The company is also looking into technologies for recovering lithium from black mass in the UK over the coming years, Fastmarkets heard.

Funding pressures continue to weigh on expansion

But funding is a key sticking point for UK companies looking to scale up across the supply chain, sources said on the sidelines of the BCSE last week, and is holding back further developments across the industry.

Today, most European and UK-origin black mass is exported, with the majority of volumes ending up in key Asian markets like South Korea, according to market sources.

Reduced lithium and nickel prices have lessened demand for NCM black mass across consumers in Europe and Asia over the last month, hampering payables for the materials.

Fastmarkets’ assessments of the black mass, NCM, payable indicator, cobalt, max 5% moisture, exw Europe, % payable Fastmarkets’ standard-grade cobalt price (low-end) and the black mass, NCM, payable indicator, nickel, max 5% moisture, exw Europe, % payable LME Nickel cash official price were both 80-85% on Wednesday July 15, unchanged week on week.

Interested in prices, news and analysis for the commodities used in EV and ESS batteries? Discover Fastmarkets’ battery raw materials suite.

Growing EV sector creates future recycling opportunities

Electric vehicle (EV) penetration levels are rising rapidly in the UK.

UK new car registrations of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) saw the most significant growth of all segments to take a 30% share in June 2026 — the highest so far this year, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) said on July 6.

A major cellmaking gigafactory in Sunderland, in northeastern England, owned by Envision AESC, started production with a capacity of 15.8 gigawatt hours in December 2025, the company said.

The plant will manufacture lithium-ion batteries for EVs made in the UK and support the launch of the new Nissan Leaf vehicle, the company said on December 16. Plans for the facility were first announced in July 2021.

Battery manufacturing company Agratas, a Tata Group-owned company, will start cellmaking production in Somerset, in southwestern England, by the end of 2027, a company source told Fastmarkets last week.

Construction on the plant is expected to be complete by the second quarter of 2027 and it is expected to have capacity of 40 GWh.

Lessons from past battery sector setbacks

But other attempts at localizing battery production, such as the Britishvolt project in northeastern England, and the AMTE Power factory in Scotland, failed back in 2023, with both companies falling into administration.

Following these cautionary tales and high-profile US cases including battery recyclers Li-Cycle and Ascend Elements, many UK firms have been more cautious to scale up in recent years, sources said on the conference sidelines.

Building a domestic recycling feedstock base

The lack of commercially operational cellmaking capacity to date has restricted the amount of materials that could be recycled in the UK, panelists said.

“In the UK, there’s not an awful lot of battery manufacturing going on,” Stanbury said.

“We get most of our [black mass] from end of life [materials],” he said on July 9. “The real growth here is in the larger stuff — it’s in the EVs.”

Recyclus currently processes a mix of industrial batteries, e-bikes, power tools, warehouse robotics batteries and EV packs, Stanbury said.

Forecasting future supply of these materials remains difficult, because recalls and insurance write-offs can create irregular inflows of material, but that this could change with new gigafactories coming online.

“Until you’re looking at and talking about the actual cell manufacturers here, so AESC, and then when Agratas comes online, most things that end up on these shores are being sold here, so you know it becomes an end of life issue,” he added.

The UK is far from an isolated case of a market with operational cellmaking capacity that lacks domestic materials supply.

Similar issues persist in the EU, where there is a startling lack of operational pCAM and CAM capacity, together with North America, which is battling similar issues.

In 2026, China is forecast to account for around 84% of globally announced CAM capacity, according to Fastmarkets’ research team. South Korea is expected to be the next largest CAM producer by country, accounting for 8.60% of globally announced CAM capacity.

This leaves supply chains in western nations heavily dependent on importing CAM from Asia.

Government support aims to close the gap

But UK authorities have shown strong willingness to back projects aiming to scale up for the battery supply chain.

Policy is centered on a combination of direct funding, industrial strategy and innovation support. This includes the 2023 UK Battery Strategy, which aims to support the design and build of manufacturing and supply chains together with bolstering its local recycling sector.

Authorities have given more than £2 billion ($2.69 billion) of automotive sector support to assist zero-emission vehicle manufacturing, battery production and battery supply chains in the UK, according to government news releases.

“I think the decisions we make now over the next few years will determine whether the UK becomes a leader in circular battery materials, or we remain dependent on importing raw materials,” Marston said.

name: Clean Energy
title: Voters Know America Needs More Energy. Solar and Storage Are the Overwhelming Choice.
description:
Delivering more affordable, homegrown solar energy will keep bills lower and also strengthen American energy independence.
Solar and energy storage bring solutions.
Solar and energy storage can be planned and deployed in a matter of months rather than years.
Solar and storage support hundreds of thousands of jobs and deliver billions in local investments and tax revenue.
From good jobs to lower bills, solar and storage offer a powerful message for candidates this November.
text:
Skyrocketing energy demand, unpredictable fuel prices, and scorching summer heatwaves are sending U.S. electricity bills through the roof. With just 100 days until the 2026 midterm elections, the window is closing for lawmakers to tackle rising costs before voters render their verdict at the ballot box. New polling released by POLITICO shows that half of all Americans find their utility bills are difficult or very difficult to afford.

Solar and storage are quick-to-build, reliable, and – importantly – low cost. In fact, if you were to take solar off the grid for the next 100 days – Americans would be on the hook for an additional $3 billion in fossil fuel costs.

In November, this growing crowd of cost-conscious Americans will be looking hard at policymakers’ energy agendas and putting their support behind candidates who can deliver low-cost solar and storage quickly.

The Most Popular Generation Source

An April Gallup poll found that 66% of Americans want policymakers to put greater emphasis on producing solar energy, compared to just 16% that want less emphasis. That same month, Pew Research found similar results.

Voter support for solar is not restricted to one party. The same April Gallup poll found that 87% of Democratic respondents want more solar, and several new surveys show that Republicans agree. Two polls conducted this spring by the firms of conservative pollsters Tony Fabrizio and Kellyanne Conway showed strong support for solar among President Trump’s voters, including in key swing states. Similarly, this month Cygnal found that adding more clean and renewable energy was the most popular grid fix among a wide variety of options given.

The popularity of these technologies is not theoretical. Just look at the elections that took place last November: Energy policy was a top issue for voters in Virginia, New Jersey, Georgia, and elsewhere. And consistently, the winners of these elections were supporters of building more solar and storage.

Building The Argument

In addition to being popular, solar and storage provide solutions to address many of the challenges that are top of mind for voters.

Affordability has dominated voters’ concerns in 2026, and solar and storage remain two of the most cost-effective ways to add new capacity to the grid. With no fuel costs, these sources are insulated from the volatile supply chains and international disruptions that sent oil and gas prices spiking this year. Delivering more affordable, homegrown solar energy will keep bills lower and also strengthen American energy independence.

Voters are also paying close attention to the skyrocketing energy demand caused by new data centers and manufacturing facilities.

As Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini noted in a recent op-ed, “lawmakers going home this summer do not need a better slogan on AI. They need a better answer on power.” Voters will not be satisfied with mere talking points on AI, they’re looking for clear, workable solutions that ensure the AI buildout will not spike their electricity bills. Solar and energy storage bring solutions.

Solar and energy storage can be planned and deployed in a matter of months rather than years. That’s why these two technologies have accounted for more than 80% of all new power added to the grid during the Trump administration. “AI won’t run on talking points,” Ruffini writes. “It will run on affordable, abundant electricity. The market is already pointing us toward the fastest, most affordable path to more power.”

The solar and energy storage industries are also job creators and economic drivers in states across the country. Solar and storage support hundreds of thousands of jobs and deliver billions in local investments and tax revenue. Since 2022, U.S. solar manufacturers have announced over $47 billion in new investments and over 190 new factories.

From good jobs to lower bills, solar and storage offer a powerful message for candidates this November. Campaigns that respond to voters’ concerns about energy by putting solar and storage at the center of their platforms will offer a tangible, common-sense solution that voters already support. Those that don’t risk missing the opportunity to champion America’s favorite energy source.

text:
WASHINGTON — A total of 278 research projects from across the nation have been chosen to begin work under the federal Genesis Mission, a program designed to use artificial intelligence to accelerate scientific research in energy, national security and other fields, Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced Wednesday.

The Department of Energy said the projects, involving institutions in all 50 states, were chosen from what officials described as the largest response ever received to a department research funding opportunity.

Wright said the selected projects would bring together scientists from the Department of Energy’s national laboratories, universities, private industry and nonprofit organizations to develop AI-enabled research methods intended to shorten the time required for scientific discovery.

“America has no shortage of bold ideas or talented scientists, and the response to the Genesis Mission proves that,” Wright said in announcing the selections.

“The 278 projects selected today represent the very best of our nation’s scientific enterprise,” he said. “The remarkable number of high-quality proposals we received demonstrates that America’s innovation pipeline is strong, and it points to even greater opportunities for future investment and continued expansion of the Genesis Mission portfolio.”

The department said the Genesis Mission is intended to combine artificial intelligence, high-performance computing and laboratory research to increase scientific productivity in fields ranging from energy technology to national security.

Officials said the selected portfolio includes 87 projects led by Department of Energy and National Nuclear Security Administration laboratories, 168 headed by universities, 19 by private companies and four by nonprofit organizations.

A total of 342 institutions are participating, including 16 federal laboratories, 142 universities, 157 companies, 13 nonprofit organizations and 14 other organizations, according to the department.

The projects will focus on research involving nuclear energy, commercial fusion, critical mineral extraction, semiconductor design and other scientific and engineering challenges.

The largest single award announced Wednesday provides $60 million over three years for research using artificial intelligence to improve the design, construction and operation of nuclear energy facilities.

Department officials said the project is intended to help reduce construction time and operating costs while improving safety and reliability.

Under Secretary for Science Dr. Darío Gil said the volume of applications reflected broad interest within the scientific community in incorporating artificial intelligence into research.

“The extraordinary response to this Genesis Mission application process demonstrates that America’s scientific community is ready to reimagine how discovery happens,” Gil said.

“Through the Genesis Mission, we are bringing together the nation’s leading researchers, institutions, and technology partners to build the next generation of scientific capability,” he said.

The department said research teams will begin developing AI-assisted scientific workflows using resources made available through the Genesis Mission platform, including artificial intelligence software, computing frameworks and high-performance computing systems located at national laboratories and partner facilities.

Officials said the platform is intended to allow researchers to rapidly design, test and refine scientific methods across multiple fields of study.

The department said additional Genesis Mission projects may be announced as the program expands.

name: Clean Energy
outlet: European Union Institute for Security Studies
title: Mining for Europe's future: Critical raw materials, public attitudes and risks in enlargement partners
description:
Enlargement partners hold substantial reserves of critical raw materials (CRMs) that the EU can leverage to achieve greater global supply autonomy.
It will not remove critical dependencies tomorrow, but it is an investment in economic security that will pay off in the longer term.
Such a perception carries a real risk of undermining the EU’s leverage in advancing both its economic security objectives and the enlargement process.
Mining projects in the Western Balkans, some associated with the EU, already create public controversy.
A similar logic applies to the Western Balkans where mining projects are often framed through the lens of resource extraction rather than broader industrial development.
text:
The technologies underpinning the EU’s green transition (batteries and wind turbines), digital transition (semiconductors) and rearmament (advanced weapons systems) rely on a narrow set of materials whose supply and processing remain concentrated in a handful of foreign countries. Around 98% of the EU’s borates supply originates in Türkiye while over 90% of rare earth elements used in permanent magnets globally are refined in China(1). This poses a critical challenge for European economic security.

The 2024 Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA)(2) aims to reduce the EU’s dependencies by promoting diversification, resilient value chains and strategic partnerships. Enlargement partners hold substantial reserves of critical raw materials (CRMs) that the EU can leverage to achieve greater global supply autonomy. Ukraine sits on significant deposits of graphite, titanium and manganese (holding the largest deposits of these three CRMs in Europe(3)) as well as lithium, cobalt, nickel, magnesium, baryte and rare earth elements. In the Western Balkans, Serbia possesses significant copper and borates reserves in addition to lithium. Bosnia and Herzegovina and North Macedonia hold important deposits of bauxite, aluminium, cobalt, copper, manganese, nickel and antimony. Albania contributes additional deposits of copper, cobalt, feldspar and nickel.

Serbia’s Jadar lithium-boron project and Ukraine’s Balakhivka graphite deposit have been recognised as strategic projects under the CRMA, enabling them to benefit from coordinated support for financing and commercial partnerships, due to their importance for European battery and clean technology supply chains. However, much of the region’s mineral deposits remain underground. Altogether, 26 out of the 34 CRMs identified by the EU can be found in Ukraine. The economic viability of exploiting some of these deposits has yet to be ascertained owing to information on depth, ore grade and byproducts being incomplete in available surveys. Moreover, access to some more significant deposits is constrained due to Russia’s war and occupation of Ukrainian territory.

This underscores the strategic value of enlargement for the EU. It will not remove critical dependencies tomorrow, but it is an investment in economic security that will pay off in the longer term. For enlargement to deliver in this strategic area will require more than securing access to CRMs. Working together with enlargement partners should include investments in localised value chains spanning refining, processing and component manufacturing. It should also be underpinned by the application of environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards. Even if this may modestly extend the lead times for new projects, it is essential to avoid the perception that the EU is a (neo-)colonial entity primarily interested in raw commodity extraction. Such a perception carries a real risk of undermining the EU’s leverage in advancing both its economic security objectives and the enlargement process.

The extraction trap

A less discussed but equally important aspect is anchoring the CRM partnerships with candidates in ESG standards. The EU promotes ESG standards as a defining feature of its approach to CRMs globally. Its commitment is reflected in the CRMA which links supply security to environmental protection, respect for human rights, socially sustainable practices and transparent business conduct. Yet ensuring the consistent implementation of these principles remains a challenge, particularly in states with weak governance, insufficient institutional capacity and low public trust. As demand for CRMs grows, there is a risk that securing supply takes precedence over governance concerns, widening the gap between formal compliance and implementation on the ground. Ukraine’s new Critical Minerals Strategy(4), a long-term roadmap for developing the country’s mineral resources released in June 2026, also emphasises a standards-based approach. However, it frames it largely in terms of geoeconomic necessity – as a condition for attracting foreign capital and ensuring foreign market access – rather than as a normative commitment to protecting the environment and local communities.

Furthermore, there is a risk that this will reinforce the portrayal of the EU as a (neo-)colonial entity primarily interested in extracting raw commodities. Such perceptions frame the EU as ‘locking partners’ into uneven and exploitative relationships, demanding perpetual reforms that are never considered sufficient, while ultimately applying pressure and double standards for its own benefit. For local communities, where the investors come from is ultimately secondary to the social, environmental and economic consequences of mining. If projects associated with the EU are perceived as falling short of the standards the Union promotes within the single market, support for enlargement may suffer.

This is not a hypothetical scenario. Mining projects in the Western Balkans, some associated with the EU, already create public controversy.

In Serbia, the Jadar project by Rio Tinto aims to produce around 58 000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium carbonate annually(5) in addition to borates, used in electric vehicle batteries, renewable energy technologies and other clean-tech industries. Its scale makes it one of Europe’s largest lithium projects. However, surveys conducted between 2024 and 2025 consistently found a majority opposed to lithium mining, rising from 55.5% in mid-2024 to 63.5% in March 2025(6). Large segments of the public perceive the project as posing risks to water resources, agricultural land and biodiversity. The controversy furthermore reflects broader concerns about governance, transparency and the extent to which strategic decisions are shaped by political elites, foreign investors and external actors. Civil society organisations warned(7) that proceeding with the project risked further undermining public confidence in EU integration. As a result, the investor, Rio Tinto, decided to place the project in a ‘care and maintenance’ phase for the time being.

The EU needs to demonstrate that its approach differs from more transactional models of resource extraction.

Developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina suggest that public resistance to CRM projects is becoming a broader regional phenomenon. In the Majevica region around Lopare, since late 2023 local authorities, residents and environmental groups have opposed lithium surveys. Around Vareš, Olovo and Zavidovići, civil society organisations and local communities have called for the termination of concessions for chromium exploration and mining since 2024, while in Tuzla Canton environmental groups continue to challenge plans that could enable future extraction of lithium, nickel, cobalt and other minerals. These developments serve as a cautionary tale for the EU, highlighting the need to demonstrate that its approach differs from more transactional models of resource extraction.

In war-torn Ukraine, the dilemma is currently linked more to the perceived need to secure as much US support as possible in the short term. The government responded to the Trump administration’s relentless interest in gaining access to Ukraine’s CRMs by agreeing to a memorandum in April 2025 that reaffirmed Ukraine’s ownership of its minerals but granted US companies preferential development and offtake rights – effectively barring third countries from receiving more favourable conditions. The risk is that, unless competition between the EU and the US is managed and deconfliction in Ukraine’s reconstruction and recovery is achieved, efforts to create a sound and predictable business environment for long-term investment will be undermined. This could tempt the EU to lower its standards in order to secure a greater role in future critical raw materials projects.

The EU can hit two targets at once

The EU should develop the linkage between economic security – a central focus of the forthcoming EU Security Strategy – and enlargement through investment in strategic CRM projects. Efforts to achieve these strategic objectives can mutually reinforce each other, but only if they are properly aligned.

The EU should engage in strategic CRM investment projects in the region. Public financing will be critical for new projects to succeed. However, it should also insist on stringent application of ESG standards as well as rule of law and governance reform in enlargement partners. These projects will not eliminate the EU’s critical dependencies tomorrow. They should instead be seen as long-term investments in the EU’s economic security. Although adherence to high standards may extend the time needed for projects to become operational, it will help preserve the EU’s credibility as a transformative actor among local populations and avoid reinforcing – already existing – (neo-)colonial narratives. Moreover, by giving up on standards the EU would hardly gain a competitive advantage over China or the US, both of which already have a growing footprint in the region. China is already deeply embedded in the mining sector in the Western Balkans. In Serbia, for example, Zijin Mining controls the Čukaru Peki mine and the Bor mining complex, which encompasses several of the country’s largest copper deposits. The US is expanding its role in prospective mining in Ukraine, including through the concession awarded for the Dobra lithium project. Short-sighted pragmatism could therefore result in strategic failure on all fronts.

The EU should regard the governance framework it brings to CRM development, together with safeguards protecting the environment and local communities, as a valuable asset rather than a burden. Properly anchored investment initiatives will provide a sustained strategic advantage over competitors that often prioritise short-term gains and face sometimes strong local resistance.

Second, the EU should support projects that develop localised value chains integrating mining, clean processing, advanced manufacturing and recycling, thereby contributing to the clean and sustainable development of the enlargement partners. Integrated value chains were already envisaged in the EU-Ukraine Strategic Partnership on Raw Materials initiated in 2021. However, the EU should put more emphasis on localising key stages of the chain – including processing chemicals or secondary production, such as phosphate fertilisers – to create greater added value in Ukraine, for example by supporting battery and defence industrial production. A similar logic applies to the Western Balkans where mining projects are often framed through the lens of resource extraction rather than broader industrial development.

Investing in local value chains is the best way in which the EU can challenge the notion that it seeks its own enrichment at the expense of living standards in partner societies, while demonstrating that CRM partnerships can serve as a pathway to sustainable development, EU membership and shared economic security. By focusing on comprehensive designs for integrated value chains, the EU can furthermore address the issue of processing monopolies held by third actors that would leave Europeans dependent even if additional extraction capacities were created. This may also contribute to deconflicting reconstruction and recovery efforts with the US in Ukraine.

Both economic security and enlargement are strategic objectives – and they should be conceived as such. CRMs in the neighbourhood will not remove EU’s strategic dependencies in the short term. With new mines taking more than 16 years on average worldwide to reach production stage, the goal is a long-term yield(8). Support for strategic CRM projects should be embedded in broader efforts to reinforce rule of law and governance reform among enlargement partners, rather than serve as an excuse to lower standards that would ultimately harm local constituencies and undermine support for enlargement. Enlargement conditionality and pre-accession funding should reinforce governance reform, build regulatory capacity, ensure democratic participation, including at the local level, and promote the consistent application of the same governance, transparency and environmental safeguards that apply within the EU. Only then can CRM partnerships strengthen both Europe’s economic security and the strategic rationale for enlargement.

References

* The authors would like to thank Josef Mayr and Alessandro Vitiello, EUISS trainees, for their invaluable research assistance.

1. Teer, J., ‘Beijing’s critical raw material weapon – and how to dismantle it’, Chaillot Paper no. 189, EUISS, May 2026.

2. European Commission, ‘Critical Raw Materials Act’, 2024.

3. Kyiv School of Economics and SYSTEMIQ, ‘Strategic Roadmap for Unlocking Ukraine’s Critical Raw Materials Potential’, 2025.

4. Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine, ‘Strategy for the Development of Industries Based on Minerals and Components of Strategic and Critical Importance’, 2026.

5. ‘Jadar lithium-borates project, Serbia – update’, Mining Weekly, 13 June 2025.

6. ‘Lithium and public opinion’, Vreme, 23 April 2025.

7. See the letter sent by a coalition of civil society organisations to European Commission officials.

text:
MARTINSVILLE, Ind. — The Hoosier State has spent $21 million so far to help remove or plug up more than 500 outdated or failing underground tanks storing gas, diesel and other hazardous materials through the nation's first proactive reimbursement program for tank closures.

That's according to the Indiana Department of Environmental Management, which in 2023 was authorized to reimburse tank owners for half of decommissioning and replacement costs.

But there are hundreds of old, potentially leaking tanks left statewide.

They're often owned by private companies, like gas stations and trucking fleets, as well as by the state and units of local government like schools, cities and counties.

Need to get in touch?

Have a news tip?

CONTACT US

Tanks are typically designed to last for about three decades, according to Tim Veatch, the petroleum branch chief for IDEM's Office of Land Quality. The potential for contamination — including to soil, indoor air and drinking water — increases every year after.

"We all go to the gas station every day, but we don't necessarily think, you know, where that gas is coming from and the potential harm to the environment," he told reporters Wednesday.

But tank removals are expensive, especially for cash-strapped small business owners and local governments.

Law enforcement officers, emergency responders and other county vehicle drivers fill up at the station next to the Morgan County Highway Department's office in Martinsville.

Department Superintendent Eddie Fisher predicts a price tag of $400,000 to $500,000 to remove a trio of 30-year-old tanks, replace them and more — which would eat up between 5% and 6% of the $8.4 million county's highway budget in one go.

He's expecting to save big once the project is completed and the state's reimbursement comes through.

The old station was dismantled and the ground largely cleared Wednesday morning, when workers carefully pried one 4,000-gallon tank lose from the earth. Fisher and other officials circled the metallic cylinder, pointing to intact stickers from the '90s.

They won't know if the old tanks leaked or not until the soil and groundwater samples are analyzed.

But: "Looks good, people. It's like the day it went in," said Carla Gill, the director of remediation services at consultant SESCO Group.

The new tanks are already in, secure under a recently poured concrete slab that now hosts the new fueling station. The spot, which was previously a parking lot, will trade uses with the old station.

"It's a big deal," Fisher said. "Quite an upgrade from what we had. Double-lined tanks is the new standard, and ours were single-walled tanks before. It's better for the environment and … the people."

The reimbursement program is in its fourth year and has never exhausted its annual $20 million allotment, disbursing $21 million of the $80 million up for grabs since its creation.

"We would like to see more applications, more projects come in, because the money is available," IDEM spokesman Allen Carter told reporters.

The dollars are set aside in the $265 million Excess Liability Trust Fund, which exists as an approved financial responsibility mechanism for tank owners and operators. It's funded by an inspection fee of one penny per gallon for fuels sold or used for motor vehicles in Indiana.

Petroleum Branch Chief Veatch said the program is advertised through petroleum marketers, contracts, consultants, an inspection program, mailers and more — but it's still news to some.

"When I reached out to the contractor and they found out about the … 50% savings, they came in and we talked about it, and felt that this is the best time to do it," Fisher said. The county decided to "save taxpayers the dollars and go ahead and take advantage of it now while we had the chance."

text:
CHINT and Octopus Energy announced the signing of two Memoranda of Cooperation (MoCs), establishing a strategic framework to expand collaboration in renewable energy infrastructure and Virtual Power Plant (VPP) solutions.

The partnership reflects both companies' shared commitment to accelerating the global energy transition through technological innovation, high-quality clean energy infrastructure and smarter energy systems.

Delivering Integrated Solutions for Renewable Energy Projects

Under the first Memorandum of Cooperation, Astronergy Europe GmbH, CHINT Power Systems Poland Sp. z o.o., and CHINT Solar Poland Spolka z ograniczona odpowiedzialnoscia will collaborate with Octopus Energy on renewable energy projects. The agreement establishes a framework under which CHINT will provide a comprehensive portfolio of renewable energy equipment including photovoltaic (PV) modules, inverters, battery energy storage systems (BESS), transformers, smart meters, cables and electric vehicle (EV) charging solutions. Subject to project-specific agreements, CHINT will also provide Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) services to support the development and delivery of renewable energy projects.

By combining CHINT's integrated manufacturing and engineering capabilities with Octopus Energy's expertise in renewable energy development and energy services, the companies aim to deliver efficient, reliable and scalable clean energy solutions for future projects.

Advancing Virtual Power Plant Innovation in China

In a second Memorandum of Cooperation, Chint Anneng Digital Power (Zhejiang) Co., Ltd. and Octopus Energy Group Limited agreed to explore comprehensive cooperation in the Virtual Power Plant (VPP) sector within the Chinese mainland market.

The collaboration will focus on evaluating opportunities across distributed energy resource aggregation, demand response, intelligent energy management and other digital energy applications. Leveraging CHINT Anneng's deep understanding of China's energy market together with Octopus Energy's international expertise in smart energy technologies and VPP operation, the companies will jointly explore innovative business models and pilot projects that support the development of a more flexible, digitalized and resilient power system.

Executive Comments

"The signing of these strategic cooperation agreements represents an important step in expanding our international partnerships and accelerating innovation in the clean energy sector," said Dr. Chuan Lu, Director of CHINT Group and Chairman of CHINT Green Energy. "By combining our strengths in equipment manufacturing, engineering and energy infrastructure with Octopus Energy's expertise in digital energy solutions, we look forward to creating long-term value for customers and supporting the global energy transition."

Greg Jackson, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Octopus Energy, said: "Building the green energy system of the future requires top-tier hardware and cutting-edge tech. Partnering with CHINT gives us access to both at an incredible scale. From accelerating infrastructure in Europe to pioneering new Virtual Power Plants in China, we’re proving that the future of energy is digital, flexible, and green."

Looking Ahead

Building on the two MoUs, the parties intend to deepen cooperation in clean energy infrastructure, engineering services and digital energy technologies. Through complementary capabilities and shared ambitions, CHINT and Octopus Energy aim to deliver innovative energy solutions, support decarbonization efforts and contribute to a more sustainable global energy future.

text:
Today, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 8800, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (NDAA). The NDAA authorizes annual funding levels for the U.S. Armed Forces and sets expenditures for the Department of War (DoW).

Included in H.R. 8800, and secured by Congressman Rick W. Allen (GA-12), is legislative text (Sections 704-705) that establishes the "prohibition on and reversal of actions to modify the scope of medical services provided at certain military medical treatment facilities," including Eisenhower Army Medical Center (EAMC).

After voting in support of the bill on the House floor, Congressman Allen issued the following statement:

"I have consistently said that the NDAA is one of the most vital pieces of legislation that comes before Congress each year. Especially so this year. I thank House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers and Congressman Joe Wilson for their support in getting this provision included in the House-passed bill."

Specifically, the Fiscal Year 2027 NDAA:

Revitalizes the Defense Industrial Base

Expands U.S. production capacity, unleashes private sector investment, opens the door to new and innovative entrants, reduces needless regulations, and creates thousands of skilled jobs for Americans.

Improves Servicemembers’ Quality of Life

Supports the President’s request to raise all servicemembers’ pay by 5 to 7% and improves housing, education, and access to childcare for military families.

Restores Lethal Capabilities

Rebuilds depleted stockpiles by providing the authorities and resources required to expedite the production and acquisition of munitions and key warfighting capabilities.

Strengthens American Deterrence

Prioritizes investment in the forces and capabilities needed to maintain a strong U.S. posture. It strengthens nuclear deterrence, expands missile defense, and targets resources and authorities to counter adversaries like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

Eliminates Waste, Fraud and Abuse

Builds on progress made in FY26 to streamline DoW operations and cut nearly $30 billion in wasteful programs. It stands up a new task force and provides new authorities to eliminate fraudulent payments and achieve a full and clean audit within 24 months.

text:
Ford Motor Co. executive chairman Bill Ford is signaling that trade barriers alone may not shield Detroit from Chinese electric vehicle competition indefinitely.

If Chinese EV brands eventually begin selling in the United States, buyers could gain cheaper choices, and longtime U.S. automakers could face a tougher test of how well they can compete.

What's happening?

A recent video from The Electric Viking (@electricviking) centered on comments from Ford, who said the industry should be ready for a future in which Chinese EV makers are no longer kept out of U.S. dealerships.

Referencing reporting from the Wall Street Journal, host Sam Evans highlighted Ford's warning. "We have to go toe-to-toe with China," Ford told the paper last week.

As BYD, Geely, and other Chinese automakers expand in overseas markets, they are doing so with EVs known for lower prices, strong battery development, and software-focused features.

In the video, Evans said Chinese brands could still one day look for ways into the North American market through countries such as Canada or Mexico, even as U.S. officials weigh tighter restrictions.

Ford has supported efforts to curb Chinese vehicle access, but the broader point was that tariffs and regulations cannot be counted on forever. As Evans said, "America's auto industry — it's relying on tariffs and regulations to block Chinese car companies."

Why does it matter?

Greater pressure from Chinese automakers could lower EV prices, giving more consumers access to vehicles that are cheaper to fuel and maintain than gas models. According to the video, Ford is working on a smaller electric pickup with a price of about $30,000.

The pressure could also push automakers to improve range, charging speed, and in-car technology more quickly.

One video viewer commented, "Too bad. We're building clunkers and China's selling well-built EVs. Very sad!"

Another added that U.S. automakers are "charging 2x prices and giving you a WAY worse vehicle."

What's being done?

According to Evans, Ford is trying to bring EV costs down with manufacturing changes such as simplified wiring and gigacasting, and it also plans to use CATL-licensed lithium iron phosphate batteries. An aim is to cut production expenses, which could eventually be reflected in vehicle prices.

Bill Ford also called for a steadier U.S. industrial strategy. Because decisions on factories, batteries, and vehicle launches are made years ahead of time, sudden policy changes can make it harder to keep affordable EV plans on track.

"Our lead times are longer than political lead times," Ford told the Wall Street Journal.

As more competition arrives, consumers could benefit from lower upfront prices, less money spent at the pump, and fewer routine maintenance costs tied to traditional combustion engines.

Ford's message was blunt: "We can't keep them out forever, and we have to be able to beat them at their own game."

authors: Jack Forrest, Leslie Bonilla Muñiz, David Montgomery
